## Preemption Design and Operation [#operation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running
jobs as needed to initiate the pending job. When
PreemptMode=SUSPEND,GANG the select plugin will initiate the pending
job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.
The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs to consider for
each pending job which is a candidate to start.
This list is sorted by either:
- QOS priority,
- Partition priority and job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or
- Job start time (with PreemptParameters=youngest_first ).

results.prompt: What can you help me with?
results.agent_response:
I’m a Slurm HPC cluster assistant that can monitor, inspect, diagnose, and explain things about your Slurm cluster. High-level capabilities and how to use me:

What I can do (read-only, immediate)
- Query the queue and job states (squeue): “What is job 12345 doing?”, “List my running jobs.”
- Inspect pending reasons and why a job is stuck (squeue → scontrol_show when needed): “Why is job 9876 pending?”
- Show partitions, node counts, and node states (sinfo): “How many GPU nodes are idle?”
- Show detailed job or node configuration and fields (scontrol show): “Show job 12345 details.”
- Provide historical job/accounting records (sacct), usage reports (sreport), fairshare/priority (sshare/sprio), reservations (scontrol reservation show), licenses (scontrol license), scheduler diagnostics (sdiag), and realtime job stats (sstat).
- Read logs or scripts you supply (read_file) for troubleshooting.
- Explain Slurm concepts, command syntax, pending/reason codes, and provide runbook-style guidance (I use the Slurm docs for reference when appropriate).

What I cannot do directly (mutating actions)
- I will not execute any action that changes cluster state (submit, cancel, hold, requeue, drain, resume, update, reconfigure, node/reservation/account changes).
- If you ask for such an action I will immediately hand the request to the operator agent (transfer_to_operator) so they can run the exact Slurm tool. For example:
  - Submissions of scripts (e.g., “submit train.sh”) → required_tool="sbatch".
  - Cancels → required_tool="scancel".
  - Node drain/down/resume → required_tool="scontrol_node".
  - Job time-limit updates → required_tool="scontrol_update", etc.
- For conditional actions (e.g., “submit if idle GPU nodes exist” or “cancel if runtime > 2h”), I will first run the minimum read-only command needed to prove the condition (sinfo for GPUs, squeue for runtime) and only hand off if the condition is met. If the condition is not met I’ll report facts and not hand off.

How I handle ambiguous action requests
- If a destructive action lacks a concrete target I’ll ask one concise clarification question and stop. e.g., “Which job ID should I cancel?” or “Which node name should I use?”
- If you say “that job” or “stop it” I’ll ask: “Which job ID should I inspect/act on?”

Examples of useful things you can ask right now
- “Why is job 12345 pending?”
- “Show GPU partition status”
- “List my jobs from the last 7 days (sacct)”
- “Show detailed info for node node01”
- “Explain pending reason ‘Resources’ and how to fix it”
- “Submit train.sh to gpu partition with 4 GPUs for 2 hours” (this is a mutating request — I will hand off to the operator to run sbatch)

If you want to proceed
- Tell me a read-only question now (include job ID or node name when relevant), or
- If you want an action, state the exact action and concrete targets (or say it’s a discovery/broad action). I’ll hand it off to the operator immediately.

What I can do (read/diagnose, directly)
- Inspect the live queue and job states (squeue) — including why a job is pending.
- Show partition/node health and availability (sinfo, sinfo_reasons, sinfo_node).
- Show detailed job and node configuration (scontrol show job/node/step).
- Check job resource usage (sstat) and historical accounting (sacct, sreport).
- Show scheduler diagnostics and priorities (sdiag, sprio, sprio_weights).
- List reservations, licenses, fairshare (scontrol_reservation_show, scontrol_license, sshare).

- Produce concise explanations, troubleshooting steps, or suggested sbatch/srun examples.

What I do when a request changes cluster state
- I cannot directly mutate cluster state in Observer. For any non-conditional action that changes the cluster (submit, cancel, hold, requeue, drain, resume, reconfigure, account/node updates, create/cancel reservations, etc.), I will immediately transfer the request to the Operator using a structured handoff call. I’ll include the exact action, required tool (e.g., sbatch, scancel, scontrol_node), and targets or target-resolution instructions.
- For conditional actions (e.g., “submit if idle GPU nodes exist” or “cancel if running >2h”), I’ll first run the minimal read-only check to prove the condition, and only transfer if the condition is met.

How to make requests (best practices)
- For job/node actions include concrete job IDs or node names. If you use “that job” or similar, I’ll ask “Which job ID should I inspect?” before proceeding.
- Tell me partition, resources, or script name when submitting (these are action parameters and will be passed to the Operator).
- For reads, a simple request like “Why is job 12345 pending?” is perfect — I’ll call squeue and scontrol_show as needed and report back.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a “good” Slurm batch script is clear, reproducible, portable, and requests only the resources you actually need. Below is a concise checklist, common pitfalls, and several short example scripts you can adapt.

Quick checklist (what to include)
- Shebang and strict shell settings: e.g., #!/bin/bash and set -euo pipefail.
- SBATCH directives (one per logical requirement) before any executable commands:
  - Job name (--job-name)
  - Partition/queue (--partition)
  - Time limit (--time)
  - Nodes / tasks / CPUs / memory (--nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task, --mem or --mem-per-cpu)
  - GPUs if needed (--gres=gpu:COUNT)
  - Account/QOS if required (--account, --qos)
  - Output and error paths (--output, --error) (include jobid and jobname in filenames)
  - Email notifications (--mail-type, --mail-user) if you need them
- Use srun to launch tasks inside the allocation (srun integrates with Slurm’s scheduler and resource accounting).
- Load modules or activate environments near the top, after SBATCH directives.
- Staging: copy input data to local (node) scratch at start; copy results back and rm scratch at end.
- Logging: redirect stdout/stderr to files and include timestamps in logs if helpful.
- Resource-conscious requests: request only what you need (over-requesting hurts throughput and delays your jobs).
- Exit/cleanup: trap signals and clean up temporary files (trap '...' EXIT).
- Use job arrays for many similar small jobs (--array).
- Add comments describing purpose, expected runtime, resource needs, and how to reproduce.

Common pitfalls
- Forgetting SBATCH directives must be at top of script (before executable commands).
- Using mpirun instead of srun on clusters that require srun (prefer srun unless documentation says otherwise).
- Not setting --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded code (leads to oversubscription).
- Not staging I/O to local fast storage (causes heavy shared filesystem load).
- Ignoring time/memory limits (causes job to be killed and lose work).
- Not testing interactively in a small debug partition before large runs.

Useful environment variables available inside the job
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_NODELIST, SLURM_NNODES, etc. Use them for logging or conditional behavior.

Testing and debugging tips
- Test interactively on a debug partition or with a small allocation: srun --pty -p debug --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 bash
- sbatch --test-only <script> to check parsing without submitting (if available on your cluster)
- Use sacct, squeue, scontrol show job, and seff (if available) to inspect job state and efficiency after runs.

Examples

1) Simple single-node CPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err

set -euo pipefail
module load python/3.10
echo "Started $SLURM_JOB_NAME ($SLURM_JOB_ID) on $(hostname) at $(date)"
srun python train.py --threads $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

2) GPU job (single GPU)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=6
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

set -euo pipefail
module load cuda/12.0
module load anaconda
source activate myenv

Short answer: write clear, minimal SBATCH directives that exactly request the resources you need, prepare the environment (modules, conda, etc.), run your job with srun (or the launcher your site prefers), capture useful environment/logging information, and make the script reproducible and testable. Below are a checklist, explanations of common options, a few short templates, and practical tips.

Checklist (what every batch script should do)
- Start with a shebang (#!/bin/bash) and safe shell options (e.g., set -euo pipefail).
- Set SBATCH directives for job-name, output, error, partition, time, nodes/ntasks/cpus-per-task, memory and GPUs (gres) as appropriate.
- Load modules / activate environments explicitly.
- cd to the intended working directory or use absolute paths.
- Stage input data and outputs (or reference shared filesystem paths).
- Use srun for the actual program (srun integrates with Slurm and sets task ranks).
- Print minimal runtime diagnostics (date, hostname, env, nproc, free -h, nvidia-smi for GPUs).
- Log stdout/stderr to files with useful names (include %j jobid or %x job name).
- Keep walltime reasonable and add safety margins; use checkpointing if long runs.
- Include cleanup/exit handling where needed (trap on TERM).

Common SBATCH options and what they mean
- --job-name=NAME : human-readable job name.
- --output=FILE, --error=FILE : files for stdout/stderr; use %j (jobid) or %x (jobname).
- --partition=PART : which partition/queue.
- --time=HH:MM:SS : walltime limit (always set).
- --nodes=N : number of nodes.
- --ntasks=NT : number of tasks total (MPI ranks).
- --cpus-per-task=M : threads per task (for OpenMP).
- --mem=MEM or --mem-per-cpu= : RAM reservation.
- --gres=gpu:K or gpu:V100:K : request GPUs.
- --exclusive : node exclusive allocation.
- --account=NAME / --qos= : accounting/QoS tags if your cluster requires them.
- --array=0-99%10 : job arrays; %10 caps concurrent tasks to 10.
- --dependency=afterok:12345 : run after another job finishes successfully.
- --mail-type=FAIL,END,BEGIN --mail-user=you@org : email notifications.

Basic single-node CPU template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G

set -euo pipefail
date
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID $SLURM_JOB_NAME"
module purge
module load python/3.10
cd /home/$USER/myproject
echo "Loaded modules:"; module list

srun python train.py --epochs 10 --data /scratch/$USER/data

GPU single-node template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu_train
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=6
#SBATCH --mem=32G

set -euo pipefail
date; hostname
module purge
module load cuda/12.0 cudnn
source ~/envs/myenv/bin/activate
nvidia-smi
srun --cpu_bind=cores python train_gpu.py --batch 64

Job array example (many similar short tasks)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array_job
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=0-99%20
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G

set -euo pipefail
TASK_ID=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
echo "Running array task $TASK_ID"
srun python process_chunk.py --chunk $TASK_ID

Good practices and tips
- Test small first: run with --time=00:05:00 and small inputs, and check logs.
- Prefer srun for MPI and parallel programs; many sites require srun rather than mpirun for correct Slurm integration.
- Distinguish ntasks vs cpus-per-task: ntasks is number of MPI ranks; cpus-per-task is threads each rank uses.
- Use --mem-per-cpu when you want memory tied to CPU count; use --mem when you want node-level memory.
- Include module list and environment information in logs for reproducibility.
- Use %j and %x in filenames so a single directory can hold many job outputs without collision.
- For GPU jobs, call nvidia-smi at start to record device allocation and status.
- Avoid hardcoding paths on ephemeral node-local scratch; copy used files in at start and copy results out at end.
- Use checkpointing (save model periodically) for long runs and consider job requeue or array/resubmit strategies for resilience.
- For debugging: run interactively (salloc or srun --pty bash) or request a short debug partition if available.
- Be explicit about licenses, accounts, QOS if cluster enforces them.

Debugging and cost control
- Always set --time; Slurm will kill jobs that exceed it.
- Keep an eye on memory: OOMs often kill jobs silently. Check sacct or job exit code for oom-kill indicators.
- Use sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed to inspect exit info after completion.
- Use sprio / sdiag if your jobs are stuck pending to see priority/backfill issues (ask admins if unexplained).

If you want, I can:
- Review one of your existing batch scripts and suggest improvements (paste it here).
- Produce a template tailored to your workload (MPI across N nodes, Data-parallel GPU, array with x tasks). Which would you like?

Read-only queries I can run now

- Node health/drain reasons (sinfo -R / sinfo_node): say which partition or node.
- Recent job history (sacct): give a user and optional time window.
- Resource usage / running-job stats (sstat + squeue): give a running job ID.

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Short answer: write a batch script with #SBATCH directives that request resources, then run sbatch myscript.sh.

What to put in the batch script (minimal example)
- Shebang and SBATCH directives (one per resource/option). Example:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob           # job name
#SBATCH --partition=gpu            # partition
#SBATCH --nodes=1                  # nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                 # MPI ranks
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4          # threads per task
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --mem=16G                  # memory
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # HH:MM:SS walltime
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out      # stdout file (%j expands to jobid)
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err       # stderr file
# Commands to run:
module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes and useful options
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh. sbatch prints the assigned job ID on success.
- Time format: HH:MM:SS (or D-HH:MM:SS).
- Memory: suffix with K/M/G (e.g., 16000M or 16G).
- GPUs: use --gres=gpu:N or cluster-specific names (ask admins if unsure).
- Job arrays: #SBATCH --array=0-9 or --array=0-99%10 and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script.
- Request particular node(s): --nodelist=node01 or -w node[01-03].
- Interactive/allocations: use salloc or srun for interactive jobs (not sbatch).
- Default output: if not set, Slurm writes slurm-<jobid>.out.
- Check status: squeue -u $USER. For finished jobs use sacct.
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>.

Cluster-specific tips
- Check partition/node availability before requesting GPUs (sinfo). Some clusters require specific gres names or accounts—if unsure, check your cluster docs or ask admins.
- If you want me to submit a script for you, tell me the exact script path and submission parameters; I will hand that over to the operator to run.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use whether you’re a user submitting jobs or learning the basics. If you want a deep dive into any section (batch scripts, GPUs, debugging, admin topics), tell me which and I’ll expand.

1) What Slurm is (very short)
- Slurm is a workload manager for scheduling batch and interactive jobs on HPC clusters. Key components: slurmctld (controller/scheduler), slurmd (node daemons), and optionally slurmdbd (accounting).

2) Common Slurm concepts
- Partition: a named group of nodes (like a queue).
- Job: a submitted workload (batch or interactive).
- Job states: PENDING (PD), RUNNING (R), COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.
- Resources: nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs, licenses, QOS, accounts.
- Job array: many similar jobs with a single submission (indexed tasks).

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a “good” Slurm batch script is clear, reproducible, requests just the resources you actually need, and launches your job in a way the scheduler expects (usually via srun). Below are concise guidelines, a compact template, several common examples, and a checklist to help you write robust, portable scripts.

Short guidelines
- Put scheduler directives in #SBATCH header lines (or pass equivalent flags to sbatch).
- Request accurate resources: nodes, ntasks, cpus-per-task, mem, time, gres (gpus), QOS/account/account.
- Use srun to launch work (preferred over plain mpirun unless your MPI vendor requires mpirun).
- Set environment (modules/conda/singularity) explicitly so the run is reproducible.
- Redirect stdout/stderr to job-specific files (use %j / %x for jobid/jobname).
- Use set -e and traps for safer failure handling and to enable cleanup.
- For arrays use --array and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; throttle massive arrays with %limit.
- Keep the walltime conservative but not excessive — underestimating causes kill; overestimating wastes queue time.

Minimal template (fill values)
# SBATCH lines:
#SBATCH --job-name=job-name
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out       # %x=jobname %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu               # or cpu/short/long etc.
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                  # if GPU needed
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# Shell setup and safety
set -euo pipefail
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST started at $(date)"

# Load modules / activate env
module purge
module load gcc/10 python/3.10 cuda/12.1
source /path/to/conda.sh && conda activate myenv

# Export threading settings when using OpenMP or BLAS
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS}

# Run the workload with srun
srun --mpi=pmix_v3 my_program --arg value

# Optional cleanup
echo "Job finished at $(date)"

Example 1 — single-node multi-threaded job
#SBATCH --job-name=py-train
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00

set -e
module load python/3.10
source activate myenv
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
srun python train.py --batch 128

Example 2 — MPI multi-node job (use srun)
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi-job
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=8
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

module load mpi/openmpi
srun --mpi=pmix_v3 ./my_mpi_executable -arg

Notes: ntasks = total ranks. ntasks-per-node × nodes = total ntasks. Use cpus-per-task for per-rank threads.

Example 3 — GPU training (single node, 4 GPUs)
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00

module load cuda/12.1 cudnn
source activate pytorch
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
srun python train_gpu.py --gpus 4

Example 4 — job array (parameter sweep)
#SBATCH --job-name=array
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G

param_file=params.txt
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $param_file)
srun python run_param.py --param "$PARAM"

Best-practice checklist
- Request actual resources: measure small runs first, then scale your requests.
- Prefer srun for execution; it integrates with the job allocation.
- Use #SBATCH --output and --error with %j/%x for unique logs.
- Set environment variables controlling thread counts (OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS).
- Use --cpus-per-task for threaded codes and --ntasks for MPI ranks.
- For GPUs, request --gres=gpu:N and ensure your framework sees the GPUs (check CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES).
- Use --time realistically (underestimate => kill; too long => long queue wait).
- Use modules or container images for reproducibility (Singularity/Apptainer).
- Add --mem or --mem-per-cpu to avoid node OOM kills. Be explicit — default may be low.
- Add small checkpoints/logging so you can resume or diagnose failures.
- For long workflows, consider --dependency options to chain jobs or --array with % limit.

Robustness and failure handling
- set -euo pipefail to stop on errors.
- trap '... cleanup ...' EXIT to copy logs or free temporary storage.
- Consider --requeue if you want the scheduler to requeue on preemption (cluster must allow).
- For very long work, use application-level checkpointing.

Debugging tips
- Test interactively first: salloc --nodes=1 --time=00:30:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1
- Use small test scripts and sbatch --test-only to check directive parsing (sbatch --test-only script.sh).
- Inspect queue with squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER.
- If pending, check reason: squeue -o "%i %t %r %P %j %u %M %D" or scontrol show job <jobid>.
- For crashed or finished jobs, use sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS.
- Capture standard output/error for failure traces.

Common pitfalls
- Mixing ntasks/cpus-per-task wrong — causes oversubscription or idle CPUs.
- Not setting OMP_NUM_THREADS when cpus-per-task > 1 (leads to oversubscribe).
- Using mpirun without srun on some clusters — can cause allocation mismatch; prefer srun.
- Forgetting --gres=gpu:X for GPU jobs; scheduler won’t allocate GPU otherwise.
- Not directing logs to unique files (overwriting previous runs).
- Requesting insufficient memory leads to OOM kill with ExitCode=137.

Quick reference commands
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc ...
- Watch queue: squeue -u $USER
- Show job: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Job accounting: sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed

If you tell me what kind of job you run (MPI, threaded Python, GPU training, array sweep) and the cluster’s scheduler constraints (partitions, typical node resources like GPUs/CPUs/memory), I can produce a ready-to-submit script tuned for that workload.

results.agent_response:
Here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use to get started, submit jobs, and debug common problems. I’ll cover core concepts, common commands, example job scripts (batch and interactive), job arrays & dependencies, resource/GPU guidance, and quick troubleshooting tips.

Core concepts
- slurmctld: the controller (scheduler) that accepts and runs jobs.
- Node / partition: nodes are compute machines; partitions are named queues (groups of nodes) you submit to.
- Job: a unit of work you submit (sbatch) or run interactively (srun/salloc).
- TRES/gres: trackable resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs). GPUs are requested via gres (e.g., --gres=gpu:1).
- QOS, accounts, fairshare: policies that control priority and limits.
- Job states: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.

Quick commands (most useful)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch job.
- srun ... — run a command inside an allocation (interactive or inside job).
- salloc ... — allocate resources interactively (gives a shell).
- squeue [-u user] [-p partition] — view queued/running jobs.
- sinfo — view partitions and node states.
- sacct — query finished job accounting/history.
- scontrol show job <id> — show detailed job info.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- sstat -j <jobid> — (running jobs) live stats (CPU, memory).
- scontrol show node <nodename> — node details.

Simple sbatch script (example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
# If you need GPUs:
# #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- %j expands to the job ID in output filenames.
- Use module load (or your site’s environment management) to set environment.
- Put srun before the main command in scripts to ensure correct allocation/smp behavior.

Interactive / debug sessions
- Quick interactive shell on a partition:
  srun --partition=debug --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 --time=00:30:00 --pty bash
- Or request an allocation and then run commands:
  salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --time=01:00:00
  Then run srun or the commands you need in the allocation shell.

Job arrays
- For many similar tasks (e.g., parameter sweeps):
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
# inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- %10 limits concurrent tasks to 10.

Job dependencies
- Submit job B after A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobidA> jobB.sh
- other options: afterany, aftercorr, singleton, etc.

Checking job status & reasons
- squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER shows pending reasons (if reported).
- If squeue doesn’t show a reason or you need more detail: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionTimeLimit, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobsPerUser.

GPU-specific tips
- Request GPUs explicitly: --gres=gpu:1 (or gpu:tesla:2 if your cluster uses types).
- Use sinfo to find GPU partitions: sinfo -o "%P %G %D %C" or ask your admin for partition names.
- When checking availability for conditional submissions, only count nodes listed as idle for GPU allocation (allocated/mixed/down/drained are not available).
- Inside job, GPU devices are typically visible via nvidia-smi; environment variables like CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES may be set.

Accounting & historical data
- sacct -j <jobid> or sacct -u <user> to view completed jobs (exit codes, elapsed, resource usage).
- sreport and sshare for usage/fairshare summaries (admin-level).

Common troubleshooting checklist
- Job stuck PENDING:
  - Run squeue to see the reason. If not present, scontrol show job <id>.
  - Check partition limits, QOS, account charges/limits.
  - Check node states with sinfo; if nodes are drained/down they reduce capacity.
- Job fails quickly with non-zero exit:
  - Inspect job-%j.err and job-%j.out.
  - Verify modules, paths, environment variables in the batch script.
  - Use small test jobs with shorter time and less memory to reproduce.
- Job out-of-memory:
  - Increase --mem or request more CPUs-per-task if memory is per-core.
  - Use ulimit or check container limits if running inside one.
- Node-specific hardware failures:
  - scontrol show node <name> and sinfo -R to see reasons/drain messages.
- No GPU seen inside job:
  - Confirm --gres is requested in sbatch/srun.
  - Check nvidia-smi; confirm module/drivers loaded.

Best practices
- Start small: request minimal resources and short walltime for testing.
- Make output and error files explicit so logs are preserved.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps rather than many individual sbatch calls.
- Use dependencies to serialize multi-stage workflows.
- Keep reproducible environment: modules, container images (Singularity/Apptainer).
- Ask your cluster admins for site-specific queues, limits, and recommended partitions.

Useful environment variables inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, SLURM_NODELIST

Where to learn more
- Your cluster’s user guide / FAQ (site-specific policies and partitions).
- Official Slurm docs (scheduling, sbatch, srun, scontrol): see slurm.schedmd.com
- For command syntax and reason codes: use lookup_slurm_docs or man pages (man sbatch, man squeue).

If you’d like, I can:
- Create a job script tailored to your application (give partition, CPUs, memory, GPUs, time).
- Walk through diagnosing a specific stuck or failed job (give job ID).
- Show example sbatch + sbatch dependency + array combined script.

Which of the above would you like next?

results.prompt: What do you do?
results.agent_response:
I’m a Slurm HPC cluster assistant: I monitor the cluster, inspect jobs/nodes/partitions, diagnose why jobs are stuck or failing, generate usage/accounting reports, and recommend fixes. I use Slurm read-only tools to gather live facts and only pass mutating requests to a human Operator.

What I can do (reads / diagnostics)
- Inspect the queue and job status (squeue) — job state, pending reason, elapsed time.
- Show partition and node state (sinfo / sinfo_node / sinfo_reasons) — allocated/idle/down/drain counts and per-node resources.
- Look up historical job accounting (sacct) — completed/failed/cancelled jobs, exit codes, elapsed, resources.
- Retrieve detailed job/node/partition configuration (scontrol show).
- Check running-job resource usage (sstat) and scheduler diagnostics (sdiag, sprio, sprio_weights).
- Produce usage reports (sreport) and fairshare info (sshare).
- Inspect licenses (scontrol_license), reservations (scontrol_reservation_show), controller config/health (scontrol show config / scontrol ping).
- Fetch Slurm reference docs for admin/command semantics (lookup_slurm_docs).

What I do NOT do directly
- I do not change cluster state myself. Any request that would mutate the cluster (submit/cancel/hold/release/requeue/update/drain/resume/reconfigure, node reservations, account changes, etc.) is immediately handed off to an Operator tool call. For conditional mutating requests, I’ll first run the minimum read-only check needed to prove the condition, then hand off only if it’s met.

How to ask effectively
- For job actions: include job ID(s). If you say “that job” I’ll ask which job ID.
- For node actions: include the node name.
- For submissions: provide the script name or resource requirements (partition, time, CPUs, GPUs, memory, QOS).
- For conditional requests: specify the exact condition (e.g., “cancel if runtime > 2 hours”).

Examples
- “Why is job 12345 pending?” — I’ll run squeue (and scontrol_show if needed) and explain the pending reason and fixes.
- “Show GPU partition node states” — I’ll run sinfo and report allocation/idle/down per node.
- “Cancel all of alice’s running jobs” — this is a mutating request and I will transfer to Operator immediately (scancel).

What would you like me to do right now?

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference: basic commands, typical sbatch examples (CPU, GPU, MPI, arrays), interactive usage, monitoring / debugging tips, and best practices.

Quick command reference
- sinfo — show partitions and node states (allocated/idle/down).
- squeue — show queued and running jobs (use -u $USER to filter).
- sbatch myjob.sh — submit a batch job script (non-interactive).
- srun — run a command inside an allocation or start tasks inside a batch job.
- salloc — request an interactive allocation (then use srun or run shell).
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job JOBID — show detailed job configuration and reason for pending.
- sacct -j JOBID — accounting info for completed jobs.
- sstat -j JOBID — runtime stats for a running job (live resource usage).
- sinfo -R — list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN with reasons.

Minimal sbatch batch script (CPU job)
- Example file: myjob.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=test
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=8G
  #SBATCH --time=01:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  module load python
  python train.py

- Submit: sbatch myjob.sh
- Output file: slurm-<JOBID>.out

Requesting GPUs
- Single-node GPU example:
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (driver depends on cluster)
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=04:00:00

MPI / multi-node parallel job
- Use mpirun / srun inside the batch script:
  #SBATCH --nodes=2
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  module load mpi
  srun my_mpi_program   # srun launches the MPI tasks across allocation

Interactive usage
- Quick interactive allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00
  srun --pty bash -i      # get an interactive shell
- Or run a single interactive command:
  srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 python -i

Job arrays (many similar tasks)
- Example (100 tasks, at most 10 concurrently):
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
- Inside the script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input per-task.

Dependencies and chaining jobs
- Submit job B to run after job A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid_A> jobB.sh

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER — show your queued/running jobs
- squeue -j <JOBID> — get state and (usually) pending reason
- If squeue does not show a useful reason, run:
  scontrol show job <JOBID>   — detailed pending reason or required resources
- For running jobs:
  sstat -j <JOBID>   — live CPU/memory usage (if enabled)
  sacct -j <JOBID>   — accounting info after job finishes (exit code, elapsed)
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionDown, QOS, License. Use scontrol show job to get the detailed reason string.

Common #SBATCH options (most used)
- --job-name=NAME
- --nodes=N, --ntasks=N, --ntasks-per-node=N
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=SIZE or --mem-per-cpu=SIZE
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS
- --gres=gpu:N
- --partition=NAME
- --output=FILE and --error=FILE (or combined with --output=slurm-%j.out)
- --mail-user=you@site --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Environment variables available in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc. Use them in scripts to adapt behavior.

Best practices
- Always test with a small, short job first (1 node, short time) to verify script and modules.
- Request realistic resources: over-requesting time or memory reduces scheduler throughput and can delay your job.
- Set --time to a sensible upper bound — shorter limits often help the job start sooner.
- Use output files named with %j (job ID) so logs don’t collide across runs.
- Capture exit codes in scripts and fail fast (set -e).
- If pending, check squeue and scontrol for the reason before contacting admins.
- For GPU jobs, confirm cluster uses gres=gpu and what GPU types are available (sinfo shows node resources).
- Keep software environment reproducible (modules, virtualenv/conda, container images if supported).

Troubleshooting tips
- Job never starts: check squeue for pending reason; check sinfo for partition/node availability.
- Job fails quickly: inspect slurm-<JOBID>.out and check the batch script for missing modules or wrong paths.
- Out-of-memory: increase --mem or detect memory leak; use sacct to see ExitCode and signal (e.g., OOM killed).
- Unexpected task placement: check --ntasks, --cpus-per-task and use srun with --cpu-bind options if needed.

Where to learn more
- The official Slurm documentation is authoritative (sacct, srun, sbatch, scontrol pages). If you want, I can fetch specific doc pages or give cluster-specific templates.

Would you like:
- a ready-to-use template for CPU, GPU, or MPI jobs tailored to your cluster defaults?
- help debugging a specific job script or a pending job ID? (If so, tell me the job ID or which template you want.)

Good — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference: basic commands, typical sbatch examples (CPU, GPU, MPI, arrays), interactive usage, monitoring / debugging tips, and best practices.

Quick command reference
- sinfo — show partitions and node states (allocated/idle/down).
- squeue — show queued and running jobs (use -u $USER to filter).
- sbatch myjob.sh — submit a batch job script (non-interactive).
- srun — run a command inside an allocation or start tasks inside a batch job.
- salloc — request an interactive allocation (then use srun or run shell).
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job JOBID — show detailed job configuration and reason for pending.
- sacct -j JOBID — accounting info for completed jobs.
- sstat -j JOBID — runtime stats for a running job (live resource usage).
- sinfo -R — list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN with reasons.

Minimal sbatch batch script (CPU job)
- Example file: myjob.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=test
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=8G
  #SBATCH --time=01:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  module load python
  python train.py

- Submit: sbatch myjob.sh
- Output file: slurm-<JOBID>.out

Requesting GPUs
- Single-node GPU example:
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (driver depends on cluster)
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=04:00:00

MPI / multi-node parallel job
- Use mpirun / srun inside the batch script:
  #SBATCH --nodes=2
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  module load mpi
  srun my_mpi_program   # srun launches the MPI tasks across allocation

Interactive usage
- Quick interactive allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00
  srun --pty bash -i      # get an interactive shell
- Or run a single interactive command:
  srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 python -i

Job arrays (many similar tasks)
- Example (100 tasks, at most 10 concurrently):
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
- Inside the script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input per-task.

Dependencies and chaining jobs
- Submit job B to run after job A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid_A> jobB.sh

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER — show your queued/running jobs
- squeue -j <JOBID> — get state and (usually) pending reason
- If squeue does not show a useful reason, run:
  scontrol show job <JOBID>   — detailed pending reason or required resources
- For running jobs:
  sstat -j <JOBID>   — live CPU/memory usage (if enabled)
  sacct -j <JOBID>   — accounting info after job finishes (exit code, elapsed)
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionDown, QOS, License. Use scontrol show job to get the detailed reason string.

Common #SBATCH options (most used)
- --job-name=NAME
- --nodes=N, --ntasks=N, --ntasks-per-node=N
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=SIZE or --mem-per-cpu=SIZE
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS
- --gres=gpu:N
- --partition=NAME
- --output=FILE and --error=FILE (or combined with --output=slurm-%j.out)
- --mail-user=you@site --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Environment variables available in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc. Use them in scripts to adapt behavior.

Best practices
- Always test with a small, short job first (1 node, short time) to verify script and modules.
- Request realistic resources: over-requesting time or memory reduces scheduler throughput and can delay your job.
- Set --time to a sensible upper bound — shorter limits often help the job start sooner.
- Use output files named with %j (job ID) so logs don’t collide across runs.
- Capture exit codes in scripts and fail fast (set -e).
- If pending, check squeue and scontrol for the reason before contacting admins.
- For GPU jobs, confirm cluster uses gres=gpu and what GPU types are available (sinfo shows node resources).
- Keep software environment reproducible (modules, virtualenv/conda, container images if supported).

Troubleshooting tips
- Job never starts: check squeue for pending reason; check sinfo for partition/node availability.
- Job fails quickly: inspect slurm-<JOBID>.out and check the batch script for missing modules or wrong paths.
- Out-of-memory: increase --mem or detect memory leak; use sacct to see ExitCode and signal (e.g., OOM killed).
- Unexpected task placement: check --ntasks, --cpus-per-task and use srun with --cpu-bind options if needed.

Where to learn more
- The official Slurm documentation is authoritative (sacct, srun, sbatch, scontrol pages). If you want, I can fetch specific doc pages or give cluster-specific templates.

- a ready-to-use template for CPU, GPU, or MPI jobs tailored to your cluster defaults?

After reviewing the Slurm cluster, good — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference: basic commands, typical sbatch examples (CPU, GPU, MPI, arrays), interactive usage, monitoring / debugging tips, and best practices.

Quick command reference
- sinfo — show partitions and node states (allocated/idle/down).
- squeue — show queued and running jobs (use -u $USER to filter).
- sbatch myjob.sh — submit a batch job script (non-interactive).
- srun — run a command inside an allocation or start tasks inside a batch job.
- salloc — request an interactive allocation (then use srun or run shell).
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job JOBID — show detailed job configuration and reason for pending.
- sacct -j JOBID — accounting info for completed jobs.
- sstat -j JOBID — runtime stats for a running job (live resource usage).
- sinfo -R — list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN with reasons.

Minimal sbatch batch script (CPU job)
- Example file: myjob.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=test
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=8G
  #SBATCH --time=01:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  module load python
  python train.py

- Submit: sbatch myjob.sh
- Output file: slurm-<JOBID>.out

Requesting GPUs
- Single-node GPU example:
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (driver depends on cluster)
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=04:00:00

MPI / multi-node parallel job
- Use mpirun / srun inside the batch script:
  #SBATCH --nodes=2
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  module load mpi
  srun my_mpi_program   # srun launches the MPI tasks across allocation

Interactive usage
- Quick interactive allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00
  srun --pty bash -i      # get an interactive shell
- Or run a single interactive command:
  srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 python -i

Job arrays (many similar tasks)
- Example (100 tasks, at most 10 concurrently):
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
- Inside the script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input per-task.

Dependencies and chaining jobs
- Submit job B to run after job A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid_A> jobB.sh

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER — show your queued/running jobs
- squeue -j <JOBID> — get state and (usually) pending reason
- If squeue does not show a useful reason, run:
  scontrol show job <JOBID>   — detailed pending reason or required resources
- For running jobs:
  sstat -j <JOBID>   — live CPU/memory usage (if enabled)
  sacct -j <JOBID>   — accounting info after job finishes (exit code, elapsed)
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionDown, QOS, License. Use scontrol show job to get the detailed reason string.

Common #SBATCH options (most used)
- --job-name=NAME
- --nodes=N, --ntasks=N, --ntasks-per-node=N
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=SIZE or --mem-per-cpu=SIZE
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS
- --gres=gpu:N
- --partition=NAME
- --output=FILE and --error=FILE (or combined with --output=slurm-%j.out)
- --mail-user=you@site --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Environment variables available in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc. Use them in scripts to adapt behavior.

Best practices
- Always test with a small, short job first (1 node, short time) to verify script and modules.
- Request realistic resources: over-requesting time or memory reduces scheduler throughput and can delay your job.
- Set --time to a sensible upper bound — shorter limits often help the job start sooner.
- Use output files named with %j (job ID) so logs don’t collide across runs.
- Capture exit codes in scripts and fail fast (set -e).
- If pending, check squeue and scontrol for the reason before contacting admins.
- For GPU jobs, confirm cluster uses gres=gpu and what GPU types are available (sinfo shows node resources).
- Keep software environment reproducible (modules, virtualenv/conda, container images if supported).

Troubleshooting tips
- Job never starts: check squeue for pending reason; check sinfo for partition/node availability.
- Job fails quickly: inspect slurm-<JOBID>.out and check the batch script for missing modules or wrong paths.
- Out-of-memory: increase --mem or detect memory leak; use sacct to see ExitCode and signal (e.g., OOM killed).
- Unexpected task placement: check --ntasks, --cpus-per-task and use srun with --cpu-bind options if needed.

Where to learn more
- The official Slurm documentation is authoritative (sacct, srun, sbatch, scontrol pages). If you want, I can fetch specific doc pages or give cluster-specific templates.

Would you like:
- a ready-to-use template for CPU, GPU, or MPI jobs tailored to your cluster defaults?
- help debugging a specific job script or a pending job ID? (If so, tell me the job ID or which template you want.)

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical guide to the basic Slurm job submission workflow and common options.

1) Prepare a job script
- Create a shell script (e.g., train.sh). Start with a shebang: #!/bin/bash
- Add SBATCH directives near the top to request resources and set job options:
  - Example directives:
    #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
    #SBATCH --partition=gpu
    #SBATCH --nodes=1
    #SBATCH --ntasks=1
    #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
    #SBATCH --mem=32G
    #SBATCH --time=02:00:00        (HH:MM:SS)
    #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1          (request GPUs)
    #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out (stdout file; %j → jobid)
    #SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err  (stderr file)
- Put the commands to run below the directives (module loads, environment setup, and the actual program).
- Make it executable (optional): chmod +x train.sh

Minimal job script example:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

2) Submit the job
- Use sbatch: sbatch train.sh
- sbatch returns a job ID (e.g., Submitted batch job 12345). Save that job ID for monitoring.

3) Monitor job status
- squeue -j <jobid>  (or squeue -u <username>) — shows RUNNING/PENDING and reasons
- scontrol show job <jobid> — detailed job information and resource allocation
- squeue --start — estimate start time for pending jobs

4) Check runtime output and history
- Output/stderr are usually written to the files you set with --output/--error (default: slurm-%j.out)
- For completed jobs or history: sacct -j <jobid>  (shows exit code, elapsed, consumed resources)

5) Interactive jobs
- For interactive allocations:
  - salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00 --partition=debug
  - Then run srun --pty bash or run commands in the allocation
- Or use srun directly for short interactive tasks: srun --partition=short --time=00:10:00 --pty bash

6) Cancelling or modifying jobs
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>
- You can change time limit or hold/release with scontrol subcommands (cluster admins may restrict these)

7) Job arrays
- For many similar tasks, use arrays:
  #SBATCH --array=1-100
- Use environment variable SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script to index work.

8) Resource request tips & common pitfalls
- Always request realistic time limits; underestimating causes TIMEOUT and overestimating can affect scheduling.
- Request CPUs/GPUs/memory using the correct flags: --cpus-per-task, --mem (per node or per CPU depending on config), --gres=gpu:N
- Check available partitions and node types with sinfo before picking a partition.
- Use modules or conda inside the script for reproducible environments.
- If a job stays PENDING, squeue will often show a REASON column (e.g., Priority, Resources, QOSLimit); scontrol show job <id> gives more detail.

9) Useful environment variables inside a job
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc.

10) Debugging strategies
- Run a small, short job first to verify environment and modules.
- Add set -x or echo statements to the script to trace execution.
- Inspect slurm-%j.out and slurm-%j.err for errors.
- Use scontrol show job to see allocated nodes and reason if job pending.

If you want, I can:
- Provide a ready-to-use job script for a specific workload (CPU, multi-node MPI, or GPU).
- Show the exact sbatch/srun commands for your cluster’s partitions — tell me the partition and resource needs.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial covering the common day‑to‑day tasks, commands, examples, and troubleshooting tips.

Basic concepts
- Slurm components you’ll use: sbatch (submit batch scripts), srun (launch job steps / interactive work), salloc (allocate interactive resources), squeue (view queue), sinfo (view partitions/nodes), sacct (accounting/history), scontrol (detailed show/change).
- Job lifecycle: submit (sbatch) → pending (waiting for resources) → running → completed/failed/timed out/cancelled.
- Resources: partition, nodes, tasks, CPUs per task, memory, GPUs (gres), time limit, QOS, account.

Simple batch script (single-node CPU job)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=normal
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py

- Save as job.sh and submit with: sbatch job.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID; job will be scheduled according to available resources and policies.

GPU job example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-job
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --output=gpu.%j.out

module load cuda
srun python train_gpu.py

- --gres=gpu:N requests N GPUs on allocated nodes.

MPI / multi-node example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=03:00:00

module load mpi
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_app

Job arrays (many similar jobs)
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
# inside script, use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input
- %10 limits concurrent tasks to 10.

Dependencies (run job B after A completes successfully)
sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 jobB.sh

After reviewing the Slurm cluster, here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial covering the common day‑to‑day tasks, commands, examples, and troubleshooting tips.

Basic concepts
- Slurm components you’ll use: sbatch (submit batch scripts), srun (launch job steps / interactive work), salloc (allocate interactive resources), squeue (view queue), sinfo (view partitions/nodes), sacct (accounting/history), scontrol (detailed show/change).
- Job lifecycle: submit (sbatch) → pending (waiting for resources) → running → completed/failed/timed out/cancelled.
- Resources: partition, nodes, tasks, CPUs per task, memory, GPUs (gres), time limit, QOS, account.

Simple batch script (single-node CPU job)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=normal
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py

- Save as job.sh and submit with: sbatch job.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID; job will be scheduled according to available resources and policies.

GPU job example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-job
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --output=gpu.%j.out

module load cuda
srun python train_gpu.py

- --gres=gpu:N requests N GPUs on allocated nodes.

MPI / multi-node example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=03:00:00

module load mpi
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_app

Job arrays (many similar jobs)
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
# inside script, use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input
- %10 limits concurrent tasks to 10.

Dependencies (run job B after A completes successfully)
sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 jobB.sh

Interactive work
- salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 bash
  (allocates resources and gives an interactive shell)
- srun --pty --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 bash
  (create an interactive job step inside allocation)

Monitoring and querying
- squeue: current queue and running jobs
  - squeue -u $USER (your jobs)
  - squeue -j JOBID (one job)
  - squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R" (custom format)
- sinfo: partition/node availability and counts
  - sinfo -s (summary)
  - sinfo -N (per-node)
- sacct: historical accounting (completed/failed jobs)
  - sacct -u alice --starttime=2024-04-01
- scontrol show job JOBID: detailed job config and reason fields
- sstat -j JOBID: live resource stats for running job (CPU/memory I/O)

Common job file directives (summary)
- --partition / -p
- --nodes / -N
- --ntasks
- --ntasks-per-node
- --cpus-per-task
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu
- --gres (e.g., gpu:1)
- --time / -t
- --job-name
- --output / --error

- Check job output and the script’s commands; many “failure” questions are solved by reading the output file.

Common pending reasons and what to check
- Resources (ReqNodeNotAvail / Resources): requested nodes/GPUs are busy—check sinfo for idle nodes.
- Priority/Backfill/Preemption (Priority): lower priority; check sprio and sshare if you need priority changes.
- QOS/Account limits (QOSMaxJobsPerUser / QOSMaxWall): site limits; contact admin or change account/QOS.
- Partition down/drained: sinfo will show nodes down/drained; ask admin to resolve.
- Dependency not satisfied: the job has --dependency set; check dependency job status.

- If a job is pending: run squeue -j JOBID (see REASON column). Use scontrol show job JOBID for more detail.
- If job fails quickly: look at job.%j.out and error file; check exit code from sacct (ExitCode).

Resubmitting & cancellation
- Cancel: scancel JOBID
- Requeue: scontrol requeue JOBID (site policy may restrict)
- To re-run failed jobs, check exit codes and logs, adjust script/resources, then sbatch again.

- Submit: sbatch script.sh
- Interactive: salloc ... or srun --pty bash

- Job history: sacct -j JOBID or sacct -u user --starttime=...
- Live stats: sstat -j JOBID
- Cancel job: scancel JOBID

- Request realistic time limits; excessive overestimates reduce scheduling flexibility and waiting times.
- Request only the resources you need (CPUs, memory, GPUs).
- Use modules to set environment; ensure env is reproducible.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks instead of separate sbatch commands.
- Keep scripts small and test interactively (salloc) before full submission.
- Use meaningful job names and --output patterns including %j to track outputs.

When to contact admin
- Nodes are down or drained for long periods (sinfo shows drains).
- You hit account/QOS or cluster-wide limits you don’t understand.
- Strange scheduler behavior (backfill anomalies) or scontrol errors.

- Show a step‑by‑step example for your exact workflow (MPI, TensorFlow, singularity/containers, etc.).
- Explain a particular Slurm error or pending reason if you paste squeue / scontrol output (tell me the job ID).

I’m the Slurm HPC cluster assistant: I monitor, analyze, and diagnose the cluster and jobs, and I help prepare or validate Slurm commands and sbatch scripts. I can run read-only Slurm queries, explain results, and recommend fixes — but I do not directly change cluster state; any mutating action is handed off to an operator per policy.

What I can do (read/diagnose):
- Show queue/job status (squeue) — include job ID and job name in answers.
- Explain why a job is pending or stuck (squeue → scontrol_show if needed).
- Show partition/node health and availability (sinfo, sinfo_reasons, sinfo_node).
- Get detailed job configs or step info (scontrol show).
- Give recent job history/accounting (sacct), usage reports (sreport), fairshare (sshare), scheduler diagnostics (sdiag, sprio).
- Inspect running-job resource usage (sstat), licenses (scontrol_license), reservations (scontrol_reservation_show).
- Read job scripts or logs you provide (read_file) and help debug sbatch scripts.
- Explain Slurm semantics, reason codes, and best practices (I consult local Slurm docs when needed).

Mutating actions (submit/cancel/hold/drain/reconfigure/etc.):
- I do NOT execute them myself. For any request that changes cluster state I will immediately transfer the action to the Operator (I’ll ask for missing targets first if needed).
- For conditional actions (e.g., “submit if a GPU node is idle”) I’ll run the minimum read-only check first, then transfer only if the condition is met.

How to ask:
- For job-specific queries: give the job ID (or I’ll ask for it).
- For node actions: give the node name.
- For broad requests like “cancel all pending jobs” no extra target is needed — I’ll treat that as an action and hand it to the Operator.

Examples you can ask right now:
- “Show me why job 12345 is pending.”
- “What GPU nodes are currently idle?”
- “Can you check recent FAILED jobs for user alice in the last 7 days?”
- “Help me debug this sbatch script” (attach the script or paste it).

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise guide to submitting jobs with Slurm (sbatch), plus common options and examples.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell shebang and SBATCH directives (or pass options on the sbatch command line).
- Example batch script (save as train.sh):
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=train-job
  #SBATCH --partition=gpu
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH -o slurm-%j.out
  #SBATCH -e slurm-%j.err

  module load cuda/12.0
  source venv/bin/activate
  srun python train.py --epochs 50

- Notes:
  - Time format: [[days-]hours:]minutes:seconds (e.g., 2:00:00 = 2 hours).
  - Job name, output (-o), and error (-e) are recommended.
  - Use srun inside the script to launch tasks (sbatch will allocate resources and run the script).

2) Submit the script
- sbatch train.sh
- sbatch prints the job ID on success.

3) Common sbatch options (can be used as #SBATCH lines or sbatch flags)
- --partition=NAME (partition/queue)
- --gres=gpu:NUM (GPUs)
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=32G or --mem-per-cpu=4G
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --job-name=NAME
- -o / -e for stdout/stderr files
- --array=1-100%10 for job arrays
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> for chaining
- --mail-type=END,FAIL and --mail-user=you@domain for email

4) One-line submit example
- sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=32G --time=02:00:00 --job-name=train train.sh

5) Interactive / testing
- For an interactive allocation: srun --pty --partition=debug --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=2 --time=00:30:00 bash
- For quick tests, use small partitions or debug queues if your cluster provides them.

6) Check job status and details
- squeue -u $USER            (list your queued/running jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid>          (check a specific job)
- scontrol show job <jobid>  (detailed job info)
- sacct -j <jobid>           (accounting/history after job completes)
- If pending and you need the reason: squeue -j <jobid> (look for the REASON column) or scontrol show job <jobid> for full details.

7) Cancel or control jobs
- scancel <jobid>            (cancel)
- sbatch --hold or scontrol hold/release <jobid> (hold/release)

8) GPU-specific note (conditional availability)
- Request GPUs with --gres=gpu:#
- Cluster policies may require certain partitions or limits—check your local docs.

9) Troubleshooting tips
- If job stays pending, check REASON from squeue or scontrol show job to see constraints (resources, dependencies, partitions, QOS limits).
- Check slurm-%j.out and stderr for runtime errors.
- Confirm modules and environment (paths, virtualenv) are set in the batch script, since the job runs in a non-interactive shell.

If you want, tell me:
- the script you plan to run (or paste it) and the resources you need (partition, GPUs, cpus, mem, time), and I can show a ready-to-submit sbatch command or example script tailored to your needs.

results.prompt: What do you do?
results.agent_response:
I’m your Slurm HPC cluster assistant — I monitor, analyze, and diagnose cluster and job state and help you act on it. Quick summary of what I do:

Read-only monitoring and diagnostics (I run Slurm read tools for live facts)
- Inspect queues, jobs, and steps (squeue, scontrol show job/step).
- Show partition and node status and reasons (sinfo, sinfo_reasons, scontrol show node).
- Check historical/accounting records (sacct, sreport, sacctmgr).
- Show scheduler diagnostics, priorities, and fairshare (sdiag, sprio, sshare).
- Show resource usage for running jobs (sstat), software licenses (scontrol_license), reservations (scontrol reservation show), and controller/config health (scontrol show config / scontrol ping).
- Fetch job scripts/logs from disk (read_file) when available.
- Look up Slurm docs or runbooks when you need command syntax or admin guidance.

Action rules and limits
- I do NOT make mutating changes directly (submits, cancels, holds, drains, node changes, reconfigure, etc.). Per workflow I will hand off any explicit/mutating request to the Operator to execute the exact Slurm command.
- For conditional actions (e.g., “submit if idle GPU nodes exist” or “cancel if runtime > 2h”) I will first run the minimum read-only check (sinfo or squeue as appropriate). If the condition is met I will then transfer to the Operator; if not, I’ll report the observed facts and stop.
- I never fabricate tool output and will show you the real Slurm outputs I use.

How to get the fastest help
- For job questions give a job ID (e.g., “why is job 12345 pending?”).
- For node actions give a node name (e.g., “drain node node07” — note this will be handed to Operator).
- For broad requests (e.g., “cancel all pending gpu jobs”, “show GPU usage last 7 days”) I can run the appropriate discovery reads or hand off as required.

Examples of things you can ask right now
- “Why is job 12345 pending?”
- “Show GPU partition node status”
- “Give me recent FAILED jobs for user alice”
- “How many GPU-hours used last 7 days?”
- “Cancel job 12345” (I will transfer this to the Operator)

- Read current cluster state (no changes)

- Explain Slurm concepts and commands

- I do not execute mutating actions myself. If you ask to submit, cancel, hold, requeue, reconfigure, drain/resume nodes, change job limits, or any state change, I immediately hand that request to an Operator tool that runs the required Slurm command (sbatch, scancel, scontrol_*, etc.).

#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL

#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
# optional job array:
# SBATCH --array=1-10%4

# --- safe shell options ---

# uncomment for verbose trace while debugging:
# set -x
umask 0022

# --- simple logging of job metadata ---

echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "CPUs/task: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, GPUs: ${SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE:-unknown}"

# uncomment for verbose trace while debugging:
# set -x
umask 0022

# --- simple logging of job metadata ---
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) started on $(date)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "CPUs/task: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, GPUs: ${SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE:-unknown}"

# --- create and use a per-job temp dir (prefer fast local scratch if available) ---
export JOB_TMP="${TMPDIR:-/scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$JOB_TMP"
cd "$JOB_TMP"

# --- cleanup handler: copy results back, kill stray children, preserve exit code ---
on_exit() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID exiting with status $rc at $(date)"
  # kill any child processes that may remain
  pkill -P $$ || true
  # copy results back (make this path valid for your site)
  rsync -a --remove-source-files ./results/ /home/$USER/results/$SLURM_JOB_ID/ || true
  exit $rc
}
trap on_exit EXIT

# --- load modules / activate envs ---
module purge
module load gcc/12 cuda/11.8        # example; use your site modules
# source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# --- run the job ---
# Prefer srun so Slurm manages distribution and accounting
# Use --cpu-bind or --hint if you need CPU affinity
srun --mpi=pmix --cpu-bind=cores ./my_program --threads "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# Or for array tasks: ./my_program --task-id $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

# explicit exit (on_exit trap will run)
exit 0

Key points / best practices
- #SBATCH directives: must appear before the first non-comment line in the script. Keep shebang (#!/bin/bash) as the first line.
- Use set -euo pipefail to fail fast and avoid surprises from unset variables; enable set -x temporarily while debugging.
- Use a trap/cleanup function (trap ... EXIT) to copy outputs back and kill stray children. Preserve and re-exit with the original exit code.
- Create and use a per-job temporary directory (local fast scratch if available) and rsync results back to a persistent filesystem at the end.
- Prefer srun for launching tasks under Slurm (srun gives proper allocation, binding, and accounting). If you must use mpirun, ensure it integrates with Slurm and uses SLURM_NTASKS/SLURM_NODELIST.
- For GPUs: request them with --gres=gpu:N and let Slurm set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES — do not hardcode GPU device assignments inside the job.
- Use --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded tasks and set memory (--mem or --mem-per-cpu) to avoid OOMs.
- Avoid long-running copies at job start on shared storage; stage inputs to local scratch where possible and rsync only outputs back at end.
- Make logs reproducible: include %j (jobid) and %x (jobname) in output filenames so parallel runs don’t clobber each other.
- Use job arrays for many similar short tasks (#SBATCH --array=...) and limit concurrent tasks with %N to avoid overloading the scheduler or filesystem.
- For debug/development jobs, set a short --time and smaller resource requests.
- Consider ulimit and umask policies if your site requires specific defaults.

results.prompt: Use official Slurm docs to explain the pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
Short answer (from the official Slurm docs)
- "Priority" as a pending reason means the scheduler considered the job but did not start it because other jobs with higher scheduling priority were chosen first. Only the reason encountered by the scheduling pass is shown; multiple reasons may apply but only the first encountered is displayed. (See "Job Reason Codes".)

What determines that priority
- Slurm’s default Multifactor Priority plugin computes a single numeric job priority as a weighted sum of several factors. The docs express it roughly as:
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_x * TRES_factor_x) - nice_factor
- Factors include: age, association (account) priority, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, specific TRES (CPU/GPU) factors, site factor, and a "nice" adjustment. Each factor is normalized (0.0–1.0) and weights are configured in slurm.conf. The final job priority is an unsigned integer (0..4294967295); larger → higher scheduling precedence. (See "Multifactor Priority Plugin".)

How to inspect why a particular job shows "Priority"
- Use sprio to view priorities and factor breakdown for queued jobs:
  - sprio -j <jobid> (shows job priority and component contributions)
- View job details (includes Priority): scontrol show job <jobid>
- squeue also shows queue state; the pending reason column will show "Priority" when that is the scheduler’s encountered cause.

What users or admins can do
- Users: reduce requested resources, request a different partition/QOS, use a higher-QOS if available, or wait until higher-priority jobs finish.
- Admins: adjust PriorityWeight* settings in slurm.conf, change association/account priorities via sacctmgr, tune fairshare settings, or modify QOS/partition priorities. After config changes, the effective priorities will change and scheduling behavior will follow the new weights.

Pointers to the official docs
- Job Reason Codes (explains pending reasons and that only the encountered reason is shown).
- Multifactor Priority Plugin (explains the priority formula, factors, and configuration).

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can run sprio and scontrol show job for that job to show its numeric priority and factor breakdown.
results.judge_reason: Used correct tool and provided accurate explanation

After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer (from the official Slurm docs)
- "Priority" as a pending reason means the scheduler considered the job but did not start it because other jobs with higher scheduling priority were chosen first. Only the reason encountered by the scheduling pass is shown; multiple reasons may apply but only the first encountered is displayed. (See "Job Reason Codes".)

What determines that priority
- Slurm’s default Multifactor Priority plugin computes a single numeric job priority as a weighted sum of several factors. The docs express it roughly as:
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_x * TRES_factor_x) - nice_factor
- Factors include: age, association (account) priority, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, specific TRES (CPU/GPU) factors, site factor, and a "nice" adjustment. Each factor is normalized (0.0–1.0) and weights are configured in slurm.conf. The final job priority is an unsigned integer (0..4294967295); larger → higher scheduling precedence. (See "Multifactor Priority Plugin".)

- Use sprio to view priorities and factor breakdown for queued jobs:
  - sprio -j <jobid> (shows job priority and component contributions)

- Users: reduce requested resources, request a different partition/QOS, use a higher-QOS if available, or wait until higher-priority jobs finish.

results.prompt: Use local Slurm docs to explain when to use sacct versus squeue
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Use squeue to view the live queue (running and pending jobs).  
- Use sacct to view accounting/history (completed, failed, cancelled jobs, exit codes, recorded resource usage).

When to pick each (doc-backed guidance)
- squeue
  - Purpose: real‑time queue view of active jobs (RUNNING, PENDING, etc.). Good for checking why a job is still pending (use the pending reason shown), seeing current node/partition allocations, and monitoring currently running jobs.
  - Typical use cases: “What is in the queue now?”, “Is job 12345 running or pending?”, “Which nodes are busy?”.
  - Common commands/examples: squeue -u alice, squeue -j 12345, squeue -p gpu.
  - Notes: squeue is fast and reads live slurmctld state.

- sacct
  - Purpose: query job accounting records stored in the job accounting log or SlurmDB (historical data about jobs and job steps). Returns exit codes, final state (COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELLED), elapsed time, requested/consumed resources, etc.
  - Typical use cases: “What exit code did my job get?”, “How long did that completed job run?”, usage/accounting reports over a time window, user/job history.
  - Common commands/examples: sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,AllocCPUs,ReqMem; sacct -u alice --starttime=2024-01-01.
  - Notes: sacct queries slurmdbd (remote procedure call). It can be slower and, if overused, can load slurmdbd — avoid calling sacct repeatedly in tight loops or scripts. sacct requires accounting storage (SlurmDB) to be configured to show historical data.

Recommended quick workflow (practical)
- Check squeue first for a job ID to see its current live state. If squeue shows no entry for that job and you need historical info (exit code, final state, elapsed), then use sacct to inspect the completed job record.
- If you need runtime resource metrics for a currently running job, use sstat (not sacct) for real‑time job resource usage; sacct is for post‑run accounting.

Other useful doc notes
- sacct shows job steps and more detailed accounting fields; use --format to tailor output.
- Because sacct contacts slurmdbd, running many sacct calls can degrade slurmdbd performance (do not loop sacct calls without limits).

If you want, I can show specific example commands for a job ID or user and explain fields you’ll see in the output.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer
- Use squeue to view the live queue (running and pending jobs).  
- Use sacct to view accounting/history (completed, failed, cancelled jobs, exit codes, recorded resource usage).

When to pick each (doc-backed guidance)
- squeue
  - Purpose: real‑time queue view of active jobs (RUNNING, PENDING, etc.). Good for checking why a job is still pending (use the pending reason shown), seeing current node/partition allocations, and monitoring currently running jobs.
  - Typical use cases: “What is in the queue now?”, “Is job 12345 running or pending?”, “Which nodes are busy?”.
  - Common commands/examples: squeue -u alice, squeue -j 12345, squeue -p gpu.
  - Notes: squeue is fast and reads live slurmctld state.

- sacct
  - Purpose: query job accounting records stored in the job accounting log or SlurmDB (historical data about jobs and job steps). Returns exit codes, final state (COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELLED), elapsed time, requested/consumed resources, etc.
  - Typical use cases: “What exit code did my job get?”, “How long did that completed job run?”, usage/accounting reports over a time window, user/job history.
  - Common commands/examples: sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,AllocCPUs,ReqMem; sacct -u alice --starttime=2024-01-01.
  - Notes: sacct queries slurmdbd (remote procedure call). It can be slower and, if overused, can load slurmdbd — avoid calling sacct repeatedly in tight loops or scripts. sacct requires accounting storage (SlurmDB) to be configured to show historical data.

Recommended quick workflow (practical)
- Check squeue first for a job ID to see its current live state. If squeue shows no entry for that job and you need historical info (exit code, final state, elapsed), then use sacct to inspect the completed job record.
- If you need runtime resource metrics for a currently running job, use sstat (not sacct) for real‑time job resource usage; sacct is for post‑run accounting.

Other useful doc notes
- sacct shows job steps and more detailed accounting fields; use --format to tailor output.
- Because sacct contacts slurmdbd, running many sacct calls can degrade slurmdbd performance (do not loop sacct calls without limits).

If you want, I can show specific example commands for a job ID or user and explain fields you’ll see in the output.
