Here’s a concise, doc‑based explanation of common QOS limits (with behavior notes and examples). Sources: Slurm QOS and Resource Limits pages (https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html, https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html).

What a QOS limit is
- A QOS limit caps a resource or submission metric for jobs that request that QOS. QOS limits mirror limits that can also be set on user/account/partition/cluster associations; when a QOS defines a limit it overrides association limits (see precedence below).

Key limits (definitions)
- MaxJobs
  - Maximum number of jobs that may be concurrently active (RUNNING or PENDING as enforced) that are associated with that QOS (or that count point in the hierarchy).
  - If a submission would cause the limit to be exceeded the job will pend unless the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit (see DenyOnLimit).
- MaxCPUs
  - Maximum number of CPUs (cores) that may be concurrently allocated to jobs using that QOS. This is enforced against the sum of CPU allocations for matching jobs.
  - CPUs are counted as integer core units (not time-weighted).
- MaxNodes / MinNodes / Max[Time|Wall]
  - Limits on node counts or job wall time. (Note: some of these limits have special precedence rules; see hierarchy note.)
- MaxSubmitJobs, MaxSubmitJobsPerUser
  - Limits on the number of jobs that may be submitted within some context (global, per-user, etc.). These control submission rate/quantity rather than resource allocation.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode
  - TRES = Trackable RESources (e.g., cpu, mem, gres/gpu). MaxTRES can set absolute limits on TRES usage (for example cpu=2000,gpu=10,mem=100000).
  - GrpTRES limits group (aggregate) usage across the QOS.
  - MaxTRESPerNode or Max[Something]PerNode is applied per node.
- MaxGRES / GRES-related limits
  - Limits specifically for GRES (Generic RESources) such as GPUs; used when you want to constrain GPU counts.
- Flags=Relative
  - When set, numeric limits are treated as percentages of total cluster resources (e.g., cpu=50 means 50% of all CPUs). Memory limits should be set without units when using Relative (1MB = 1%).

Behavioral rules and enforcement
- Hierarchy / precedence
  - Limits are enforced according to a fixed hierarchy (partition QOS, job QOS, user association, account association(s) ascending, root/cluster association, partition limit, none). The first place a limit is defined in this list is used. You can change partition-vs-job QOS precedence with Flags=OverPartQOS.
- What happens when a limit would be exceeded
  - Default: a job that would violate a Max* limit will pend until resources are available.
  - If Flags=DenyOnLimit is set on the QOS, jobs that would violate the QOS “Max” limits will be denied at submission time (rejected), rather than pended.
  - Group (Grp) limits are treated as Max limits when DenyOnLimit is applied.
- Interaction with partitions and associations
  - A Partition QOS (a QOS attached to a partition) carries the QOS limits into the partition view and (by default) is applied before a job’s requested QOS. OverPartQOS reverses that order.
- Relative QOS nuance
  - With Flags=Relative, limits are percentages and may be computed either cluster-wide or relative to a partition when used as a partition QOS; slurmctld must be reconfigured/restarted to pick up some flag changes.
- Units and types
  - CPU limits are counts. Memory limits are normally specified with units (MB/GB) but when using Relative you should set memory with no units so it’s treated as a percentage.

Examples (from docs)
- If a partition QOS sets MaxJobs=20 and a user-association sets MaxJobs=4, the partition QOS value (20) takes effect because of the hierarchy—unless OverPartQOS is used to reverse precedence.
- If a QOS has cpu=50 and Flags=Relative, that means jobs using the QOS can consume up to 50% of total cluster CPUs (values above 100 are treated as 100).

Practical notes for admins and users
- Use MaxTRES (or specific MaxCPUs/MaxGRES) when you need precise control over specific resource types (CPUs vs GPUs vs memory).
- Use DenyOnLimit when you prefer immediate rejection at submission instead of a job silently queueing/pend-ing.
- Remember the hierarchy: setting limits at the right level (partition vs QOS vs association) matters.
- When changing QOS flags or limits, reconfiguration may be required for some flags (e.g., Relative) to take effect.

- Resource limits and hierarchy: https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run

the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.

to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,

Based on the current cluster state, here’s a concise, doc‑based explanation of common QOS limits (with behavior notes and examples). Sources: Slurm QOS and Resource Limits pages (https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html, https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html).

What a QOS limit is
- A QOS limit caps a resource or submission metric for jobs that request that QOS. QOS limits mirror limits that can also be set on user/account/partition/cluster associations; when a QOS defines a limit it overrides association limits (see precedence below).

Key limits (definitions)
- MaxJobs
  - Maximum number of jobs that may be concurrently active (RUNNING or PENDING as enforced) that are associated with that QOS (or that count point in the hierarchy).
  - If a submission would cause the limit to be exceeded the job will pend unless the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit (see DenyOnLimit).
- MaxCPUs
  - Maximum number of CPUs (cores) that may be concurrently allocated to jobs using that QOS. This is enforced against the sum of CPU allocations for matching jobs.
  - CPUs are counted as integer core units (not time-weighted).
- MaxNodes / MinNodes / Max[Time|Wall]
  - Limits on node counts or job wall time. (Note: some of these limits have special precedence rules; see hierarchy note.)
- MaxSubmitJobs, MaxSubmitJobsPerUser
  - Limits on the number of jobs that may be submitted within some context (global, per-user, etc.). These control submission rate/quantity rather than resource allocation.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode
  - TRES = Trackable RESources (e.g., cpu, mem, gres/gpu). MaxTRES can set absolute limits on TRES usage (for example cpu=2000,gpu=10,mem=100000).
  - GrpTRES limits group (aggregate) usage across the QOS.
  - MaxTRESPerNode or Max[Something]PerNode is applied per node.
- MaxGRES / GRES-related limits
  - Limits specifically for GRES (Generic RESources) such as GPUs; used when you want to constrain GPU counts.
- Flags=Relative
  - When set, numeric limits are treated as percentages of total cluster resources (e.g., cpu=50 means 50% of all CPUs). Memory limits should be set without units when using Relative (1MB = 1%).

Behavioral rules and enforcement
- Hierarchy / precedence
  - Limits are enforced according to a fixed hierarchy (partition QOS, job QOS, user association, account association(s) ascending, root/cluster association, partition limit, none). The first place a limit is defined in this list is used. You can change partition-vs-job QOS precedence with Flags=OverPartQOS.
- What happens when a limit would be exceeded
  - Default: a job that would violate a Max* limit will pend until resources are available.
  - If Flags=DenyOnLimit is set on the QOS, jobs that would violate the QOS “Max” limits will be denied at submission time (rejected), rather than pended.
  - Group (Grp) limits are treated as Max limits when DenyOnLimit is applied.
- Interaction with partitions and associations
  - A Partition QOS (a QOS attached to a partition) carries the QOS limits into the partition view and (by default) is applied before a job’s requested QOS. OverPartQOS reverses that order.
- Relative QOS nuance
  - With Flags=Relative, limits are percentages and may be computed either cluster-wide or relative to a partition when used as a partition QOS; slurmctld must be reconfigured/restarted to pick up some flag changes.
- Units and types
  - CPU limits are counts. Memory limits are normally specified with units (MB/GB) but when using Relative you should set memory with no units so it’s treated as a percentage.

Examples (from docs)
- If a partition QOS sets MaxJobs=20 and a user-association sets MaxJobs=4, the partition QOS value (20) takes effect because of the hierarchy—unless OverPartQOS is used to reverse precedence.
- If a QOS has cpu=50 and Flags=Relative, that means jobs using the QOS can consume up to 50% of total cluster CPUs (values above 100 are treated as 100).

Practical notes for admins and users
- Use MaxTRES (or specific MaxCPUs/MaxGRES) when you need precise control over specific resource types (CPUs vs GPUs vs memory).
- Use DenyOnLimit when you prefer immediate rejection at submission instead of a job silently queueing/pend-ing.
- Remember the hierarchy: setting limits at the right level (partition vs QOS vs association) matters.
- When changing QOS flags or limits, reconfiguration may be required for some flags (e.g., Relative) to take effect.

- QOS reference and options: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Resource limits and hierarchy: https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step

What a QOS limit is
- A QOS limit caps a resource or submission metric for jobs that request that QOS. QOS limits mirror limits that can also be set on user/account/partition/cluster associations; when a QOS defines a limit it overrides association limits (see precedence below).

Key limits (definitions)
- MaxJobs
  - Maximum number of jobs that may be concurrently active (RUNNING or PENDING as enforced) that are associated with that QOS (or that count point in the hierarchy).
  - If a submission would cause the limit to be exceeded the job will pend unless the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit (see DenyOnLimit).
- MaxCPUs
  - Maximum number of CPUs (cores) that may be concurrently allocated to jobs using that QOS. This is enforced against the sum of CPU allocations for matching jobs.
  - CPUs are counted as integer core units (not time-weighted).
- MaxNodes / MinNodes / Max[Time|Wall]
  - Limits on node counts or job wall time. (Note: some of these limits have special precedence rules; see hierarchy note.)
- MaxSubmitJobs, MaxSubmitJobsPerUser
  - Limits on the number of jobs that may be submitted within some context (global, per-user, etc.). These control submission rate/quantity rather than resource allocation.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode
  - TRES = Trackable RESources (e.g., cpu, mem, gres/gpu). MaxTRES can set absolute limits on TRES usage (for example cpu=2000,gpu=10,mem=100000).
  - GrpTRES limits group (aggregate) usage across the QOS.
  - MaxTRESPerNode or Max[Something]PerNode is applied per node.
- MaxGRES / GRES-related limits
  - Limits specifically for GRES (Generic RESources) such as GPUs; used when you want to constrain GPU counts.
- Flags=Relative
  - When set, numeric limits are treated as percentages of total cluster resources (e.g., cpu=50 means 50% of all CPUs). Memory limits should be set without units when using Relative (1MB = 1%).

Behavioral rules and enforcement
- Hierarchy / precedence
  - Limits are enforced according to a fixed hierarchy (partition QOS, job QOS, user association, account association(s) ascending, root/cluster association, partition limit, none). The first place a limit is defined in this list is used. You can change partition-vs-job QOS precedence with Flags=OverPartQOS.
- What happens when a limit would be exceeded
  - Default: a job that would violate a Max* limit will pend until resources are available.
  - If Flags=DenyOnLimit is set on the QOS, jobs that would violate the QOS “Max” limits will be denied at submission time (rejected), rather than pended.
  - Group (Grp) limits are treated as Max limits when DenyOnLimit is applied.
- Interaction with partitions and associations
  - A Partition QOS (a QOS attached to a partition) carries the QOS limits into the partition view and (by default) is applied before a job’s requested QOS. OverPartQOS reverses that order.
- Relative QOS nuance
  - With Flags=Relative, limits are percentages and may be computed either cluster-wide or relative to a partition when used as a partition QOS; slurmctld must be reconfigured/restarted to pick up some flag changes.
- Units and types
  - CPU limits are counts. Memory limits are normally specified with units (MB/GB) but when using Relative you should set memory with no units so it’s treated as a percentage.

Examples (from docs)
- If a partition QOS sets MaxJobs=20 and a user-association sets MaxJobs=4, the partition QOS value (20) takes effect because of the hierarchy—unless OverPartQOS is used to reverse precedence.
- If a QOS has cpu=50 and Flags=Relative, that means jobs using the QOS can consume up to 50% of total cluster CPUs (values above 100 are treated as 100).

Practical notes for admins and users
- Use MaxTRES (or specific MaxCPUs/MaxGRES) when you need precise control over specific resource types (CPUs vs GPUs vs memory).
- Use DenyOnLimit when you prefer immediate rejection at submission instead of a job silently queueing/pend-ing.
- Remember the hierarchy: setting limits at the right level (partition vs QOS vs association) matters.
- When changing QOS flags or limits, reconfiguration may be required for some flags (e.g., Relative) to take effect.

Where to read more
- QOS reference and options: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Resource limits and hierarchy: https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor) to compute a single numeric job priority as a weighted sum of independent factors. Three of the most important pieces that control queue ordering are: the fairshare factor (how much a user/account has recently consumed), the Fair Tree algorithm (how fairshare is computed across accounts/users), and the configured PriorityWeight* values (how strongly each factor influences ordering).

How job priority is computed (conceptual)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X)
  - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating value (roughly 0.0–1.0). The PriorityWeight* entries are unsigned integers; together they scale each factor’s contribution before the total is converted to the final integer priority (0 .. 4294967295).

Fairshare factor — what it means and how it behaves
- Fairshare reduces priority for users/accounts that have used more of the cluster recently; it raises priority for users/accounts that have used less.
- Fairshare values are derived from historical usage per association/account/user and are normalized into a factor used in the multifactor formula.
- Two key configuration knobs:
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: controls how quickly past usage “decays” (short half-life forgets history quickly; long half-life keeps historical usage influential). A value of 0 disables decay (must then use PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optionally reset usage counters on a schedule (useful for enforcing quotas or fixed-period fairness).
- Tools to inspect fairshare: sshare (shows effective shares and usage) and sprio (shows factor contributions for pending jobs).

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Since Slurm 19.05 the Fair Tree algorithm is the default method used to convert historical usage into fairshare factors.
- Fair Tree is hierarchical: if two sibling accounts A and B are ordered by fairshare, then all children of A rank above all children of B. This preserves account-level ordering and avoids precision/tie problems seen in the older Classic algorithm.
- Benefits: stable ordering across account hierarchies, predictable behavior when account coordinators adjust shares, and reduced numerical tie/precision issues.
- If you need the older "classic" behavior you can still configure that explicitly, but Fair Tree is typically preferred.

Priority weights — how to make a factor matter (or not)
- PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, and per-TRES weights determine how strongly each factor affects final priority.
- If a weight is set to zero the corresponding factor contributes nothing.
- Typical default pattern: make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to others so fairshare has strong influence (examples in docs use PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, others 1000).
- Example effects:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare >> PriorityWeightAge, then users’ historical usage dominates scheduling (new jobs from under-used users jump ahead of old heavy users).
  - If PriorityWeightAge is high, long-waiting jobs will eventually win even if a user has been heavy.
- TRES weights allow bias by resource type (e.g., make GPU usage count differently than CPU usage in the fairshare calculations).

Practical tuning and debugging tips
- Decide policy first: do you want strict account-level fairness, or to allow aging to override recent usage?
- Typical levers:
  - Increase PriorityWeightFairshare to favor historical fairness.
  - Decrease PriorityDecayHalfLife to forget older usage sooner (helps new users recover).
  - Use PriorityUsageResetPeriod for hard periodic resets (monthly allocations, semester quotas).
  - Tune TRES weights to reflect relative cost/importance of GPUs vs CPUs.
- Inspect what Slurm is doing:
  - sshare — view current fairshare/usage for accounts and users.
  - sprio [--all] — show the numeric priority and per-factor contributions for pending jobs.
  - scontrol show config — see configured PriorityWeight* and decay/reset settings.
- When debugging why a particular job is low in the queue, run sprio (or scontrol show job) to see the fairshare_factor and all other factor contributions.

Short examples
- Two accounts A and B, equal job size mix, but A has consumed 4× more resources in the past week:
  - With PriorityWeightFairshare high, jobs from B will be scheduled ahead of A until usage evens out.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is short (e.g., 1 day), A’s advantage/penalty fades quickly and A’s jobs recover sooner.
- If PriorityWeightAge is large, even a user with poor fairshare will eventually have jobs win after waiting long enough.

Bottom line
- Fairshare (via Fair Tree) determines how recent historical consumption penalizes or boosts users/accounts.
- Priority weights control how much that fairshare (and other factors like age, job size, QOS, TRES) influence final queue ordering.
- Use sshare and sprio to inspect current effective shares and factor contributions; tune PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife/PriorityUsageResetPeriod to match your site’s fairness vs responsiveness goals.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current configured PriorityWeight* and fairshare settings from your cluster (scontrol show config and sshare/sprio).

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The following slurm.conf parameters are used to configure the Multifactor Job
Priority Plugin. See slurm.conf(5) man page for more details.
PriorityType
Set this value to "priority/multifactor" to enable the Multifactor Job
Priority Plugin.
PriorityDecayHalfLife
This determines the contribution of historical usage on the
composite usage value. The larger the number, the longer past usage

Short answer
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor) to compute a single numeric job priority as a weighted sum of independent factors. Three of the most important pieces that control queue ordering are: the fairshare factor (how much a user/account has recently consumed), the Fair Tree algorithm (how fairshare is computed across accounts/users), and the configured PriorityWeight* values (how strongly each factor influences ordering).

How job priority is computed (conceptual)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X)
  - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating value (roughly 0.0–1.0). The PriorityWeight* entries are unsigned integers; together they scale each factor’s contribution before the total is converted to the final integer priority (0 .. 4294967295).

Fairshare factor — what it means and how it behaves
- Fairshare reduces priority for users/accounts that have used more of the cluster recently; it raises priority for users/accounts that have used less.
- Fairshare values are derived from historical usage per association/account/user and are normalized into a factor used in the multifactor formula.
- Two key configuration knobs:
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: controls how quickly past usage “decays” (short half-life forgets history quickly; long half-life keeps historical usage influential). A value of 0 disables decay (must then use PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optionally reset usage counters on a schedule (useful for enforcing quotas or fixed-period fairness).
- Tools to inspect fairshare: sshare (shows effective shares and usage) and sprio (shows factor contributions for pending jobs).

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Since Slurm 19.05 the Fair Tree algorithm is the default method used to convert historical usage into fairshare factors.
- Fair Tree is hierarchical: if two sibling accounts A and B are ordered by fairshare, then all children of A rank above all children of B. This preserves account-level ordering and avoids precision/tie problems seen in the older Classic algorithm.
- Benefits: stable ordering across account hierarchies, predictable behavior when account coordinators adjust shares, and reduced numerical tie/precision issues.
- If you need the older "classic" behavior you can still configure that explicitly, but Fair Tree is typically preferred.

Priority weights — how to make a factor matter (or not)
- PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, and per-TRES weights determine how strongly each factor affects final priority.
- If a weight is set to zero the corresponding factor contributes nothing.
- Typical default pattern: make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to others so fairshare has strong influence (examples in docs use PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, others 1000).
- Example effects:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare >> PriorityWeightAge, then users’ historical usage dominates scheduling (new jobs from under-used users jump ahead of old heavy users).
  - If PriorityWeightAge is high, long-waiting jobs will eventually win even if a user has been heavy.
- TRES weights allow bias by resource type (e.g., make GPU usage count differently than CPU usage in the fairshare calculations).

Practical tuning and debugging tips
- Decide policy first: do you want strict account-level fairness, or to allow aging to override recent usage?
- Typical levers:
  - Increase PriorityWeightFairshare to favor historical fairness.
  - Decrease PriorityDecayHalfLife to forget older usage sooner (helps new users recover).
  - Use PriorityUsageResetPeriod for hard periodic resets (monthly allocations, semester quotas).
  - Tune TRES weights to reflect relative cost/importance of GPUs vs CPUs.
- Inspect what Slurm is doing:
  - sshare — view current fairshare/usage for accounts and users.
  - sprio [--all] — show the numeric priority and per-factor contributions for pending jobs.
  - scontrol show config — see configured PriorityWeight* and decay/reset settings.
- When debugging why a particular job is low in the queue, run sprio (or scontrol show job) to see the fairshare_factor and all other factor contributions.

Short examples
- Two accounts A and B, equal job size mix, but A has consumed 4× more resources in the past week:
  - With PriorityWeightFairshare high, jobs from B will be scheduled ahead of A until usage evens out.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is short (e.g., 1 day), A’s advantage/penalty fades quickly and A’s jobs recover sooner.
- If PriorityWeightAge is large, even a user with poor fairshare will eventually have jobs win after waiting long enough.

Bottom line
- Fairshare (via Fair Tree) determines how recent historical consumption penalizes or boosts users/accounts.
- Priority weights control how much that fairshare (and other factors like age, job size, QOS, TRES) influence final queue ordering.
- Use sshare and sprio to inspect current effective shares and factor contributions; tune PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife/PriorityUsageResetPeriod to match your site’s fairness vs responsiveness goals.

- Two accounts A and B, equal job size mix, but A has consumed 4× more resources in the past week:
  - With PriorityWeightFairshare high, jobs from B will be scheduled ahead of A until usage evens out.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is short (e.g., 1 day), A’s advantage/penalty fades quickly and A’s jobs recover sooner.
- If PriorityWeightAge is large, even a user with poor fairshare will eventually have jobs win after waiting long enough.

Bottom line
- Fairshare (via Fair Tree) determines how recent historical consumption penalizes or boosts users/accounts.
- Priority weights control how much that fairshare (and other factors like age, job size, QOS, TRES) influence final queue ordering.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain pending reasons Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, and QOS limits
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, doc-backed explanations (what the reason means, common causes, quick checks, and typical fixes) for the pending reasons you asked about. References: Slurm Job Reason Codes, Resource Limits, Priority (multifactor) and QOS docs.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - The scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to place the job (CPUs, memory, GPUs, nodes, sockets, or matching TRES/GRES).
- Common causes
  - No nodes with the requested TRES (e.g., --gres=gpu:...), not enough CPUs or memory on any single node, fragmentation across nodes, or all suitable nodes are already allocated.
  - Constraints like node features (-C / --constraint) or topology/heterogeneous requests that can't be satisfied.
- What to check
  - sinfo to see partition/node idle counts and TRES/GRES availability.
  - squeue to see what is currently running/allocating.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested resources.
- Typical fixes
  - Relax resources/constraints (fewer GPUs, less memory, fewer specific features).
  - Submit with a different partition or different GRES type.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or enable preemption if policy allows.

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is eligible but lower-priority jobs are ahead; higher-priority workload(s) currently prevent this job from being scheduled.
- Common causes
  - Other queued jobs have higher multifactor priority (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, partition weight, etc.).
  - QOS/association priority settings or recent account usage (fairshare) favor other jobs.
- What to check
  - sprio (shows priority components for queued jobs) and sprio --weights (configured weights).
  - squeue to identify higher-priority jobs on the partition.
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage.
- Typical fixes
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust QOS/priority weights or run under a QOS that allows preemption.
  - Wait — priority factors (age/fairshare) may escalate the job over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node characteristics that are currently not available or usable, so the scheduler cannot allocate them.
- Common causes
  - The job used explicit node requests (e.g., --nodelist, -w, heterogeneous node lists) and those nodes are down/drained/allocated or reserved.
  - A reservation prevents taking those nodes, or the nodes have been placed into maintenance/power-off states.
  - Node feature/constraint mismatch where nodes matching constraints are unavailable.
- What to check
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the exact node request.
  - sinfo (and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons) or sinfo --Node to inspect node states (down/drain/reserved).
  - squeue --reservation=<name> if a reservation might be blocking nodes.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node list or relax constraints.
  - Wait for the nodes to come back (or ask admins to bring nodes up or clear the reservation).
  - If a reservation blocks the nodes, either use a different partition/QOS or coordinate with the reservation owner/admin.

4) QOS limits (pending reasons that indicate limit enforcement)
- What it means
  - The job would exceed a configured resource or count limit on a QOS, account, user association or partition; the scheduler set a limit-related pending reason (e.g., Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp*, MaxTRESPerUser).
- Common causes
  - Per-QOS or partition limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser (GPU/CPU hours or counts), MaxNodes, MaxWall, etc. A job can pend when it would breach a limit unless DenyOnLimit is set (then it would be denied at submission).
  - Hierarchical enforcement: Partition QOS limits are evaluated first by default; job QOS and association limits follow (OverPartQOS can change precedence).
- What to check
  - sacctmgr (sacctmgr list associations / sacctmgr show qos) to inspect QOS and association limits.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the job's QOS/association.
  - Resource Limits documentation to map the pending reason to the exact configured limit name.
- Typical fixes
  - Use a different QOS or partition with sufficient limits.
  - Request limit increases from admins (via sacctmgr).
  - Change the job request (smaller resource request, fewer concurrent jobs) to fit within limits.
  - If DenyOnLimit is set and you keep hitting rejects at submit, adjust the job/QOS or ask admins to change DenyOnLimit.

Short diagnostic checklist you can run (commands)
- scontrol show job <jobid>        # job’s requested resources, QOS, node list
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R"  # queue row + reason
- sinfo -l / sinfo --Node          # partition and node availability, TRES/GRES
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons        # nodes in drain/down and the reasons
- sprio                             # priority breakdown for pending jobs
- sshare                            # fairshare / effective shares
- sacctmgr list qos / sacctmgr show qos  # QOS limits and flags

If you want, tell me one example JOBID and I can show the exact squeue / scontrol fields and the scheduler-assigned pending reason and give a targeted remediation.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order

flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit

- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy

- Partition limit

- Common causes
  - No nodes with the requested TRES (e.g., --gres=gpu:...), not enough CPUs or memory on any single node, fragmentation across nodes, or all suitable nodes are already allocated.
  - Constraints like node features (-C / --constraint) or topology/heterogeneous requests that can't be satisfied.
- What to check
  - sinfo to see partition/node idle counts and TRES/GRES availability.
  - squeue to see what is currently running/allocating.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested resources.
- Typical fixes
  - Relax resources/constraints (fewer GPUs, less memory, fewer specific features).
  - Submit with a different partition or different GRES type.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or enable preemption if policy allows.

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is eligible but lower-priority jobs are ahead; higher-priority workload(s) currently prevent this job from being scheduled.
- Common causes
  - Other queued jobs have higher multifactor priority (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, partition weight, etc.).
  - QOS/association priority settings or recent account usage (fairshare) favor other jobs.
- What to check
  - sprio (shows priority components for queued jobs) and sprio --weights (configured weights).
  - squeue to identify higher-priority jobs on the partition.
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage.
- Typical fixes
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust QOS/priority weights or run under a QOS that allows preemption.
  - Wait — priority factors (age/fairshare) may escalate the job over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node characteristics that are currently not available or usable, so the scheduler cannot allocate them.
- Common causes
  - The job used explicit node requests (e.g., --nodelist, -w, heterogeneous node lists) and those nodes are down/drained/allocated or reserved.
  - A reservation prevents taking those nodes, or the nodes have been placed into maintenance/power-off states.
  - Node feature/constraint mismatch where nodes matching constraints are unavailable.
- What to check
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the exact node request.
  - sinfo (and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons) or sinfo --Node to inspect node states (down/drain/reserved).
  - squeue --reservation=<name> if a reservation might be blocking nodes.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node list or relax constraints.
  - Wait for the nodes to come back (or ask admins to bring nodes up or clear the reservation).
  - If a reservation blocks the nodes, either use a different partition/QOS or coordinate with the reservation owner/admin.

4) QOS limits (pending reasons that indicate limit enforcement)
- What it means
  - The job would exceed a configured resource or count limit on a QOS, account, user association or partition; the scheduler set a limit-related pending reason (e.g., Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp*, MaxTRESPerUser).
- Common causes
  - Per-QOS or partition limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser (GPU/CPU hours or counts), MaxNodes, MaxWall, etc. A job can pend when it would breach a limit unless DenyOnLimit is set (then it would be denied at submission).
  - Hierarchical enforcement: Partition QOS limits are evaluated first by default; job QOS and association limits follow (OverPartQOS can change precedence).
- What to check
  - sacctmgr (sacctmgr list associations / sacctmgr show qos) to inspect QOS and association limits.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the job's QOS/association.
  - Resource Limits documentation to map the pending reason to the exact configured limit name.
- Typical fixes
  - Use a different QOS or partition with sufficient limits.
  - Request limit increases from admins (via sacctmgr).
  - Change the job request (smaller resource request, fewer concurrent jobs) to fit within limits.
  - If DenyOnLimit is set and you keep hitting rejects at submit, adjust the job/QOS or ask admins to change DenyOnLimit.

Short diagnostic checklist you can run (commands)
- scontrol show job <jobid>        # job’s requested resources, QOS, node list
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R"  # queue row + reason
- sinfo -l / sinfo --Node          # partition and node availability, TRES/GRES
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons        # nodes in drain/down and the reasons
- sprio                             # priority breakdown for pending jobs
- sshare                            # fairshare / effective shares
- sacctmgr list qos / sacctmgr show qos  # QOS limits and flags

If you want, tell me one example JOBID and I can show the exact squeue / scontrol fields and the scheduler-assigned pending reason and give a targeted remediation.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Based on the current cluster state, below are concise, doc-backed explanations (what the reason means, common causes, quick checks, and typical fixes) for the pending reasons you asked about. References: Slurm Job Reason Codes, Resource Limits, Priority (multifactor) and QOS docs.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - The scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to place the job (CPUs, memory, GPUs, nodes, sockets, or matching TRES/GRES).
- Common causes
  - No nodes with the requested TRES (e.g., --gres=gpu:...), not enough CPUs or memory on any single node, fragmentation across nodes, or all suitable nodes are already allocated.
  - Constraints like node features (-C / --constraint) or topology/heterogeneous requests that can't be satisfied.
- What to check
  - sinfo to see partition/node idle counts and TRES/GRES availability.
  - squeue to see what is currently running/allocating.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested resources.
- Typical fixes
  - Relax resources/constraints (fewer GPUs, less memory, fewer specific features).
  - Submit with a different partition or different GRES type.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or enable preemption if policy allows.

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is eligible but lower-priority jobs are ahead; higher-priority workload(s) currently prevent this job from being scheduled.
- Common causes
  - Other queued jobs have higher multifactor priority (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, partition weight, etc.).
  - QOS/association priority settings or recent account usage (fairshare) favor other jobs.
- What to check
  - sprio (shows priority components for queued jobs) and sprio --weights (configured weights).
  - squeue to identify higher-priority jobs on the partition.
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage.
- Typical fixes
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust QOS/priority weights or run under a QOS that allows preemption.
  - Wait — priority factors (age/fairshare) may escalate the job over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node characteristics that are currently not available or usable, so the scheduler cannot allocate them.
- Common causes
  - The job used explicit node requests (e.g., --nodelist, -w, heterogeneous node lists) and those nodes are down/drained/allocated or reserved.
  - A reservation prevents taking those nodes, or the nodes have been placed into maintenance/power-off states.
  - Node feature/constraint mismatch where nodes matching constraints are unavailable.
- What to check
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the exact node request.
  - sinfo (and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons) or sinfo --Node to inspect node states (down/drain/reserved).
  - squeue --reservation=<name> if a reservation might be blocking nodes.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node list or relax constraints.
  - Wait for the nodes to come back (or ask admins to bring nodes up or clear the reservation).
  - If a reservation blocks the nodes, either use a different partition/QOS or coordinate with the reservation owner/admin.

4) QOS limits (pending reasons that indicate limit enforcement)
- What it means
  - The job would exceed a configured resource or count limit on a QOS, account, user association or partition; the scheduler set a limit-related pending reason (e.g., Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp*, MaxTRESPerUser).
- Common causes
  - Per-QOS or partition limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser (GPU/CPU hours or counts), MaxNodes, MaxWall, etc. A job can pend when it would breach a limit unless DenyOnLimit is set (then it would be denied at submission).
  - Hierarchical enforcement: Partition QOS limits are evaluated first by default; job QOS and association limits follow (OverPartQOS can change precedence).
- What to check
  - sacctmgr (sacctmgr list associations / sacctmgr show qos) to inspect QOS and association limits.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the job's QOS/association.
  - Resource Limits documentation to map the pending reason to the exact configured limit name.
- Typical fixes
  - Use a different QOS or partition with sufficient limits.
  - Request limit increases from admins (via sacctmgr).
  - Change the job request (smaller resource request, fewer concurrent jobs) to fit within limits.
  - If DenyOnLimit is set and you keep hitting rejects at submit, adjust the job/QOS or ask admins to change DenyOnLimit.

Short diagnostic checklist you can run (commands)
- scontrol show job <jobid>        # job’s requested resources, QOS, node list
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R"  # queue row + reason
- sinfo -l / sinfo --Node          # partition and node availability, TRES/GRES
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons        # nodes in drain/down and the reasons
- sprio                             # priority breakdown for pending jobs
- sshare                            # fairshare / effective shares
- sacctmgr list qos / sacctmgr show qos  # QOS limits and flags

If you want, tell me one example JOBID and I can show the exact squeue / scontrol fields and the scheduler-assigned pending reason and give a targeted remediation.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

After reviewing the Slurm cluster, below are concise, doc-backed explanations (what the reason means, common causes, quick checks, and typical fixes) for the pending reasons you asked about. References: Slurm Job Reason Codes, Resource Limits, Priority (multifactor) and QOS docs.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - The scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to place the job (CPUs, memory, GPUs, nodes, sockets, or matching TRES/GRES).
- Common causes
  - No nodes with the requested TRES (e.g., --gres=gpu:...), not enough CPUs or memory on any single node, fragmentation across nodes, or all suitable nodes are already allocated.
  - Constraints like node features (-C / --constraint) or topology/heterogeneous requests that can't be satisfied.
- What to check
  - sinfo to see partition/node idle counts and TRES/GRES availability.
  - squeue to see what is currently running/allocating.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested resources.
- Typical fixes
  - Relax resources/constraints (fewer GPUs, less memory, fewer specific features).
  - Submit with a different partition or different GRES type.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or enable preemption if policy allows.

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is eligible but lower-priority jobs are ahead; higher-priority workload(s) currently prevent this job from being scheduled.
- Common causes
  - Other queued jobs have higher multifactor priority (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, partition weight, etc.).
  - QOS/association priority settings or recent account usage (fairshare) favor other jobs.
- What to check
  - sprio (shows priority components for queued jobs) and sprio --weights (configured weights).
  - squeue to identify higher-priority jobs on the partition.
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage.
- Typical fixes
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust QOS/priority weights or run under a QOS that allows preemption.
  - Wait — priority factors (age/fairshare) may escalate the job over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node characteristics that are currently not available or usable, so the scheduler cannot allocate them.
- Common causes
  - The job used explicit node requests (e.g., --nodelist, -w, heterogeneous node lists) and those nodes are down/drained/allocated or reserved.
  - A reservation prevents taking those nodes, or the nodes have been placed into maintenance/power-off states.
  - Node feature/constraint mismatch where nodes matching constraints are unavailable.
- What to check
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the exact node request.
  - sinfo (and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons) or sinfo --Node to inspect node states (down/drain/reserved).
  - squeue --reservation=<name> if a reservation might be blocking nodes.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node list or relax constraints.
  - Wait for the nodes to come back (or ask admins to bring nodes up or clear the reservation).
  - If a reservation blocks the nodes, either use a different partition/QOS or coordinate with the reservation owner/admin.

4) QOS limits (pending reasons that indicate limit enforcement)
- What it means
  - The job would exceed a configured resource or count limit on a QOS, account, user association or partition; the scheduler set a limit-related pending reason (e.g., Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp*, MaxTRESPerUser).
- Common causes
  - Per-QOS or partition limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser (GPU/CPU hours or counts), MaxNodes, MaxWall, etc. A job can pend when it would breach a limit unless DenyOnLimit is set (then it would be denied at submission).
  - Hierarchical enforcement: Partition QOS limits are evaluated first by default; job QOS and association limits follow (OverPartQOS can change precedence).
- What to check
  - sacctmgr (sacctmgr list associations / sacctmgr show qos) to inspect QOS and association limits.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the job's QOS/association.
  - Resource Limits documentation to map the pending reason to the exact configured limit name.
- Typical fixes
  - Use a different QOS or partition with sufficient limits.

- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons        # nodes in drain/down and the reasons
- sprio                             # priority breakdown for pending jobs
- sshare                            # fairshare / effective shares
- sacctmgr list qos / sacctmgr show qos  # QOS limits and flags

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None

the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS

- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.

SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin

in order to optimize performance.

and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.

restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished

`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to compare afterok, afterany, afternotok, and singleton dependencies
results.agent_response:
I looked up the official Slurm sbatch/manual docs and summarized the four dependency types you asked about. Short definitions, when they trigger, examples and typical uses:

1) after
- What it means: make the job eligible to start after the specified job(s) have started (i.e., after the referenced job(s) begin execution).
- Triggers: when the referenced job(s) have started running (does not wait for completion).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=after:12345 myjob.sh
- Use case: start something that can run concurrently once a producer has begun (e.g., start a consumer once producer is running), or coordinate start ordering without waiting for completion.

2) afterok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have completed successfully (exit code 0).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have terminated with success (zero exit code).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next-step.sh
- Use case: multi-step workflows where later steps must run only if earlier steps succeed (build → test → deploy).

3) afterany
- What it means: start after the specified job(s) have terminated, regardless of their exit code (success or failure).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have finished in any terminal state.
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 postprocess.sh
- Use case: always-run follow-up tasks (e.g., archive logs or collect metrics) whether the upstream job succeeded or failed.

4) afternotok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have terminated with a non‑zero (failing) exit code.
- Triggers: when any/all referenced jobs have finished and returned a non‑zero exit (i.e., failed).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345 failure_handler.sh
- Use case: run remediation/alerting/cleanup only when an upstream job fails.

5) singleton (special)
- What it means: no job ID is passed; the job is held until all previously submitted jobs with the same user and job name have finished. Ensures only one job with that name/user runs at a time.
- Triggers: the new job becomes eligible after earlier jobs with the same name and user have terminated.
- Example: sbatch --job-name=data_proc --dependency=singleton data_proc.sh
- Use case: serialize repeated submissions of the same job (avoid parallel runs of the same job-name by the same user).

Notes and tips
- Syntax: --dependency=type:jobid[:jobid...] (singleton has no jobid).
- Combine dependencies: you can specify multiple dependencies (comma-separated) to express complex conditions.
- Choose afterok for success-only chaining, afterany when you must always continue, afternotok for failure-only handlers, after when you only need start ordering, and singleton to serialize same-name jobs.
- These definitions come from the sbatch man page / Slurm documentation.

If you want, I can show exact sbatch examples for a concrete workflow (e.g., build→test→deploy with success/failure handlers) or look up how dependencies interact with job arrays. Which would you like?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

I looked up the official Slurm sbatch/manual docs and summarized the four dependency types you asked about. Short definitions, when they trigger, examples and typical uses:

1) after
- What it means: make the job eligible to start after the specified job(s) have started (i.e., after the referenced job(s) begin execution).
- Triggers: when the referenced job(s) have started running (does not wait for completion).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=after:12345 myjob.sh
- Use case: start something that can run concurrently once a producer has begun (e.g., start a consumer once producer is running), or coordinate start ordering without waiting for completion.

2) afterok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have completed successfully (exit code 0).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have terminated with success (zero exit code).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next-step.sh
- Use case: multi-step workflows where later steps must run only if earlier steps succeed (build → test → deploy).

3) afterany
- What it means: start after the specified job(s) have terminated, regardless of their exit code (success or failure).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have finished in any terminal state.
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 postprocess.sh
- Use case: always-run follow-up tasks (e.g., archive logs or collect metrics) whether the upstream job succeeded or failed.

4) afternotok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have terminated with a non‑zero (failing) exit code.
- Triggers: when any/all referenced jobs have finished and returned a non‑zero exit (i.e., failed).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345 failure_handler.sh
- Use case: run remediation/alerting/cleanup only when an upstream job fails.

5) singleton (special)
- What it means: no job ID is passed; the job is held until all previously submitted jobs with the same user and job name have finished. Ensures only one job with that name/user runs at a time.
- Triggers: the new job becomes eligible after earlier jobs with the same name and user have terminated.
- Example: sbatch --job-name=data_proc --dependency=singleton data_proc.sh
- Use case: serialize repeated submissions of the same job (avoid parallel runs of the same job-name by the same user).

Notes and tips
- Syntax: --dependency=type:jobid[:jobid...] (singleton has no jobid).
- Combine dependencies: you can specify multiple dependencies (comma-separated) to express complex conditions.
- Choose afterok for success-only chaining, afterany when you must always continue, afternotok for failure-only handlers, after when you only need start ordering, and singleton to serialize same-name jobs.
- These definitions come from the sbatch man page / Slurm documentation.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
