## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, i looked up the official Slurm sbatch/manual docs and summarized the four dependency types you asked about. Short definitions, when they trigger, examples and typical uses:

1) after
- What it means: make the job eligible to start after the specified job(s) have started (i.e., after the referenced job(s) begin execution).
- Triggers: when the referenced job(s) have started running (does not wait for completion).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=after:12345 myjob.sh
- Use case: start something that can run concurrently once a producer has begun (e.g., start a consumer once producer is running), or coordinate start ordering without waiting for completion.

2) afterok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have completed successfully (exit code 0).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have terminated with success (zero exit code).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next-step.sh
- Use case: multi-step workflows where later steps must run only if earlier steps succeed (build → test → deploy).

3) afterany
- What it means: start after the specified job(s) have terminated, regardless of their exit code (success or failure).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have finished in any terminal state.
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 postprocess.sh
- Use case: always-run follow-up tasks (e.g., archive logs or collect metrics) whether the upstream job succeeded or failed.

4) afternotok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have terminated with a non‑zero (failing) exit code.
- Triggers: when any/all referenced jobs have finished and returned a non‑zero exit (i.e., failed).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345 failure_handler.sh
- Use case: run remediation/alerting/cleanup only when an upstream job fails.

5) singleton (special)
- What it means: no job ID is passed; the job is held until all previously submitted jobs with the same user and job name have finished. Ensures only one job with that name/user runs at a time.
- Triggers: the new job becomes eligible after earlier jobs with the same name and user have terminated.
- Example: sbatch --job-name=data_proc --dependency=singleton data_proc.sh
- Use case: serialize repeated submissions of the same job (avoid parallel runs of the same job-name by the same user).

Notes and tips
- Syntax: --dependency=type:jobid[:jobid...] (singleton has no jobid).
- Combine dependencies: you can specify multiple dependencies (comma-separated) to express complex conditions.
- Choose afterok for success-only chaining, afterany when you must always continue, afternotok for failure-only handlers, after when you only need start ordering, and singleton to serialize same-name jobs.
- These definitions come from the sbatch man page / Slurm documentation.

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.

either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## Slurm Configuration [#SLURM_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html)
PrologFlags=contain must be set in the slurm.conf. This sets up the
"extern" step into which ssh-launched processes will be adopted. You must also
enable the task/cgroup plugin in slurm.conf. See the
[Slurm cgroups guide.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroups.html)
CAUTION This option must be in place before using this module.
The module bases its checks on local steps that have already been launched. Jobs
launched without this option do not have an extern step, so pam_slurm_adopt will
not have access to those jobs.
LaunchParameters=ulimit_pam_adopt will set RLIMIT_RSS in processes
adopted by the external step, similar to tasks running in regular steps.
The UsePAM option in slurm.conf is not related to pam_slurm_adopt.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

1) after
- What it means: make the job eligible to start after the specified job(s) have started (i.e., after the referenced job(s) begin execution).
- Triggers: when the referenced job(s) have started running (does not wait for completion).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=after:12345 myjob.sh
- Use case: start something that can run concurrently once a producer has begun (e.g., start a consumer once producer is running), or coordinate start ordering without waiting for completion.

2) afterok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have completed successfully (exit code 0).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have terminated with success (zero exit code).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next-step.sh
- Use case: multi-step workflows where later steps must run only if earlier steps succeed (build → test → deploy).

3) afterany
- What it means: start after the specified job(s) have terminated, regardless of their exit code (success or failure).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have finished in any terminal state.
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 postprocess.sh
- Use case: always-run follow-up tasks (e.g., archive logs or collect metrics) whether the upstream job succeeded or failed.

4) afternotok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have terminated with a non‑zero (failing) exit code.
- Triggers: when any/all referenced jobs have finished and returned a non‑zero exit (i.e., failed).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345 failure_handler.sh
- Use case: run remediation/alerting/cleanup only when an upstream job fails.

5) singleton (special)
- What it means: no job ID is passed; the job is held until all previously submitted jobs with the same user and job name have finished. Ensures only one job with that name/user runs at a time.
- Triggers: the new job becomes eligible after earlier jobs with the same name and user have terminated.
- Example: sbatch --job-name=data_proc --dependency=singleton data_proc.sh
- Use case: serialize repeated submissions of the same job (avoid parallel runs of the same job-name by the same user).

Notes and tips
- Syntax: --dependency=type:jobid[:jobid...] (singleton has no jobid).
- Combine dependencies: you can specify multiple dependencies (comma-separated) to express complex conditions.
- Choose afterok for success-only chaining, afterany when you must always continue, afternotok for failure-only handlers, after when you only need start ordering, and singleton to serialize same-name jobs.
- These definitions come from the sbatch man page / Slurm documentation.

If you want, I can show exact sbatch examples for a concrete workflow (e.g., build→test→deploy with success/failure handlers) or look up how dependencies interact with job arrays. Which would you like?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV
records defined within the cluster itself.

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Summary — how Slurm orders the queue
- Slurm’s default is the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor). A job’s priority is a weighted sum of multiple factors (age, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, TRES, site, nice, …). The larger the resulting integer, the higher the job is ordered in the queue and the sooner it is eligible to run.

High-level formula (concept)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge  * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X )
  - nice_factor
- Each factor produces a floating value roughly in [0.0, 1.0] (implementation-dependent). The configured PriorityWeight* values scale each factor’s contribution; weights are integers and the final priority is an integer (0 .. 2^32-1).

Fairshare (what it does)
- Purpose: prevent users/accounts that consumed many resources recently from always winning the scheduler. Fairshare reduces priority for heavy recent users and increases it for under-used users.
- It is driven by historical usage tracked per association (user/account), decayed over time by PriorityDecayHalfLife so older usage matters less.
- Key config knobs:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare: how strongly fairshare influences final priority (higher = more influence).
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: how quickly historical usage decays (e.g., 7-0 is 7 days). Smaller half-life → recent use matters more.
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optional periodic reset of usage counters (useful if you want hard resets).
- You can inspect fairshare-related usage with sshare (reports effective shares/usage).

Fair Tree (Fair-share algorithm starting ~19.05)
- Fair Tree is the modern fairshare algorithm used by the multifactor plugin by default.
- Behavior:
  - Hierarchical: it respects account/user/account-group hierarchies so that if parent account A ranks ahead of sibling B, then all children of A rank ahead of all children of B. That prevents accidental local re-ordering inside an account that would hurt cross-account fairness.
  - Produces stable, rank-based fairshare factors and avoids precision issues and undesirable inversions that could occur in the older Classic algorithm.
  - Tie-handling is explicit and deterministic (but ties are permitted).
- Use when you have hierarchical accounting (accounts with subaccounts) and want consistent inter-account ordering.

Configured priority weights (how they change behavior)
- Weights are the administrator’s control knobs; they scale each factor’s effect on final priority:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare (commonly big, e.g., 10000): strong influence of fairshare.
  - PriorityWeightAge (e.g., 1000): lets jobs that waited a long time climb the queue (prevents starvation).
  - PriorityWeightJobSize (e.g., 1000): can favor smaller or larger jobs depending on how job_size_factor is defined.
  - PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS etc.: let you prefer jobs in particular partitions or QOS classes.
  - TRES weights (TRESWeight) let CPU, GPU, memory costs change priority (e.g., deprioritize GPU-heavy jobs).
- Example numeric intuition:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare = 10000 and fairshare_factor for alice = 0.8, that contributes ≈ 8000 points.
  - If PriorityWeightAge = 1000 and age_factor = 0.5, that contributes ≈ 500 points.
  - Final priority is the sum of all such contributions (site + assoc + fairshare + …) minus nice_factor.
- Practical tuning guidance:
  - If fairness matters most, make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to other weights.
  - If you want long-waiting jobs to eventually run despite fairshare, increase PriorityWeightAge.
  - If small jobs should be favored to improve throughput, tune PriorityWeightJobSize or PriorityFavorSmall.
  - Use PriorityDecayHalfLife to define how much history you want (short half-life = recent use matters; long half-life = long-term quotas).
  - Avoid making all weights zero or heavily skewing one factor unless intentional.

Diagnostics and inspection
- sprio: shows per-job priority and breakdown by factor (useful to see which factors contribute most).
- sshare: shows usage and effective shares for accounts/users (helps understand fairshare state).
- scontrol show config: view the Priority* settings in slurm.conf.
- sdiag and scheduler logs: for deeper scheduler behavior and backfill diagnostics.

Common interactions and gotchas
- Fairshare vs Age: a very large fairshare weight can cause a new or low-usage user’s job to jump ahead of long-waiting jobs unless you also raise PriorityWeightAge.
- TRES weights: assigning large positive weights to a TRES increases priority for jobs consuming that TRES (or the inverse, depending on factor setup); be careful when combining TRES weights with fairshare.
- QOS and partition factors can override account-level fairness for special classes (e.g., interactive or emergency QOS).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife = 0 disables decay (usage never decays) so the usage counters must be reset periodically with PriorityUsageResetPeriod or manually.
- Priority calculations use integers and limited precision; extremely large or tiny weights can lead to unintuitive ordering—test changes in a staging environment.

If you want, I can:
- show example slurm.conf snippets with recommended starting weights, or
- explain how to interpret sprio output for one or more real jobs, or
- suggest a tuning recipe for a cluster profile (research, bursty GPU, or throughput-focused). Which would you like?

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, summary — how Slurm orders the queue
- Slurm’s default is the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor). A job’s priority is a weighted sum of multiple factors (age, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, TRES, site, nice, …). The larger the resulting integer, the higher the job is ordered in the queue and the sooner it is eligible to run.

High-level formula (concept)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge  * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X )
  - nice_factor
- Each factor produces a floating value roughly in [0.0, 1.0] (implementation-dependent). The configured PriorityWeight* values scale each factor’s contribution; weights are integers and the final priority is an integer (0 .. 2^32-1).

Fairshare (what it does)
- Purpose: prevent users/accounts that consumed many resources recently from always winning the scheduler. Fairshare reduces priority for heavy recent users and increases it for under-used users.
- It is driven by historical usage tracked per association (user/account), decayed over time by PriorityDecayHalfLife so older usage matters less.
- Key config knobs:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare: how strongly fairshare influences final priority (higher = more influence).
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: how quickly historical usage decays (e.g., 7-0 is 7 days). Smaller half-life → recent use matters more.
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optional periodic reset of usage counters (useful if you want hard resets).
- You can inspect fairshare-related usage with sshare (reports effective shares/usage).

Fair Tree (Fair-share algorithm starting ~19.05)
- Fair Tree is the modern fairshare algorithm used by the multifactor plugin by default.
- Behavior:
  - Hierarchical: it respects account/user/account-group hierarchies so that if parent account A ranks ahead of sibling B, then all children of A rank ahead of all children of B. That prevents accidental local re-ordering inside an account that would hurt cross-account fairness.
  - Produces stable, rank-based fairshare factors and avoids precision issues and undesirable inversions that could occur in the older Classic algorithm.
  - Tie-handling is explicit and deterministic (but ties are permitted).
- Use when you have hierarchical accounting (accounts with subaccounts) and want consistent inter-account ordering.

Configured priority weights (how they change behavior)
- Weights are the administrator’s control knobs; they scale each factor’s effect on final priority:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare (commonly big, e.g., 10000): strong influence of fairshare.
  - PriorityWeightAge (e.g., 1000): lets jobs that waited a long time climb the queue (prevents starvation).
  - PriorityWeightJobSize (e.g., 1000): can favor smaller or larger jobs depending on how job_size_factor is defined.
  - PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS etc.: let you prefer jobs in particular partitions or QOS classes.
  - TRES weights (TRESWeight) let CPU, GPU, memory costs change priority (e.g., deprioritize GPU-heavy jobs).
- Example numeric intuition:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare = 10000 and fairshare_factor for alice = 0.8, that contributes ≈ 8000 points.
  - If PriorityWeightAge = 1000 and age_factor = 0.5, that contributes ≈ 500 points.
  - Final priority is the sum of all such contributions (site + assoc + fairshare + …) minus nice_factor.
- Practical tuning guidance:
  - If fairness matters most, make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to other weights.
  - If you want long-waiting jobs to eventually run despite fairshare, increase PriorityWeightAge.
  - If small jobs should be favored to improve throughput, tune PriorityWeightJobSize or PriorityFavorSmall.
  - Use PriorityDecayHalfLife to define how much history you want (short half-life = recent use matters; long half-life = long-term quotas).
  - Avoid making all weights zero or heavily skewing one factor unless intentional.

Diagnostics and inspection
- sprio: shows per-job priority and breakdown by factor (useful to see which factors contribute most).
- sshare: shows usage and effective shares for accounts/users (helps understand fairshare state).
- scontrol show config: view the Priority* settings in slurm.conf.
- sdiag and scheduler logs: for deeper scheduler behavior and backfill diagnostics.

Common interactions and gotchas
- Fairshare vs Age: a very large fairshare weight can cause a new or low-usage user’s job to jump ahead of long-waiting jobs unless you also raise PriorityWeightAge.
- TRES weights: assigning large positive weights to a TRES increases priority for jobs consuming that TRES (or the inverse, depending on factor setup); be careful when combining TRES weights with fairshare.
- QOS and partition factors can override account-level fairness for special classes (e.g., interactive or emergency QOS).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife = 0 disables decay (usage never decays) so the usage counters must be reset periodically with PriorityUsageResetPeriod or manually.
- Priority calculations use integers and limited precision; extremely large or tiny weights can lead to unintuitive ordering—test changes in a staging environment.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain burst buffer directives and stage-in or stage-out behavior
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, doc-based summary of Slurm burst-buffer directives and how stage‑in / stage‑out behave. I used the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) as the source.

What burst‑buffer directives are and where to put them
- Burst‑buffer directives are comment lines placed in batch scripts (they begin with #) that tell Slurm’s burst‑buffer plugin what storage to allocate and what data movement to run for the job.
- Directives may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- The same directives can be supplied on the command line: sbatch/srun/salloc accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (a file of burst‑buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers; --bbf points to a file formatted like the script directives.

Plugin differences (affects directive names and exact fields)
- DataWarp plugin: common directive names are #DW (job‑specific burst buffer directives) and #BB (used for persistent‑buffer create/destroy with DataWarp). DataWarp has extra, vendor-specific options; consult DataWarp docs for details.
- Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable via burst_buffer.conf). The lua plugin is generic and relies on a site-provided burst_buffer.lua implementation for exact behavior.
- Exact token names and the allowed fields (stage_in, stage_out, capacity, pool, access, type, etc.) depend on the plugin; the guide documents the general fields but plugin docs (or your cluster’s burst_buffer.lua) define the precise syntax.

Job vs persistent burst buffers
- Job‑specific burst buffers: allocated for a job and released afterwards. Many plugins require a capacity; if a job requests a job‑specific buffer without specifying capacity the job may be rejected.
- Persistent burst buffers: (DataWarp only) may be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent and survive beyond a single job.

Stage‑in / stage‑out behavior and lifecycle
- Staging occurs at defined points in the job lifecycle. Slurm tracks burst buffer states such as: pending, allocating, allocated, staging‑in, staged‑in, pre‑run, running, staging‑out, post‑run, teardown, complete (these appear in the BurstBufferState shown by scontrol show job).
- Stage‑in: data movement from the backing filesystem into the allocated burst buffer is run before the job enters the running state (the job will wait for stage‑in to finish). After successful stage‑in the job proceeds to pre‑run / run.
- Stage‑out: after the job finishes running, post‑run hooks run to move data from the burst buffer back to the target filesystem (stage‑out). Stage‑out runs during the job’s post‑run / teardown phases (the job’s completion may be delayed until stage‑out finishes).
- Timeouts: plugins expose timeout controls (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout in the burst‑buffer configuration/status). If staging times out or fails, the burst‑buffer plugin’s behavior depends on plugin/config (failure can lead to teardown or teardown‑fail states).
- Heterogeneous jobs: burst‑buffer hooks are run per job component that has directives — components without directives do not get burst‑buffer stages.

Typical directive components (conceptual, plugin-specific syntax varies)
- capacity=<size> (required for many job‑specific buffers)
- pool=<pool-name> (which pool to allocate from)
- stage_in=<source>:<bb-path> (request staging of source data into the buffer)
- stage_out=<bb-path>:<destination> (request staging of results out of the buffer)
- access=, type=, link/move/copy semantics — some plugins support copy vs link vs move semantics; exact names/options are plugin dependent

How to check status / diagnostics
- scontrol show job <jobid> includes a BurstBufferState field for jobs that requested burst buffers.
- scontrol show burst (or sview Burst Buffer tab) shows configured burst pools, allocated buffers, per‑job allocations, and plugin timeouts (StageInTimeout / StageOutTimeout).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf increases burst‑buffer logging for debugging.

Practical notes and best practices
- Because stage‑in must finish before the job runs, large stage‑in operations can delay job start — account for that in scheduling and timeouts.
- Stage‑out can extend job completion time (post‑run); set StageOutTimeout appropriately and avoid leaving long, unneeded data in buffers.
- Request only the capacity you need; burst‑buffer size may affect scheduling.
- For cluster‑specific behavior and exact directive syntax/examples, consult your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf, burst_buffer.lua (if used), and the DataWarp/Lua plugin documentation in the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide.

Where to read the exact syntax
- See the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) for:
  - job submission directives and command‑line options (--bb / --bbf),
  - DataWarp and Lua plugin sections,
  - persistent buffer create/destroy (#BB create_persistent ...),
  - the list of burst buffer states and example scontrol output.

If you want, I can:
- paste the exact directive examples from the guide for the plugin your site uses (DataWarp or Lua), or
- check your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf and burst_buffer.lua (if you give me the file paths) to show the exact directive name and supported fields your cluster expects. Which would you prefer?

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a

- post-run

What burst‑buffer directives are and where to put them
- Burst‑buffer directives are comment lines placed in batch scripts (they begin with #) that tell Slurm’s burst‑buffer plugin what storage to allocate and what data movement to run for the job.
- Directives may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- The same directives can be supplied on the command line: sbatch/srun/salloc accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (a file of burst‑buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers; --bbf points to a file formatted like the script directives.

Plugin differences (affects directive names and exact fields)
- DataWarp plugin: common directive names are #DW (job‑specific burst buffer directives) and #BB (used for persistent‑buffer create/destroy with DataWarp). DataWarp has extra, vendor-specific options; consult DataWarp docs for details.
- Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable via burst_buffer.conf). The lua plugin is generic and relies on a site-provided burst_buffer.lua implementation for exact behavior.
- Exact token names and the allowed fields (stage_in, stage_out, capacity, pool, access, type, etc.) depend on the plugin; the guide documents the general fields but plugin docs (or your cluster’s burst_buffer.lua) define the precise syntax.

Job vs persistent burst buffers
- Job‑specific burst buffers: allocated for a job and released afterwards. Many plugins require a capacity; if a job requests a job‑specific buffer without specifying capacity the job may be rejected.
- Persistent burst buffers: (DataWarp only) may be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent and survive beyond a single job.

Stage‑in / stage‑out behavior and lifecycle
- Staging occurs at defined points in the job lifecycle. Slurm tracks burst buffer states such as: pending, allocating, allocated, staging‑in, staged‑in, pre‑run, running, staging‑out, post‑run, teardown, complete (these appear in the BurstBufferState shown by scontrol show job).
- Stage‑in: data movement from the backing filesystem into the allocated burst buffer is run before the job enters the running state (the job will wait for stage‑in to finish). After successful stage‑in the job proceeds to pre‑run / run.
- Stage‑out: after the job finishes running, post‑run hooks run to move data from the burst buffer back to the target filesystem (stage‑out). Stage‑out runs during the job’s post‑run / teardown phases (the job’s completion may be delayed until stage‑out finishes).
- Timeouts: plugins expose timeout controls (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout in the burst‑buffer configuration/status). If staging times out or fails, the burst‑buffer plugin’s behavior depends on plugin/config (failure can lead to teardown or teardown‑fail states).
- Heterogeneous jobs: burst‑buffer hooks are run per job component that has directives — components without directives do not get burst‑buffer stages.

Typical directive components (conceptual, plugin-specific syntax varies)
- capacity=<size> (required for many job‑specific buffers)
- pool=<pool-name> (which pool to allocate from)
- stage_in=<source>:<bb-path> (request staging of source data into the buffer)
- stage_out=<bb-path>:<destination> (request staging of results out of the buffer)
- access=, type=, link/move/copy semantics — some plugins support copy vs link vs move semantics; exact names/options are plugin dependent

How to check status / diagnostics
- scontrol show job <jobid> includes a BurstBufferState field for jobs that requested burst buffers.
- scontrol show burst (or sview Burst Buffer tab) shows configured burst pools, allocated buffers, per‑job allocations, and plugin timeouts (StageInTimeout / StageOutTimeout).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf increases burst‑buffer logging for debugging.

Practical notes and best practices
- Because stage‑in must finish before the job runs, large stage‑in operations can delay job start — account for that in scheduling and timeouts.
- Stage‑out can extend job completion time (post‑run); set StageOutTimeout appropriately and avoid leaving long, unneeded data in buffers.
- Request only the capacity you need; burst‑buffer size may affect scheduling.
- For cluster‑specific behavior and exact directive syntax/examples, consult your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf, burst_buffer.lua (if used), and the DataWarp/Lua plugin documentation in the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide.

Where to read the exact syntax
- See the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) for:
  - job submission directives and command‑line options (--bb / --bbf),
  - DataWarp and Lua plugin sections,
  - persistent buffer create/destroy (#BB create_persistent ...),
  - the list of burst buffer states and example scontrol output.

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

## Advanced Reservations [#reservation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Burst buffer resources can be placed in an advanced reservation using the
BurstBuffer option.
The argument consists of four elements:
`[plugin:][pool:]#[units]`
- plugin is the burst buffer plugin name, currently either "datawarp" or "lua".
- pool specifies a burst buffer resource pool. If "type" is not specified, the number is a measure of storage space.
- # (meaning number) should be replaced with a positive integer.
- units has the same format as the suffix of capacity in the [Job Submission Commands](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html) section.
Jobs using this reservation are not restricted to these burst buffer
resources, but may use these reserved resources plus any which are generally
available. Some examples follow.

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

- pending

- allocated
- deleting
- deleted

- staged-in
- pre-run
- alloc-revoke

- suspended
- post-run
- staging-out
- teardown
- teardown-fail
- complete

a burst buffer. The states `allocating`, `allocated`,

state `alloc-revoke` happens if a failure in Slurm's select plugin

Based on the current cluster state, below is a concise, doc-based summary of Slurm burst-buffer directives and how stage‑in / stage‑out behave. I used the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) as the source.

What burst‑buffer directives are and where to put them
- Burst‑buffer directives are comment lines placed in batch scripts (they begin with #) that tell Slurm’s burst‑buffer plugin what storage to allocate and what data movement to run for the job.
- Directives may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- The same directives can be supplied on the command line: sbatch/srun/salloc accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (a file of burst‑buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers; --bbf points to a file formatted like the script directives.

Plugin differences (affects directive names and exact fields)
- DataWarp plugin: common directive names are #DW (job‑specific burst buffer directives) and #BB (used for persistent‑buffer create/destroy with DataWarp). DataWarp has extra, vendor-specific options; consult DataWarp docs for details.
- Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable via burst_buffer.conf). The lua plugin is generic and relies on a site-provided burst_buffer.lua implementation for exact behavior.
- Exact token names and the allowed fields (stage_in, stage_out, capacity, pool, access, type, etc.) depend on the plugin; the guide documents the general fields but plugin docs (or your cluster’s burst_buffer.lua) define the precise syntax.

Job vs persistent burst buffers
- Job‑specific burst buffers: allocated for a job and released afterwards. Many plugins require a capacity; if a job requests a job‑specific buffer without specifying capacity the job may be rejected.
- Persistent burst buffers: (DataWarp only) may be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent and survive beyond a single job.

Stage‑in / stage‑out behavior and lifecycle
- Staging occurs at defined points in the job lifecycle. Slurm tracks burst buffer states such as: pending, allocating, allocated, staging‑in, staged‑in, pre‑run, running, staging‑out, post‑run, teardown, complete (these appear in the BurstBufferState shown by scontrol show job).
- Stage‑in: data movement from the backing filesystem into the allocated burst buffer is run before the job enters the running state (the job will wait for stage‑in to finish). After successful stage‑in the job proceeds to pre‑run / run.
- Stage‑out: after the job finishes running, post‑run hooks run to move data from the burst buffer back to the target filesystem (stage‑out). Stage‑out runs during the job’s post‑run / teardown phases (the job’s completion may be delayed until stage‑out finishes).
- Timeouts: plugins expose timeout controls (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout in the burst‑buffer configuration/status). If staging times out or fails, the burst‑buffer plugin’s behavior depends on plugin/config (failure can lead to teardown or teardown‑fail states).
- Heterogeneous jobs: burst‑buffer hooks are run per job component that has directives — components without directives do not get burst‑buffer stages.

Typical directive components (conceptual, plugin-specific syntax varies)
- capacity=<size> (required for many job‑specific buffers)
- pool=<pool-name> (which pool to allocate from)
- stage_in=<source>:<bb-path> (request staging of source data into the buffer)
- stage_out=<bb-path>:<destination> (request staging of results out of the buffer)
- access=, type=, link/move/copy semantics — some plugins support copy vs link vs move semantics; exact names/options are plugin dependent

How to check status / diagnostics
- scontrol show job <jobid> includes a BurstBufferState field for jobs that requested burst buffers.
- scontrol show burst (or sview Burst Buffer tab) shows configured burst pools, allocated buffers, per‑job allocations, and plugin timeouts (StageInTimeout / StageOutTimeout).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf increases burst‑buffer logging for debugging.

Practical notes and best practices
- Because stage‑in must finish before the job runs, large stage‑in operations can delay job start — account for that in scheduling and timeouts.
- Stage‑out can extend job completion time (post‑run); set StageOutTimeout appropriately and avoid leaving long, unneeded data in buffers.
- Request only the capacity you need; burst‑buffer size may affect scheduling.
- For cluster‑specific behavior and exact directive syntax/examples, consult your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf, burst_buffer.lua (if used), and the DataWarp/Lua plugin documentation in the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide.

Where to read the exact syntax
- See the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) for:

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

BurstBuffer option.

resources, but may use these reserved resources plus any which are generally

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

After reviewing the Slurm cluster, below is a concise, doc-based summary of Slurm burst-buffer directives and how stage‑in / stage‑out behave. I used the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) as the source.

What burst‑buffer directives are and where to put them
- Burst‑buffer directives are comment lines placed in batch scripts (they begin with #) that tell Slurm’s burst‑buffer plugin what storage to allocate and what data movement to run for the job.
- Directives may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- The same directives can be supplied on the command line: sbatch/srun/salloc accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (a file of burst‑buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers; --bbf points to a file formatted like the script directives.

Plugin differences (affects directive names and exact fields)
- DataWarp plugin: common directive names are #DW (job‑specific burst buffer directives) and #BB (used for persistent‑buffer create/destroy with DataWarp). DataWarp has extra, vendor-specific options; consult DataWarp docs for details.
- Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable via burst_buffer.conf). The lua plugin is generic and relies on a site-provided burst_buffer.lua implementation for exact behavior.
- Exact token names and the allowed fields (stage_in, stage_out, capacity, pool, access, type, etc.) depend on the plugin; the guide documents the general fields but plugin docs (or your cluster’s burst_buffer.lua) define the precise syntax.

Job vs persistent burst buffers
- Job‑specific burst buffers: allocated for a job and released afterwards. Many plugins require a capacity; if a job requests a job‑specific buffer without specifying capacity the job may be rejected.
- Persistent burst buffers: (DataWarp only) may be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent and survive beyond a single job.

Stage‑in / stage‑out behavior and lifecycle
- Staging occurs at defined points in the job lifecycle. Slurm tracks burst buffer states such as: pending, allocating, allocated, staging‑in, staged‑in, pre‑run, running, staging‑out, post‑run, teardown, complete (these appear in the BurstBufferState shown by scontrol show job).
- Stage‑in: data movement from the backing filesystem into the allocated burst buffer is run before the job enters the running state (the job will wait for stage‑in to finish). After successful stage‑in the job proceeds to pre‑run / run.
- Stage‑out: after the job finishes running, post‑run hooks run to move data from the burst buffer back to the target filesystem (stage‑out). Stage‑out runs during the job’s post‑run / teardown phases (the job’s completion may be delayed until stage‑out finishes).
- Timeouts: plugins expose timeout controls (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout in the burst‑buffer configuration/status). If staging times out or fails, the burst‑buffer plugin’s behavior depends on plugin/config (failure can lead to teardown or teardown‑fail states).
- Heterogeneous jobs: burst‑buffer hooks are run per job component that has directives — components without directives do not get burst‑buffer stages.

Typical directive components (conceptual, plugin-specific syntax varies)
- capacity=<size> (required for many job‑specific buffers)
- pool=<pool-name> (which pool to allocate from)
- stage_in=<source>:<bb-path> (request staging of source data into the buffer)
- stage_out=<bb-path>:<destination> (request staging of results out of the buffer)
- access=, type=, link/move/copy semantics — some plugins support copy vs link vs move semantics; exact names/options are plugin dependent

How to check status / diagnostics
- scontrol show job <jobid> includes a BurstBufferState field for jobs that requested burst buffers.
- scontrol show burst (or sview Burst Buffer tab) shows configured burst pools, allocated buffers, per‑job allocations, and plugin timeouts (StageInTimeout / StageOutTimeout).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf increases burst‑buffer logging for debugging.

Practical notes and best practices
- Because stage‑in must finish before the job runs, large stage‑in operations can delay job start — account for that in scheduling and timeouts.
- Stage‑out can extend job completion time (post‑run); set StageOutTimeout appropriately and avoid leaving long, unneeded data in buffers.
- Request only the capacity you need; burst‑buffer size may affect scheduling.
- For cluster‑specific behavior and exact directive syntax/examples, consult your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf, burst_buffer.lua (if used), and the DataWarp/Lua plugin documentation in the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide.

Where to read the exact syntax
- See the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) for:
  - job submission directives and command‑line options (--bb / --bbf),
  - DataWarp and Lua plugin sections,
  - persistent buffer create/destroy (#BB create_persistent ...),
  - the list of burst buffer states and example scontrol output.

- paste the exact directive examples from the guide for the plugin your site uses (DataWarp or Lua), or
- check your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf and burst_buffer.lua (if you give me the file paths) to show the exact directive name and supported fields your cluster expects. Which would you prefer?

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

Burst buffer resources can be placed in an advanced reservation using the
BurstBuffer option.
The argument consists of four elements:
`[plugin:][pool:]#[units]`

- pool specifies a burst buffer resource pool. If "type" is not specified, the number is a measure of storage space.

- units has the same format as the suffix of capacity in the [Job Submission Commands](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html) section.

resources, but may use these reserved resources plus any which are generally
available. Some examples follow.

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

These are the different possible burst buffer states:
- pending

- allocated
- deleting
- deleted
- staging-in
- staged-in

- alloc-revoke

- suspended
- post-run
- staging-out
- teardown
- teardown-fail
- complete

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain pending reasons Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, and QOS limits
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four common pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, how to diagnose them, and common ways to resolve them.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - Slurm could not find sufficient free resources that match the job request (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, or node features/constraints). This includes cases where no single node satisfies a per‑node request (e.g., --mem-per-cpu, --ntasks-per-node) or where the requested combination of resources is not available.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (look at ReqTRES, NumNodes, MinNodes, NodeList/Constraints).
  - See cluster/node availability: sinfo -Nel (per-node free/alloc counts), sinfo (partition summary).
  - Check queue rows: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %t %R %C %m" (reason column, requested resources).
- Typical fixes
  - Reduce resources requested (fewer CPUs, less memory, fewer GPUs, smaller node count).
  - Remove or relax constraints/--constraint/--nodelist/--exclude that force specific nodes.
  - Use a different partition with suitable nodes.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask users/admins to free nodes.
  - For per‑node packing problems, change job layout (--ntasks-per-node, --nodes).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The scheduler found one or more higher‑priority jobs which must run before this job. Slurm reports the first encountered blocking reason as "Priority".
- How to diagnose
  - Show job priority values: scontrol show job <jobid> (Priority field).
  - Inspect priority factors and queue ordering: sprio (or sprio -l / sprio -u <user>), sshare (fairshare usage).
  - Look for many older/higher‑QOS jobs in the same partition: squeue -p <partition> --sort=-p (or sort by priority/age).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit with a higher QOS (if permitted) or ask admin to adjust QOS/priority.
  - Reduce job size/time so it is scheduled sooner by the policy.
  - Wait—priority often resolves as higher priority jobs finish or as the job ages/fairshare changes.
  - Admin actions: change priority weights, adjust fairshare or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The specific nodes requested by the job (via --nodelist, --exclude, or a constraint that pins nodes) are not available for allocation (they may be DOWN, DRAINED, allocated to other jobs, in a reservation, or otherwise unavailable).
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (NodeList, Exclude, Constraint).
  - Check node states: sinfo -Nel or sinfo --Node (or sinfo_reasons to list down/drain nodes and reasons).
  - For a named node: scontrol show node <nodename> to see state/reason.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node requests or exclusions so the scheduler can choose available nodes.
  - Choose a different partition without the unavailable nodes.
  - Wait for the named nodes to come back online or be released from other jobs.
  - If nodes are down/drained, contact the cluster admin to repair/bring them back.

4) QOS limits (jobs blocked by QOS/account limits)
- What it means
  - The job is blocked because it would violate a QOS or association/account limit. Slurm reason codes related to QOS/limits include Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp, AssocMax and similar. Limits can be per‑QOS, per‑user, per‑account, or TRES (CPU/GPU/time) caps.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job fields: scontrol show job <jobid> (QOS, Account, ReqTRES).
  - Check accounting/association limits: sacctmgr show assoc / sacctmgr list associations (or ask admin to run those).
  - See fairshare/usage: sshare and sprio may help show why QOS choice affects priority.
  - The squeue reason text will often indicate the specific limit name (e.g., MaxJobsPerUser).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit under a different QOS or account with higher limits (if you have access).
  - Reduce requested resources/time to stay within the QOS limits.
  - Wait until other jobs reduce your account's current usage (free up slots).
  - Request admin changes to the QOS/account limits (this is an administrative change).

Notes and troubleshooting tips
- Only one pending reason is shown (the reason encountered during scheduling); there can be multiple underlying causes. If you need the exact, low‑level scheduler decision you can combine scontrol show job <id>, sprio, sshare, and sinfo.
- Useful quick commands: squeue -j <id> -o "%i %P %u %t %R %l %M" ; scontrol show job <id> ; sinfo -Nel ; sprio ; sshare ; sacctmgr show assoc.
- If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact squeue/scontrol outputs you should check and what they likely mean.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

trials.agent_response:
Below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four common pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, how to diagnose them, and common ways to resolve them.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - Slurm could not find sufficient free resources that match the job request (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, or node features/constraints). This includes cases where no single node satisfies a per‑node request (e.g., --mem-per-cpu, --ntasks-per-node) or where the requested combination of resources is not available.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (look at ReqTRES, NumNodes, MinNodes, NodeList/Constraints).
  - See cluster/node availability: sinfo -Nel (per-node free/alloc counts), sinfo (partition summary).
  - Check queue rows: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %t %R %C %m" (reason column, requested resources).
- Typical fixes
  - Reduce resources requested (fewer CPUs, less memory, fewer GPUs, smaller node count).
  - Remove or relax constraints/--constraint/--nodelist/--exclude that force specific nodes.
  - Use a different partition with suitable nodes.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask users/admins to free nodes.
  - For per‑node packing problems, change job layout (--ntasks-per-node, --nodes).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The scheduler found one or more higher‑priority jobs which must run before this job. Slurm reports the first encountered blocking reason as "Priority".
- How to diagnose
  - Show job priority values: scontrol show job <jobid> (Priority field).
  - Inspect priority factors and queue ordering: sprio (or sprio -l / sprio -u <user>), sshare (fairshare usage).
  - Look for many older/higher‑QOS jobs in the same partition: squeue -p <partition> --sort=-p (or sort by priority/age).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit with a higher QOS (if permitted) or ask admin to adjust QOS/priority.
  - Reduce job size/time so it is scheduled sooner by the policy.
  - Wait—priority often resolves as higher priority jobs finish or as the job ages/fairshare changes.
  - Admin actions: change priority weights, adjust fairshare or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The specific nodes requested by the job (via --nodelist, --exclude, or a constraint that pins nodes) are not available for allocation (they may be DOWN, DRAINED, allocated to other jobs, in a reservation, or otherwise unavailable).
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (NodeList, Exclude, Constraint).
  - Check node states: sinfo -Nel or sinfo --Node (or sinfo_reasons to list down/drain nodes and reasons).
  - For a named node: scontrol show node <nodename> to see state/reason.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node requests or exclusions so the scheduler can choose available nodes.
  - Choose a different partition without the unavailable nodes.
  - Wait for the named nodes to come back online or be released from other jobs.
  - If nodes are down/drained, contact the cluster admin to repair/bring them back.

4) QOS limits (jobs blocked by QOS/account limits)
- What it means
  - The job is blocked because it would violate a QOS or association/account limit. Slurm reason codes related to QOS/limits include Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp, AssocMax and similar. Limits can be per‑QOS, per‑user, per‑account, or TRES (CPU/GPU/time) caps.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job fields: scontrol show job <jobid> (QOS, Account, ReqTRES).
  - Check accounting/association limits: sacctmgr show assoc / sacctmgr list associations (or ask admin to run those).
  - See fairshare/usage: sshare and sprio may help show why QOS choice affects priority.

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One

defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four common pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, how to diagnose them, and common ways to resolve them.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - Slurm could not find sufficient free resources that match the job request (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, or node features/constraints). This includes cases where no single node satisfies a per‑node request (e.g., --mem-per-cpu, --ntasks-per-node) or where the requested combination of resources is not available.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (look at ReqTRES, NumNodes, MinNodes, NodeList/Constraints).
  - See cluster/node availability: sinfo -Nel (per-node free/alloc counts), sinfo (partition summary).
  - Check queue rows: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %t %R %C %m" (reason column, requested resources).
- Typical fixes
  - Reduce resources requested (fewer CPUs, less memory, fewer GPUs, smaller node count).
  - Remove or relax constraints/--constraint/--nodelist/--exclude that force specific nodes.
  - Use a different partition with suitable nodes.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask users/admins to free nodes.
  - For per‑node packing problems, change job layout (--ntasks-per-node, --nodes).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The scheduler found one or more higher‑priority jobs which must run before this job. Slurm reports the first encountered blocking reason as "Priority".
- How to diagnose
  - Show job priority values: scontrol show job <jobid> (Priority field).
  - Inspect priority factors and queue ordering: sprio (or sprio -l / sprio -u <user>), sshare (fairshare usage).
  - Look for many older/higher‑QOS jobs in the same partition: squeue -p <partition> --sort=-p (or sort by priority/age).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit with a higher QOS (if permitted) or ask admin to adjust QOS/priority.
  - Reduce job size/time so it is scheduled sooner by the policy.
  - Wait—priority often resolves as higher priority jobs finish or as the job ages/fairshare changes.
  - Admin actions: change priority weights, adjust fairshare or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The specific nodes requested by the job (via --nodelist, --exclude, or a constraint that pins nodes) are not available for allocation (they may be DOWN, DRAINED, allocated to other jobs, in a reservation, or otherwise unavailable).
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (NodeList, Exclude, Constraint).
  - Check node states: sinfo -Nel or sinfo --Node (or sinfo_reasons to list down/drain nodes and reasons).
  - For a named node: scontrol show node <nodename> to see state/reason.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node requests or exclusions so the scheduler can choose available nodes.
  - Choose a different partition without the unavailable nodes.
  - Wait for the named nodes to come back online or be released from other jobs.
  - If nodes are down/drained, contact the cluster admin to repair/bring them back.

4) QOS limits (jobs blocked by QOS/account limits)
- What it means
  - The job is blocked because it would violate a QOS or association/account limit. Slurm reason codes related to QOS/limits include Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp, AssocMax and similar. Limits can be per‑QOS, per‑user, per‑account, or TRES (CPU/GPU/time) caps.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job fields: scontrol show job <jobid> (QOS, Account, ReqTRES).
  - Check accounting/association limits: sacctmgr show assoc / sacctmgr list associations (or ask admin to run those).
  - See fairshare/usage: sshare and sprio may help show why QOS choice affects priority.
  - The squeue reason text will often indicate the specific limit name (e.g., MaxJobsPerUser).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit under a different QOS or account with higher limits (if you have access).
  - Reduce requested resources/time to stay within the QOS limits.
  - Wait until other jobs reduce your account's current usage (free up slots).
  - Request admin changes to the QOS/account limits (this is an administrative change).

Notes and troubleshooting tips
- Only one pending reason is shown (the reason encountered during scheduling); there can be multiple underlying causes. If you need the exact, low‑level scheduler decision you can combine scontrol show job <id>, sprio, sshare, and sinfo.
- Useful quick commands: squeue -j <id> -o "%i %P %u %t %R %l %M" ; scontrol show job <id> ; sinfo -Nel ; sprio ; sshare ; sacctmgr show assoc.
- If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact squeue/scontrol outputs you should check and what they likely mean.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Snippet:
# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four common pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, how to diagnose them, and common ways to resolve them.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - Slurm could not find sufficient free resources that match the job request (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, or node features/constraints). This includes cases where no single node satisfies a per‑node request (e.g., --mem-per-cpu, --ntasks-per-node) or where the requested combination of resources is not available.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (look at ReqTRES, NumNodes, MinNodes, NodeList/Constraints).
  - See cluster/node availability: sinfo -Nel (per-node free/alloc counts), sinfo (partition summary).
  - Check queue rows: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %t %R %C %m" (reason column, requested resources).
- Typical fixes
  - Reduce resources requested (fewer CPUs, less memory, fewer GPUs, smaller node count).
  - Remove or relax constraints/--constraint/--nodelist/--exclude that force specific nodes.
  - Use a different partition with suitable nodes.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask users/admins to free nodes.
  - For per‑node packing problems, change job layout (--ntasks-per-node, --nodes).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The scheduler found one or more higher‑priority jobs which must run before this job. Slurm reports the first encountered blocking reason as "Priority".
- How to diagnose
  - Show job priority values: scontrol show job <jobid> (Priority field).
  - Inspect priority factors and queue ordering: sprio (or sprio -l / sprio -u <user>), sshare (fairshare usage).
  - Look for many older/higher‑QOS jobs in the same partition: squeue -p <partition> --sort=-p (or sort by priority/age).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit with a higher QOS (if permitted) or ask admin to adjust QOS/priority.
  - Reduce job size/time so it is scheduled sooner by the policy.
  - Wait—priority often resolves as higher priority jobs finish or as the job ages/fairshare changes.
  - Admin actions: change priority weights, adjust fairshare or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The specific nodes requested by the job (via --nodelist, --exclude, or a constraint that pins nodes) are not available for allocation (they may be DOWN, DRAINED, allocated to other jobs, in a reservation, or otherwise unavailable).
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (NodeList, Exclude, Constraint).
  - Check node states: sinfo -Nel or sinfo --Node (or sinfo_reasons to list down/drain nodes and reasons).
  - For a named node: scontrol show node <nodename> to see state/reason.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node requests or exclusions so the scheduler can choose available nodes.
  - Choose a different partition without the unavailable nodes.
  - Wait for the named nodes to come back online or be released from other jobs.
  - If nodes are down/drained, contact the cluster admin to repair/bring them back.

4) QOS limits (jobs blocked by QOS/account limits)
- What it means
  - The job is blocked because it would violate a QOS or association/account limit. Slurm reason codes related to QOS/limits include Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp, AssocMax and similar. Limits can be per‑QOS, per‑user, per‑account, or TRES (CPU/GPU/time) caps.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job fields: scontrol show job <jobid> (QOS, Account, ReqTRES).
  - Check accounting/association limits: sacctmgr show assoc / sacctmgr list associations (or ask admin to run those).
  - See fairshare/usage: sshare and sprio may help show why QOS choice affects priority.
  - The squeue reason text will often indicate the specific limit name (e.g., MaxJobsPerUser).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit under a different QOS or account with higher limits (if you have access).
  - Reduce requested resources/time to stay within the QOS limits.
  - Wait until other jobs reduce your account's current usage (free up slots).
  - Request admin changes to the QOS/account limits (this is an administrative change).

Notes and troubleshooting tips
- Only one pending reason is shown (the reason encountered during scheduling); there can be multiple underlying causes. If you need the exact, low‑level scheduler decision you can combine scontrol show job <id>, sprio, sshare, and sinfo.
- Useful quick commands: squeue -j <id> -o "%i %P %u %t %R %l %M" ; scontrol show job <id> ; sinfo -Nel ; sprio ; sshare ; sacctmgr show assoc.
- If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact squeue/scontrol outputs you should check and what they likely mean.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Snippet:
# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.
