trials.agent_response:
Summary (official Slurm behavior)
- Purpose: the afterok dependency makes a job wait until one or more specified jobs have finished successfully (exit code 0).
- Syntax (common forms):
  - CLI: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid>...]
  - In a script: #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:<jobid>
  - (The docs also show --depend as a short form: --depend=afterok:<jobid>.)
- Multiple job IDs: list them after the colon (colon-separated in examples in the official docs).
- Effect: the dependent job will remain pending until each referenced job has completed with exit code 0. If any referenced job fails/cancels/returns nonzero, the afterok dependency for that referenced job is not satisfied.

Key official-doc details and edge cases
- Job arrays:
  - If you depend on a job array ID, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. The documentation notes that for arrays the interpretation of afterok is based on the highest exit code from any task in the array (so any nonzero exit causes afterok to be unsatisfied).
  - You can depend on specific array elements (examples in the job-array docs).
- Burst buffers:
  - If both jobs use burst buffers, an afterok dependency will wait for the producing job to finish and its burst-buffer stage-out to complete. If the dependent job does not use a burst buffer, it will not wait for stage-out; use afterburstbuffer if you need that.
- Related dependency types (for different semantics):
  - afterany: wait until referenced job(s) complete (regardless of exit code).
  - afternotok: wait until referenced job(s) complete and at least one task fails (nonzero exit).
  - aftercorr: for array jobs, wait for the corresponding element to complete successfully.
  - afterburstbuffer: wait for burst-buffer stage-out to finish (see burst-buffer docs).

Short examples (from docs-style usage)
- Single job:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myscript.sh
- Multiple jobs:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 myscript.sh
- Job array (wait for all elements to succeed):
  - sbatch --depend=afterok:67890 followup.sh

Official references
- sbatch manual (options and --dependency): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job array dependency semantics (afterok behavior with arrays): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst buffer note about dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html

- show the exact man-page section text for --dependency, or
- give examples for array-element dependencies (e.g., 123_4), or
- help convert an existing submission script to use afterok. Which would you like?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PAM Slurm Adopt plugin on cgroup v2 [#pam_slurm_adopt](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
The [pam_slurm_adopt plugin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html) has a
dependency with the API of cgroup/v1 because in some situations it relied
on the job's cgroup creation time for choosing which job id should be picked to
add your sshd pid into. With v2 we wanted to remove this dependency and not
rely on the cgroup filesystem, but simply on the job id. This won't guarantee
that the sshd session is inserted into the youngest job, but will guarantee it
will be put into the largest job id. Thanks to this we removed the dependency of
the plugin against the specific cgroup hierarchy.

Based on the current cluster state, summary (official Slurm behavior)
- Purpose: the afterok dependency makes a job wait until one or more specified jobs have finished successfully (exit code 0).
- Syntax (common forms):
  - CLI: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid>...]
  - In a script: #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:<jobid>
  - (The docs also show --depend as a short form: --depend=afterok:<jobid>.)
- Multiple job IDs: list them after the colon (colon-separated in examples in the official docs).
- Effect: the dependent job will remain pending until each referenced job has completed with exit code 0. If any referenced job fails/cancels/returns nonzero, the afterok dependency for that referenced job is not satisfied.

Key official-doc details and edge cases
- Job arrays:
  - If you depend on a job array ID, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. The documentation notes that for arrays the interpretation of afterok is based on the highest exit code from any task in the array (so any nonzero exit causes afterok to be unsatisfied).
  - You can depend on specific array elements (examples in the job-array docs).
- Burst buffers:
  - If both jobs use burst buffers, an afterok dependency will wait for the producing job to finish and its burst-buffer stage-out to complete. If the dependent job does not use a burst buffer, it will not wait for stage-out; use afterburstbuffer if you need that.
- Related dependency types (for different semantics):
  - afterany: wait until referenced job(s) complete (regardless of exit code).
  - afternotok: wait until referenced job(s) complete and at least one task fails (nonzero exit).
  - aftercorr: for array jobs, wait for the corresponding element to complete successfully.
  - afterburstbuffer: wait for burst-buffer stage-out to finish (see burst-buffer docs).

Short examples (from docs-style usage)
- Single job:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myscript.sh
- Multiple jobs:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 myscript.sh
- Job array (wait for all elements to succeed):
  - sbatch --depend=afterok:67890 followup.sh

Official references
- sbatch manual (options and --dependency): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job array dependency semantics (afterok behavior with arrays): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst buffer note about dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html

- show the exact man-page section text for --dependency, or
- give examples for array-element dependencies (e.g., 123_4), or
- help convert an existing submission script to use afterok. Which would you like?

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

The [pam_slurm_adopt plugin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html) has a

will be put into the largest job id. Thanks to this we removed the dependency of
the plugin against the specific cgroup hierarchy.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, summary (official Slurm behavior)
- Purpose: the afterok dependency makes a job wait until one or more specified jobs have finished successfully (exit code 0).
- Syntax (common forms):
  - CLI: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid>...]
  - In a script: #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:<jobid>
  - (The docs also show --depend as a short form: --depend=afterok:<jobid>.)
- Multiple job IDs: list them after the colon (colon-separated in examples in the official docs).
- Effect: the dependent job will remain pending until each referenced job has completed with exit code 0. If any referenced job fails/cancels/returns nonzero, the afterok dependency for that referenced job is not satisfied.

Key official-doc details and edge cases
- Job arrays:
  - If you depend on a job array ID, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. The documentation notes that for arrays the interpretation of afterok is based on the highest exit code from any task in the array (so any nonzero exit causes afterok to be unsatisfied).
  - You can depend on specific array elements (examples in the job-array docs).
- Burst buffers:
  - If both jobs use burst buffers, an afterok dependency will wait for the producing job to finish and its burst-buffer stage-out to complete. If the dependent job does not use a burst buffer, it will not wait for stage-out; use afterburstbuffer if you need that.
- Related dependency types (for different semantics):
  - afterany: wait until referenced job(s) complete (regardless of exit code).
  - afternotok: wait until referenced job(s) complete and at least one task fails (nonzero exit).
  - aftercorr: for array jobs, wait for the corresponding element to complete successfully.
  - afterburstbuffer: wait for burst-buffer stage-out to finish (see burst-buffer docs).

Short examples (from docs-style usage)
- Single job:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myscript.sh
- Multiple jobs:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 myscript.sh
- Job array (wait for all elements to succeed):
  - sbatch --depend=afterok:67890 followup.sh

Official references
- sbatch manual (options and --dependency): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job array dependency semantics (afterok behavior with arrays): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst buffer note about dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html

- show the exact man-page section text for --dependency, or
- give examples for array-element dependencies (e.g., 123_4), or

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.

The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PAM Slurm Adopt plugin on cgroup v2 [#pam_slurm_adopt](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
The [pam_slurm_adopt plugin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html) has a
dependency with the API of cgroup/v1 because in some situations it relied
on the job's cgroup creation time for choosing which job id should be picked to
add your sshd pid into. With v2 we wanted to remove this dependency and not
rely on the cgroup filesystem, but simply on the job id. This won't guarantee
that the sshd session is inserted into the youngest job, but will guarantee it
will be put into the largest job id. Thanks to this we removed the dependency of
the plugin against the specific cgroup hierarchy.

### Data Collection [#collection](https://slurm.schedmd.com/hdf5_profile_user_guide.html)
The --profile option on salloc|sbatch|srun controls whether data is
collected and what type of data is collected. If --profile is not specified
no data collected unless the ProfileHDF5Default
option is used in acct_gather.conf. --profile on the command line overrides
any value specified in the configuration file.
--profile =<all|none|[energy[,|task[,|filesystem[,|network]]]]>
Enables detailed data collection by the acct_gather_profile plugin.
Detailed data are typically time-series that are stored in a HDF5 file for
the job.
All
All data types are collected. (Cannot be combined with other values.)
None
No data types are collected. This is the default. (Cannot be
combined with other values.)
Energy
Energy data is collected.
Filesystem
Filesystem data is collected. Currently only

results.prompt: Explain afterany and afternotok dependency semantics in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Short answer

- afterany: the dependent job is released when each job named in the dependency has terminated — in any final state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). It does not care about exit status, only that the jobs have finished.

- afternotok: the dependent job is released only when every job named in the dependency has terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they did not finish successfully). If any dependency job finished successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition for that dependent job is not satisfied.

Details and examples

- Syntax (example): sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 myjob.sh or sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345,12346 myjob.sh

- afterany semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have reached a terminal state. Terminal states include COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.
  - The dependent job becomes eligible regardless of whether the predecessors succeeded or failed.
  - If a listed job is still running or pending, the dependent job stays in PENDING with reason "Dependency".

- afternotok semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have terminated and each terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they failed, timed out, were cancelled with a non‑zero exit code, etc.).
  - If any listed job finishes successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition is not met for that dependent job; the dependency is effectively unsatisfiable (the job will remain pending unless you change/cancel it).
  - Common use: run a follow-up only when prior jobs fail.

- Contrast to related types:
  - afterok: releases only if all listed jobs finished successfully (exit code 0).
  - after: releases when listed jobs have started (not when they finish).

Practical notes
- You can list multiple job IDs separated by commas. All listed jobs must satisfy the dependency rule.
- If a dependency job already finished before you submit the dependent job, its terminal state is used immediately when evaluating the dependency.
- For troubleshooting, check squeue (active queue) and sacct (historical exit codes) to see predecessors’ final states and exit codes.

If you want, I can show how to check the predecessor jobs’ states/exit codes (squeue/sacct examples) or craft a concrete sbatch example for your workflow.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, short answer

- afterany: the dependent job is released when each job named in the dependency has terminated — in any final state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). It does not care about exit status, only that the jobs have finished.

- afternotok: the dependent job is released only when every job named in the dependency has terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they did not finish successfully). If any dependency job finished successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition for that dependent job is not satisfied.

Details and examples

- Syntax (example): sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 myjob.sh or sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345,12346 myjob.sh

- afterany semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have reached a terminal state. Terminal states include COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.
  - The dependent job becomes eligible regardless of whether the predecessors succeeded or failed.
  - If a listed job is still running or pending, the dependent job stays in PENDING with reason "Dependency".

- afternotok semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have terminated and each terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they failed, timed out, were cancelled with a non‑zero exit code, etc.).
  - If any listed job finishes successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition is not met for that dependent job; the dependency is effectively unsatisfiable (the job will remain pending unless you change/cancel it).
  - Common use: run a follow-up only when prior jobs fail.

- Contrast to related types:
  - afterok: releases only if all listed jobs finished successfully (exit code 0).
  - after: releases when listed jobs have started (not when they finish).

Practical notes
- You can list multiple job IDs separated by commas. All listed jobs must satisfy the dependency rule.
- If a dependency job already finished before you submit the dependent job, its terminal state is used immediately when evaluating the dependency.
- For troubleshooting, check squeue (active queue) and sacct (historical exit codes) to see predecessors’ final states and exit codes.

If you want, I can show how to check the predecessor jobs’ states/exit codes (squeue/sacct examples) or craft a concrete sbatch example for your workflow.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer

- afterany: the dependent job is released when each job named in the dependency has terminated — in any final state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). It does not care about exit status, only that the jobs have finished.

- afternotok: the dependent job is released only when every job named in the dependency has terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they did not finish successfully). If any dependency job finished successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition for that dependent job is not satisfied.

Details and examples

- Syntax (example): sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 myjob.sh or sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345,12346 myjob.sh

- afterany semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have reached a terminal state. Terminal states include COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.
  - The dependent job becomes eligible regardless of whether the predecessors succeeded or failed.
  - If a listed job is still running or pending, the dependent job stays in PENDING with reason "Dependency".

- afternotok semantics:
  - Waits until all listed jobs have terminated and each terminated with a non‑zero / non‑OK result (i.e., they failed, timed out, were cancelled with a non‑zero exit code, etc.).
  - If any listed job finishes successfully (exit code 0), the afternotok condition is not met for that dependent job; the dependency is effectively unsatisfiable (the job will remain pending unless you change/cancel it).
  - Common use: run a follow-up only when prior jobs fail.

- Contrast to related types:
  - afterok: releases only if all listed jobs finished successfully (exit code 0).
  - after: releases when listed jobs have started (not when they finish).

Practical notes
- You can list multiple job IDs separated by commas. All listed jobs must satisfy the dependency rule.
- If a dependency job already finished before you submit the dependent job, its terminal state is used immediately when evaluating the dependency.
- For troubleshooting, check squeue (active queue) and sacct (historical exit codes) to see predecessors’ final states and exit codes.

If you want, I can show how to check the predecessor jobs’ states/exit codes (squeue/sacct examples) or craft a concrete sbatch example for your workflow.

results.prompt: Explain afterany and afternotok dependency semantics in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Short answer

- afterany: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished, regardless of their exit codes (success or failure).
- afternotok: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished only if at least one of them did NOT complete successfully (i.e., at least one finished with a non‑zero/failed exit).

Details and examples

- Basic single-job dependencies
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated (RUN -> DONE/FAILED/CANCELLED/etc.). Exit code of 123 is ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated and its termination indicates failure (non‑zero/unsuccessful). If job 123 exited with code 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Multiple job IDs (colon-separated list)
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both job 123 and job 124 have terminated (both must finish). The exit codes are ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both 123 and 124 have terminated, and at least one of them must have a non‑zero/failed result. If both exit 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Job arrays
  - When you depend on a job array, semantics apply to the array as a whole:
    - afterany on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete (regardless of individual exit codes).
    - afternotok on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete and at least one task failed (i.e., at least one had a non‑zero exit).
    - (Implementation note in the docs: interpretation of afterok/afternotok for an array is based on the tasks’ exit codes taken together — effectively looking at whether any task had a non‑zero exit.)

Notes / edge cases
- “Finished” means the specified job(s) have reached a terminal state (DONE, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). CANCELLED/TIMEOUT produce non‑zero terminal states and will satisfy afternotok (they count as “not OK”).
- afterany differs from afterok: afterok requires successful (zero) completion of the specified jobs before the dependent job can start; afternotok requires at least one non‑successful completion.
- You can combine dependency types in more complex dependency expressions (see sbatch --dependency docs for syntax options).

If you want, I can show concrete sbatch commands for a particular workflow (single jobs vs arrays, or mixed success/failure behavior).

If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest

The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and

The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a

A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run

handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.

trials.agent_response:
Short answer

- afterany: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished, regardless of their exit codes (success or failure).
- afternotok: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished only if at least one of them did NOT complete successfully (i.e., at least one finished with a non‑zero/failed exit).

Details and examples

- Basic single-job dependencies
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated (RUN -> DONE/FAILED/CANCELLED/etc.). Exit code of 123 is ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated and its termination indicates failure (non‑zero/unsuccessful). If job 123 exited with code 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Multiple job IDs (colon-separated list)
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both job 123 and job 124 have terminated (both must finish). The exit codes are ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both 123 and 124 have terminated, and at least one of them must have a non‑zero/failed result. If both exit 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Job arrays
  - When you depend on a job array, semantics apply to the array as a whole:
    - afterany on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete (regardless of individual exit codes).
    - afternotok on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete and at least one task failed (i.e., at least one had a non‑zero exit).
    - (Implementation note in the docs: interpretation of afterok/afternotok for an array is based on the tasks’ exit codes taken together — effectively looking at whether any task had a non‑zero exit.)

Notes / edge cases
- “Finished” means the specified job(s) have reached a terminal state (DONE, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). CANCELLED/TIMEOUT produce non‑zero terminal states and will satisfy afternotok (they count as “not OK”).
- afterany differs from afterok: afterok requires successful (zero) completion of the specified jobs before the dependent job can start; afternotok requires at least one non‑successful completion.
- You can combine dependency types in more complex dependency expressions (see sbatch --dependency docs for syntax options).

If you want, I can show concrete sbatch commands for a particular workflow (single jobs vs arrays, or mixed success/failure behavior).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.

begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.

job to complete.

complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, short answer

- afterany: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished, regardless of their exit codes (success or failure).
- afternotok: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished only if at least one of them did NOT complete successfully (i.e., at least one finished with a non‑zero/failed exit).

Details and examples

- Basic single-job dependencies
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated (RUN -> DONE/FAILED/CANCELLED/etc.). Exit code of 123 is ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated and its termination indicates failure (non‑zero/unsuccessful). If job 123 exited with code 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Multiple job IDs (colon-separated list)
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both job 123 and job 124 have terminated (both must finish). The exit codes are ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both 123 and 124 have terminated, and at least one of them must have a non‑zero/failed result. If both exit 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Job arrays
  - When you depend on a job array, semantics apply to the array as a whole:
    - afterany on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete (regardless of individual exit codes).
    - afternotok on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete and at least one task failed (i.e., at least one had a non‑zero exit).
    - (Implementation note in the docs: interpretation of afterok/afternotok for an array is based on the tasks’ exit codes taken together — effectively looking at whether any task had a non‑zero exit.)

Notes / edge cases
- “Finished” means the specified job(s) have reached a terminal state (DONE, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). CANCELLED/TIMEOUT produce non‑zero terminal states and will satisfy afternotok (they count as “not OK”).
- afterany differs from afterok: afterok requires successful (zero) completion of the specified jobs before the dependent job can start; afternotok requires at least one non‑successful completion.
- You can combine dependency types in more complex dependency expressions (see sbatch --dependency docs for syntax options).

If you want, I can show concrete sbatch commands for a particular workflow (single jobs vs arrays, or mixed success/failure behavior).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer

- afterany: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished, regardless of their exit codes (success or failure).
- afternotok: start the dependent job after the specified job(s) have finished only if at least one of them did NOT complete successfully (i.e., at least one finished with a non‑zero/failed exit).

Details and examples

- Basic single-job dependencies
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated (RUN -> DONE/FAILED/CANCELLED/etc.). Exit code of 123 is ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh becomes eligible only after job 123 has terminated and its termination indicates failure (non‑zero/unsuccessful). If job 123 exited with code 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Multiple job IDs (colon-separated list)
  - sbatch --dependency=afterany:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both job 123 and job 124 have terminated (both must finish). The exit codes are ignored.
  - sbatch --dependency=afternotok:123:124 myjob.sh
    - myjob.sh waits until both 123 and 124 have terminated, and at least one of them must have a non‑zero/failed result. If both exit 0, the dependency is not satisfied.

- Job arrays
  - When you depend on a job array, semantics apply to the array as a whole:
    - afterany on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete (regardless of individual exit codes).
    - afternotok on an array is satisfied after all array tasks complete and at least one task failed (i.e., at least one had a non‑zero exit).
    - (Implementation note in the docs: interpretation of afterok/afternotok for an array is based on the tasks’ exit codes taken together — effectively looking at whether any task had a non‑zero exit.)

Notes / edge cases
- “Finished” means the specified job(s) have reached a terminal state (DONE, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.). CANCELLED/TIMEOUT produce non‑zero terminal states and will satisfy afternotok (they count as “not OK”).
- afterany differs from afterok: afterok requires successful (zero) completion of the specified jobs before the dependent job can start; afternotok requires at least one non‑successful completion.
- You can combine dependency types in more complex dependency expressions (see sbatch --dependency docs for syntax options).

If you want, I can show concrete sbatch commands for a particular workflow (single jobs vs arrays, or mixed success/failure behavior).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_state_codes.html)
In the Slurm code, there are base states and state flags .
Each job has a base state and may have additional state flags set. When using
the [REST API](https://slurm.schedmd.com/rest_quickstart.html), both the base state and current
flag(s) will be returned.
When the [squeue](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html) and [sacct](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
command report a job state, they represent it as a single state. Both will
recognize all base states but not all state flags. If a recognized flag is

results.prompt: Explain the singleton dependency type for Slurm jobs
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- dependency=singleton serializes jobs so only one job from the same “singleton group” can be active at a time. Use it by passing --dependency=singleton to sbatch or srun for batch submissions.

What it does (semantics)
- When you submit a job with --dependency=singleton, Slurm will not start that job while another job in the same singleton group is still active (pending or running). The newly submitted job is held in the queue and becomes eligible only after the earlier job has finished (regardless of that job’s exit code).
- In practice the singleton group is determined by the submitting user and the job name (the job-name given with --job-name / -J). In other words, jobs with the same user and same job name are serialized by singleton.

How it differs from other dependencies
- singleton waits for completion of the earlier job(s) regardless of success or failure. Contrast that with afterok (which requires the predecessor to exit successfully) or afterany (which requires completion but is expressed with explicit job IDs).
- singleton is about preventing concurrent runs of “the same” job, not about sequencing specific job IDs.

Typical uses
- Prevent overlapping runs of a periodic task or workflow (for example, ensure a nightly data-processing job never runs concurrently with a previous run).
- Ensure only one instance of a named worker/ingest job is active per user.

Usage example
- sbatch --job-name=myjob --dependency=singleton myjob.sh

Notes and caveats
- singleton does not stop multiple submissions; it only delays start time so jobs run one at a time.
- It is enforced by the scheduler; it does not change job exit behavior or automatically cancel jobs.
- If you need sequencing that depends on success/failure, use afterok/afternotok/afterany instead.

If you want, I can show an example workflow or compare singleton behavior with a real pending job using squeue.

trials.agent_response:
Short answer
- dependency=singleton serializes jobs so only one job from the same “singleton group” can be active at a time. Use it by passing --dependency=singleton to sbatch or srun for batch submissions.

What it does (semantics)
- When you submit a job with --dependency=singleton, Slurm will not start that job while another job in the same singleton group is still active (pending or running). The newly submitted job is held in the queue and becomes eligible only after the earlier job has finished (regardless of that job’s exit code).
- In practice the singleton group is determined by the submitting user and the job name (the job-name given with --job-name / -J). In other words, jobs with the same user and same job name are serialized by singleton.

How it differs from other dependencies
- singleton waits for completion of the earlier job(s) regardless of success or failure. Contrast that with afterok (which requires the predecessor to exit successfully) or afterany (which requires completion but is expressed with explicit job IDs).
- singleton is about preventing concurrent runs of “the same” job, not about sequencing specific job IDs.

Typical uses
- Prevent overlapping runs of a periodic task or workflow (for example, ensure a nightly data-processing job never runs concurrently with a previous run).
- Ensure only one instance of a named worker/ingest job is active per user.

Usage example
- sbatch --job-name=myjob --dependency=singleton myjob.sh

Notes and caveats
- singleton does not stop multiple submissions; it only delays start time so jobs run one at a time.
- It is enforced by the scheduler; it does not change job exit behavior or automatically cancel jobs.
- If you need sequencing that depends on success/failure, use afterok/afternotok/afterany instead.

If you want, I can show an example workflow or compare singleton behavior with a real pending job using squeue.

results.prompt: What does sbatch --parsable return and why is it useful?
results.agent_response:
sbatch --parsable makes sbatch emit a single machine-readable token (the assigned Slurm job id information) instead of the human-readable line ("Submitted batch job 12345"). For plain submissions that token is the job id; for array submissions it contains the job/array identifiers in a compact, parseable form.

Why it’s useful
- easy to capture in scripts: JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable job.sh)
- safe to feed to other Slurm commands (scancel, squeue, scontrol, or sbatch --dependency=afterok:$JOBID) without brittle text parsing
- avoids locale/human-message changes and extra text that break automation

Example (script-friendly): 
JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable my_job.sh)
squeue -j "$JOBID"

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in

in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, sbatch --parsable makes sbatch emit a single machine-readable token (the assigned Slurm job id information) instead of the human-readable line ("Submitted batch job 12345"). For plain submissions that token is the job id; for array submissions it contains the job/array identifiers in a compact, parseable form.

Why it’s useful
- easy to capture in scripts: JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable job.sh)
- safe to feed to other Slurm commands (scancel, squeue, scontrol, or sbatch --dependency=afterok:$JOBID) without brittle text parsing
- avoids locale/human-message changes and extra text that break automation

Example (script-friendly): 
JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable my_job.sh)
squeue -j "$JOBID"

results.prompt: Explain Slurm exit code and derived exit code fields from accounting
results.agent_response:
Summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode (accounting field): the exit status recorded for the job (the value Slurm shows for the job or step). It is printed as "exit:signal" (for example 0:0, 1:0, 0:9). The first number is the 8‑bit exit code (0–255); the second number is the signal number if termination was by signal (0 if none).
- DerivedExitCode (accounting field): an additional field Slurm maintains in the job record that reflects Slurm’s computed/aggregated exit status for the job (initially set to the highest non‑zero exit code returned by any of the job’s steps). It has the same "code:signal" format and a free‑text comment string may be attached.

Key details and interpretation
- Format: both fields use "EXIT:SIG". Examples:
  - 0:0 → exited normally with code 0 (success).
  - 1:0 → process exited with status 1.
  - 0:9 → terminated by signal 9 (SIGKILL).
  - 255 → negative return values are shown as unsigned 0–255.
- ExitCode vs DerivedExitCode:
  - ExitCode reflects the recorded exit of the job (for sbatch this is the batch script’s return; for srun it’s the invoked command).
  - DerivedExitCode is computed by Slurm from the job’s steps (highest non‑zero step exit) so it can capture internal step failures even when the top‑level script returned 0.
- Job state implications:
  - Slurm treats a non‑zero exit as a failure (job states and reasons like FAILED / NonZeroExitCode will be set when appropriate).
  - DerivedExitCode is intended to make step failures visible in accounting even if the top‑level exit was zero.
- Admin correction:
  - An administrator can view and edit the derived fields with sjobexitmod (sjobexitmod -l <jobid> to list; -e / -r to set exit/comment). This updates the DB record (used for accounting/visibility).
- Viewing the fields:
  - sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode
  - scontrol show job <jobid> (shows ExitCode in scontrol output)
  - sjobexitmod -l <jobid> (shows/edits derived exit and comment)

Practical notes
- Use DerivedExitCode when you want Slurm’s view of step‑level failures (useful for postmortem/accounting) and compare it with ExitCode to find mismatches (e.g., script returned 0 but steps failed).
- For job arrays / heterogeneous jobs, derived code is computed across the relevant steps/tasks (sacct can show per-task step ExitCode lines).
- If you need to correct accounting for a finished job (for example, mark it with an OOM code or add a comment), ask an admin to run sjobexitmod (this changes the DB record).

References
- Slurm job exit codes doc (ExitCode format, signals, derived exit code and sjobexitmod) — see Slurm documentation (sacct, job_exit_code, sjobexitmod).

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

trials.agent_response:
Summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode (accounting field): the exit status recorded for the job (the value Slurm shows for the job or step). It is printed as "exit:signal" (for example 0:0, 1:0, 0:9). The first number is the 8‑bit exit code (0–255); the second number is the signal number if termination was by signal (0 if none).
- DerivedExitCode (accounting field): an additional field Slurm maintains in the job record that reflects Slurm’s computed/aggregated exit status for the job (initially set to the highest non‑zero exit code returned by any of the job’s steps). It has the same "code:signal" format and a free‑text comment string may be attached.

Key details and interpretation
- Format: both fields use "EXIT:SIG". Examples:
  - 0:0 → exited normally with code 0 (success).
  - 1:0 → process exited with status 1.
  - 0:9 → terminated by signal 9 (SIGKILL).
  - 255 → negative return values are shown as unsigned 0–255.
- ExitCode vs DerivedExitCode:
  - ExitCode reflects the recorded exit of the job (for sbatch this is the batch script’s return; for srun it’s the invoked command).
  - DerivedExitCode is computed by Slurm from the job’s steps (highest non‑zero step exit) so it can capture internal step failures even when the top‑level script returned 0.
- Job state implications:
  - Slurm treats a non‑zero exit as a failure (job states and reasons like FAILED / NonZeroExitCode will be set when appropriate).
  - DerivedExitCode is intended to make step failures visible in accounting even if the top‑level exit was zero.
- Admin correction:
  - An administrator can view and edit the derived fields with sjobexitmod (sjobexitmod -l <jobid> to list; -e / -r to set exit/comment). This updates the DB record (used for accounting/visibility).
- Viewing the fields:
  - sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode
  - scontrol show job <jobid> (shows ExitCode in scontrol output)
  - sjobexitmod -l <jobid> (shows/edits derived exit and comment)

Practical notes
- Use DerivedExitCode when you want Slurm’s view of step‑level failures (useful for postmortem/accounting) and compare it with ExitCode to find mismatches (e.g., script returned 0 but steps failed).
- For job arrays / heterogeneous jobs, derived code is computed across the relevant steps/tasks (sacct can show per-task step ExitCode lines).
- If you need to correct accounting for a finished job (for example, mark it with an OOM code or add a comment), ask an admin to run sjobexitmod (this changes the DB record).

References
- Slurm job exit codes doc (ExitCode format, signals, derived exit code and sjobexitmod) — see Slurm documentation (sacct, job_exit_code, sjobexitmod).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

Based on the current cluster state, summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode (accounting field): the exit status recorded for the job (the value Slurm shows for the job or step). It is printed as "exit:signal" (for example 0:0, 1:0, 0:9). The first number is the 8‑bit exit code (0–255); the second number is the signal number if termination was by signal (0 if none).
- DerivedExitCode (accounting field): an additional field Slurm maintains in the job record that reflects Slurm’s computed/aggregated exit status for the job (initially set to the highest non‑zero exit code returned by any of the job’s steps). It has the same "code:signal" format and a free‑text comment string may be attached.

Key details and interpretation
- Format: both fields use "EXIT:SIG". Examples:
  - 0:0 → exited normally with code 0 (success).
  - 1:0 → process exited with status 1.
  - 0:9 → terminated by signal 9 (SIGKILL).
  - 255 → negative return values are shown as unsigned 0–255.
- ExitCode vs DerivedExitCode:
  - ExitCode reflects the recorded exit of the job (for sbatch this is the batch script’s return; for srun it’s the invoked command).
  - DerivedExitCode is computed by Slurm from the job’s steps (highest non‑zero step exit) so it can capture internal step failures even when the top‑level script returned 0.
- Job state implications:
  - Slurm treats a non‑zero exit as a failure (job states and reasons like FAILED / NonZeroExitCode will be set when appropriate).
  - DerivedExitCode is intended to make step failures visible in accounting even if the top‑level exit was zero.
- Admin correction:
  - An administrator can view and edit the derived fields with sjobexitmod (sjobexitmod -l <jobid> to list; -e / -r to set exit/comment). This updates the DB record (used for accounting/visibility).
- Viewing the fields:
  - sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode
  - scontrol show job <jobid> (shows ExitCode in scontrol output)
  - sjobexitmod -l <jobid> (shows/edits derived exit and comment)

Practical notes
- Use DerivedExitCode when you want Slurm’s view of step‑level failures (useful for postmortem/accounting) and compare it with ExitCode to find mismatches (e.g., script returned 0 but steps failed).
- For job arrays / heterogeneous jobs, derived code is computed across the relevant steps/tasks (sacct can show per-task step ExitCode lines).
- If you need to correct accounting for a finished job (for example, mark it with an OOM code or add a comment), ask an admin to run sjobexitmod (this changes the DB record).

References
- Slurm job exit codes doc (ExitCode format, signals, derived exit code and sjobexitmod) — see Slurm documentation (sacct, job_exit_code, sjobexitmod).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode (accounting field): the exit status recorded for the job (the value Slurm shows for the job or step). It is printed as "exit:signal" (for example 0:0, 1:0, 0:9). The first number is the 8‑bit exit code (0–255); the second number is the signal number if termination was by signal (0 if none).
- DerivedExitCode (accounting field): an additional field Slurm maintains in the job record that reflects Slurm’s computed/aggregated exit status for the job (initially set to the highest non‑zero exit code returned by any of the job’s steps). It has the same "code:signal" format and a free‑text comment string may be attached.

Key details and interpretation
- Format: both fields use "EXIT:SIG". Examples:
  - 0:0 → exited normally with code 0 (success).
  - 1:0 → process exited with status 1.
  - 0:9 → terminated by signal 9 (SIGKILL).
  - 255 → negative return values are shown as unsigned 0–255.
- ExitCode vs DerivedExitCode:
  - ExitCode reflects the recorded exit of the job (for sbatch this is the batch script’s return; for srun it’s the invoked command).
  - DerivedExitCode is computed by Slurm from the job’s steps (highest non‑zero step exit) so it can capture internal step failures even when the top‑level script returned 0.
- Job state implications:
  - Slurm treats a non‑zero exit as a failure (job states and reasons like FAILED / NonZeroExitCode will be set when appropriate).
  - DerivedExitCode is intended to make step failures visible in accounting even if the top‑level exit was zero.
- Admin correction:
  - An administrator can view and edit the derived fields with sjobexitmod (sjobexitmod -l <jobid> to list; -e / -r to set exit/comment). This updates the DB record (used for accounting/visibility).
- Viewing the fields:
  - sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode
  - scontrol show job <jobid> (shows ExitCode in scontrol output)
  - sjobexitmod -l <jobid> (shows/edits derived exit and comment)

Practical notes
- Use DerivedExitCode when you want Slurm’s view of step‑level failures (useful for postmortem/accounting) and compare it with ExitCode to find mismatches (e.g., script returned 0 but steps failed).
- For job arrays / heterogeneous jobs, derived code is computed across the relevant steps/tasks (sacct can show per-task step ExitCode lines).
- If you need to correct accounting for a finished job (for example, mark it with an OOM code or add a comment), ask an admin to run sjobexitmod (this changes the DB record).

References
- Slurm job exit codes doc (ExitCode format, signals, derived exit code and sjobexitmod) — see Slurm documentation (sacct, job_exit_code, sjobexitmod).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
"Priority" as a Slurm pending reason means: the scheduler attempted to place the job but chose other jobs first because they have higher scheduling priority. It does not by itself mean a resource limit, dependency, or begin time — it means the job lost the scheduling comparison to one or more other jobs.

What it implies
- Your job is eligible to run (no unmet dependency, begin time, or explicit account/limit block was detected for the scheduling attempt), but other jobs ranked higher and consumed the available scheduling opportunity.
- The scheduler ranks jobs by a numeric priority; higher numeric priority => scheduled earlier.

How Slurm computes that numeric priority
- By default Slurm uses the Multifactor Priority plugin. Job_priority is a weighted sum of factors such as:
  - age (how long the job has waited)
  - association/account priority
  - fairshare (historical usage)
  - job size
  - partition priority
  - QOS priority
  - TRES factors (CPU/GPU weights)
  - site/nice factors
- Each factor is normalized and multiplied by configured weights (see PriorityWeight* settings). The final priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger is better.

What to check when you see "Priority"
- Inspect the job's numeric priority and the queue ordering:
  - sprio — shows computed priority factors (per-job priority and contributing factors).
  - squeue (include PRIORITY and REASON columns) — shows which jobs are ahead of yours.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> — shows the job's Priority= value and other properties (QOS, account, nice, TRES).
- Check fairshare and effective shares:
  - sshare — to see account/user fairshare usage that may lower/increase priority.
- Check QOS and partition weights:
  - QOS or partition settings may give other jobs elevated priority (or your job lower priority).
- If preemption or backfill is in use, high-priority jobs may preempt or block lower-priority jobs from starting.

Common causes
- Many recent/high-weight jobs were submitted with higher QOS/account priority.
- Your account has low fairshare (used up entitlement), so fairshare factor reduces your priority.
- Partition or association priorities favor other users or partitions.
- Your job is large (job_size factor) and the scheduler is preferring many smaller/higher-priority jobs first (configurable by weights).

If you want help diagnosing a specific job, tell me the job ID and I can show the priority value and the jobs currently ahead of it (I'll run the appropriate Slurm reads).

What it implies
- Your job is eligible to run (no unmet dependency, begin time, or explicit account/limit block was detected for the scheduling attempt), but other jobs ranked higher and consumed the available scheduling opportunity.
- The scheduler ranks jobs by a numeric priority; higher numeric priority => scheduled earlier.

How Slurm computes that numeric priority
- By default Slurm uses the Multifactor Priority plugin. Job_priority is a weighted sum of factors such as:
  - age (how long the job has waited)
  - association/account priority
  - fairshare (historical usage)
  - job size
  - partition priority
  - QOS priority
  - TRES factors (CPU/GPU weights)
  - site/nice factors
- Each factor is normalized and multiplied by configured weights (see PriorityWeight* settings). The final priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger is better.

What to check when you see "Priority"
- Inspect the job's numeric priority and the queue ordering:
  - sprio — shows computed priority factors (per-job priority and contributing factors).
  - squeue (include PRIORITY and REASON columns) — shows which jobs are ahead of yours.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> — shows the job's Priority= value and other properties (QOS, account, nice, TRES).
- Check fairshare and effective shares:
  - sshare — to see account/user fairshare usage that may lower/increase priority.
- Check QOS and partition weights:
  - QOS or partition settings may give other jobs elevated priority (or your job lower priority).
- If preemption or backfill is in use, high-priority jobs may preempt or block lower-priority jobs from starting.

- Many recent/high-weight jobs were submitted with higher QOS/account priority.
- Your account has low fairshare (used up entitlement), so fairshare factor reduces your priority.
- Partition or association priorities favor other users or partitions.
- Your job is large (job_size factor) and the scheduler is preferring many smaller/higher-priority jobs first (configurable by weights).

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer first: there is no official job-reason named "QOSMaxJobsPerUser" in the Slurm job-reason list. QOS job-count limits are implemented with QOS attributes (MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs / GrpJobs / active_jobs in the REST API, etc.) and when those limits block a job the scheduler reports one of the standard association/limit reason codes (for example AssociationJobLimit, AssocGrp*, AssocMax*, Max*PerAccount). The QOS may also use the DenyOnLimit flag to reject jobs at submission instead of letting them pend.

What the pieces mean and how they map to pending reasons
- QOS limits (where you set them with sacctmgr show/modify qos) can include:
  - MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs (job-count style limits),
  - GrpJobs (group/aggregate job-count),
  - GrpTRES / MaxTRES (aggregate resource caps),
  - other Max* or Grp* limits (per-node, per-account TRES, wall time, nodes, …),
  - Flags such as DenyOnLimit or OverPartQOS.
  (The REST API exposes similar fields such as jobs and active_jobs for a QOS.)
- Enforcement and precedence:
  - Limits are applied in the documented hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account association, cluster, partition). A limit defined earlier in the precedence chain wins.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would exceed a QOS 'Max' limit are denied at submission (rejected) rather than queued.
- How those limits show up as squeue/scontrol reasons:
  - AssociationJobLimit — the job's association has reached its maximum job count (common when a per-user/per-account job-count limit is active).
  - AssocGrp* — an aggregate/group limit (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) has been reached.
  - AssocMax* / AssocMax…Limit / Max*PerAccount — a requested value exceeds a defined maximum for the association/QOS (the job would violate a Max limit).
  - Max*PerAccount (or Max*PerUser variants shown by some installs) appear when a per-account/per-user maximum (on TRES, jobs, nodes, etc.) is violated.
  - (The job_reason_codes documentation lists all reason-code names and short descriptions — use that to match the reason string you see.)
- Important behavior notes:
  - If a QOS limit only becomes true when considering multiple jobs together (group limits), affected jobs will pend with a group/association reason (not necessarily a QOS-named reason).
  - Only the single reason encountered by the attempted scheduling method is shown; other applicable limits may also exist but are not displayed.

How to diagnose a job pending for a QOS limit
- First look at the queue reason: squeue (the pending Reason column) for the job ID.
- If you need more detail: scontrol show job <JOBID> will show the job's QOS, association, and any limit-related fields the scheduler considered.
- Inspect configured limits:
  - sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos) to view the QOS attributes (MaxJobs, GrpJobs, DenyOnLimit, …).
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> (or account=<acct>) to see user/account association limits that may override/augment the QOS.
- If a job was rejected at submission, check sbatch/srun error text and whether the QOS has DenyOnLimit enabled.

If you want, tell me a specific job ID (or show the squeue Reason line) and I can walk through the exact mapping and the sacctmgr/scontrol queries to find which configured limit is blocking it.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

## SPECIFICATIONS FOR QOS[#SECTION_SPECIFICATIONS-FOR-QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
A QOS can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for a QOS.
NOTE : The group limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) are tested when a job is
being considered for being allocated resources.
If starting a job would cause any of its group limit to be exceeded,
that job will not be considered for scheduling even if that job might preempt
other jobs which would release sufficient group resources for the pending
job to be initiated.

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.
For configuration information, see the
[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

sbatch , salloc , and srun commands.
