### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

trials.agent_response:
Short answer first: there is no official job-reason named "QOSMaxJobsPerUser" in the Slurm job-reason list. QOS job-count limits are implemented with QOS attributes (MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs / GrpJobs / active_jobs in the REST API, etc.) and when those limits block a job the scheduler reports one of the standard association/limit reason codes (for example AssociationJobLimit, AssocGrp*, AssocMax*, Max*PerAccount). The QOS may also use the DenyOnLimit flag to reject jobs at submission instead of letting them pend.

What the pieces mean and how they map to pending reasons
- QOS limits (where you set them with sacctmgr show/modify qos) can include:
  - MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs (job-count style limits),
  - GrpJobs (group/aggregate job-count),
  - GrpTRES / MaxTRES (aggregate resource caps),
  - other Max* or Grp* limits (per-node, per-account TRES, wall time, nodes, …),
  - Flags such as DenyOnLimit or OverPartQOS.
  (The REST API exposes similar fields such as jobs and active_jobs for a QOS.)
- Enforcement and precedence:
  - Limits are applied in the documented hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account association, cluster, partition). A limit defined earlier in the precedence chain wins.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would exceed a QOS 'Max' limit are denied at submission (rejected) rather than queued.
- How those limits show up as squeue/scontrol reasons:
  - AssociationJobLimit — the job's association has reached its maximum job count (common when a per-user/per-account job-count limit is active).
  - AssocGrp* — an aggregate/group limit (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) has been reached.
  - AssocMax* / AssocMax…Limit / Max*PerAccount — a requested value exceeds a defined maximum for the association/QOS (the job would violate a Max limit).
  - Max*PerAccount (or Max*PerUser variants shown by some installs) appear when a per-account/per-user maximum (on TRES, jobs, nodes, etc.) is violated.
  - (The job_reason_codes documentation lists all reason-code names and short descriptions — use that to match the reason string you see.)
- Important behavior notes:
  - If a QOS limit only becomes true when considering multiple jobs together (group limits), affected jobs will pend with a group/association reason (not necessarily a QOS-named reason).
  - Only the single reason encountered by the attempted scheduling method is shown; other applicable limits may also exist but are not displayed.

How to diagnose a job pending for a QOS limit
- First look at the queue reason: squeue (the pending Reason column) for the job ID.
- If you need more detail: scontrol show job <JOBID> will show the job's QOS, association, and any limit-related fields the scheduler considered.
- Inspect configured limits:
  - sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos) to view the QOS attributes (MaxJobs, GrpJobs, DenyOnLimit, …).
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> (or account=<acct>) to see user/account association limits that may override/augment the QOS.
- If a job was rejected at submission, check sbatch/srun error text and whether the QOS has DenyOnLimit enabled.

If you want, tell me a specific job ID (or show the squeue Reason line) and I can walk through the exact mapping and the sacctmgr/scontrol queries to find which configured limit is blocking it.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.

[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.

$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0

```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, short answer first: there is no official job-reason named "QOSMaxJobsPerUser" in the Slurm job-reason list. QOS job-count limits are implemented with QOS attributes (MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs / GrpJobs / active_jobs in the REST API, etc.) and when those limits block a job the scheduler reports one of the standard association/limit reason codes (for example AssociationJobLimit, AssocGrp*, AssocMax*, Max*PerAccount). The QOS may also use the DenyOnLimit flag to reject jobs at submission instead of letting them pend.

What the pieces mean and how they map to pending reasons
- QOS limits (where you set them with sacctmgr show/modify qos) can include:
  - MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs (job-count style limits),
  - GrpJobs (group/aggregate job-count),
  - GrpTRES / MaxTRES (aggregate resource caps),
  - other Max* or Grp* limits (per-node, per-account TRES, wall time, nodes, …),
  - Flags such as DenyOnLimit or OverPartQOS.
  (The REST API exposes similar fields such as jobs and active_jobs for a QOS.)
- Enforcement and precedence:
  - Limits are applied in the documented hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account association, cluster, partition). A limit defined earlier in the precedence chain wins.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would exceed a QOS 'Max' limit are denied at submission (rejected) rather than queued.
- How those limits show up as squeue/scontrol reasons:
  - AssociationJobLimit — the job's association has reached its maximum job count (common when a per-user/per-account job-count limit is active).
  - AssocGrp* — an aggregate/group limit (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) has been reached.
  - AssocMax* / AssocMax…Limit / Max*PerAccount — a requested value exceeds a defined maximum for the association/QOS (the job would violate a Max limit).
  - Max*PerAccount (or Max*PerUser variants shown by some installs) appear when a per-account/per-user maximum (on TRES, jobs, nodes, etc.) is violated.
  - (The job_reason_codes documentation lists all reason-code names and short descriptions — use that to match the reason string you see.)
- Important behavior notes:
  - If a QOS limit only becomes true when considering multiple jobs together (group limits), affected jobs will pend with a group/association reason (not necessarily a QOS-named reason).
  - Only the single reason encountered by the attempted scheduling method is shown; other applicable limits may also exist but are not displayed.

How to diagnose a job pending for a QOS limit
- First look at the queue reason: squeue (the pending Reason column) for the job ID.
- If you need more detail: scontrol show job <JOBID> will show the job's QOS, association, and any limit-related fields the scheduler considered.
- Inspect configured limits:
  - sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos) to view the QOS attributes (MaxJobs, GrpJobs, DenyOnLimit, …).
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> (or account=<acct>) to see user/account association limits that may override/augment the QOS.
- If a job was rejected at submission, check sbatch/srun error text and whether the QOS has DenyOnLimit enabled.

If you want, tell me a specific job ID (or show the squeue Reason line) and I can walk through the exact mapping and the sacctmgr/scontrol queries to find which configured limit is blocking it.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.

[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

# Quality of Service (QOS)
One can specify a Quality of Service (QOS) for each job submitted
to Slurm. The QOSs are defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr
command. Jobs request a QOS using the "--qos=" option to the
sbatch , salloc , and srun commands.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0
```
Add a new QOS
```text
$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```
Set QOS priority
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10
```
Set some other limits
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos z...

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer first: there is no official job-reason named "QOSMaxJobsPerUser" in the Slurm job-reason list. QOS job-count limits are implemented with QOS attributes (MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs / GrpJobs / active_jobs in the REST API, etc.) and when those limits block a job the scheduler reports one of the standard association/limit reason codes (for example AssociationJobLimit, AssocGrp*, AssocMax*, Max*PerAccount). The QOS may also use the DenyOnLimit flag to reject jobs at submission instead of letting them pend.

What the pieces mean and how they map to pending reasons
- QOS limits (where you set them with sacctmgr show/modify qos) can include:
  - MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs (job-count style limits),
  - GrpJobs (group/aggregate job-count),
  - GrpTRES / MaxTRES (aggregate resource caps),
  - other Max* or Grp* limits (per-node, per-account TRES, wall time, nodes, …),
  - Flags such as DenyOnLimit or OverPartQOS.
  (The REST API exposes similar fields such as jobs and active_jobs for a QOS.)
- Enforcement and precedence:
  - Limits are applied in the documented hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account association, cluster, partition). A limit defined earlier in the precedence chain wins.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would exceed a QOS 'Max' limit are denied at submission (rejected) rather than queued.
- How those limits show up as squeue/scontrol reasons:
  - AssociationJobLimit — the job's association has reached its maximum job count (common when a per-user/per-account job-count limit is active).
  - AssocGrp* — an aggregate/group limit (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) has been reached.
  - AssocMax* / AssocMax…Limit / Max*PerAccount — a requested value exceeds a defined maximum for the association/QOS (the job would violate a Max limit).
  - Max*PerAccount (or Max*PerUser variants shown by some installs) appear when a per-account/per-user maximum (on TRES, jobs, nodes, etc.) is violated.
  - (The job_reason_codes documentation lists all reason-code names and short descriptions — use that to match the reason string you see.)
- Important behavior notes:
  - If a QOS limit only becomes true when considering multiple jobs together (group limits), affected jobs will pend with a group/association reason (not necessarily a QOS-named reason).
  - Only the single reason encountered by the attempted scheduling method is shown; other applicable limits may also exist but are not displayed.

How to diagnose a job pending for a QOS limit
- First look at the queue reason: squeue (the pending Reason column) for the job ID.
- If you need more detail: scontrol show job <JOBID> will show the job's QOS, association, and any limit-related fields the scheduler considered.
- Inspect configured limits:
  - sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos) to view the QOS attributes (MaxJobs, GrpJobs, DenyOnLimit, …).
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> (or account=<acct>) to see user/account association limits that may override/augment the QOS.
- If a job was rejected at submission, check sbatch/srun error text and whether the QOS has DenyOnLimit enabled.

If you want, tell me a specific job ID (or show the squeue Reason line) and I can walk through the exact mapping and the sacctmgr/scontrol queries to find which configured limit is blocking it.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One

defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.

multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even
if the job is enforced with...

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or similarly named association field shown by sacctmgr) refers to the association-level group limits that apply specifically to GRES (Generic RESources — e.g., GPUs, licenses, burst buffers). It is how Slurm records or displays the GRES-related group/TRES limits for a user/account/association.

What association (group) GRES/TRES limits are
- TRES = Trackable RESource. GRES is the TRES type for generic resources (typically gpu, license, etc.).
- Association/group limits control aggregate and per-entity use of resources for an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition).
- Common GRES-related limits:
  - GrpTRES (or Assoc group TRES): aggregate limits for the association, e.g. GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8 (at most 8 GPUs in total across that association).
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPerAcct: per-user or per-account maximums (can be type- and model-qualified, e.g. gres/gpu:tesla=1).
  - MaxTRESPerJob: limit of a TRES per single job (e.g. a job cannot request > 4 GPUs).
  - Other related fields: GrpJobs, MaxJobs, etc., which affect job counts rather than TRES counts.

How the limits are expressed (syntax)
- Limits are given as comma-separated TRES=VALUE pairs. Example forms:
  - GrpTRES=cpu=128,mem=512G,gres/gpu=8
  - MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
  - MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=4
- GRES type qualification: you can qualify a GRES by model/type: gres/gpu:tesla or simply gres/gpu. The qualified form targets a specific GRES subtype.

Enforcement and precedence
- When Slurm considers starting a job, it checks association/group limits. If starting that job would exceed any applicable group limit, the job is not considered for allocation (remains pending).
- Precedence order for limits: job QOS / partition QOS and association levels are checked in a defined hierarchy. In general the first-defined limit in the precedence list is used (user association → account association(s) → cluster defaults), with some exceptions documented for certain limits (see Slurm docs).
- Changing limits:
  - If you lower a limit, running jobs are not killed to satisfy the new limit; the new limit is enforced for new allocations.
  - If you delete an association, jobs belonging to it are cancelled immediately.

Important GRES caveat (common pitfall)
- Type-specific limits vs generic requests: if you set a limit for a specific GRES type (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) but a user submits with --gres=gpu (no model specified), Slurm may not enforce the type-specific limit. In short: a type-specific limit will not block a generic request for a different/unspecified type. This is a known design limitation; if you need strict enforcement, require users to request specific types (via job_submit plugin or policies).

How to view and change these limits
- View defined GRES types: sacctmgr show tres
- View association limits: sacctmgr show association (use format options to display TRES/GrpTRES/MaxTRES* fields)
- Set/modify limits via sacctmgr. Example (run as admin):
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16
  - sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
- To remove a TRES limit assign -1 (or use sacctmgr syntax to remove that entry).

Recommendations / best practices
- Decide whether you want generic or model-specific enforcement. If model-specific enforcement is required, either:
  - require users to request a model in --gres (enforce with job_submit plugin), or
  - implement a lua job_submit plugin to rewrite/validate requests.
- Use sacctmgr show tres and show association formats regularly to audit active limits.
- Use GrpTRES for aggregate quotas and MaxTRESPerUser/MaxTRESPerJob for per-user or per-job caps.

References / where to read more
- sacctmgr and resource_limits docs in the Slurm manual (commands: sacctmgr show tres, sacctmgr show association; docs: "Resource Limits" and "sacctmgr" pages).

If you want, I can:
- show the current GRES and association limits on your cluster (sac t mgr / sacctmgr queries), or
- give exact sacctmgr command examples tailored to a user/account name you supply.

3. The option specified for the cluster.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.
Note: The precedence order specified above is respected except for the
following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even

When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this
situation an additional lua job submit plugin to check the user request may
become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a
limit set of MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 , the limit won't be
enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.
This is due to a design limitation. The only way to enforce such a limit
is to combine the specification of the limit with a job submit plugin that

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the

Note that the GRES specification for each node works in the same fashion
as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.

## AutoDetect [#AutoDetect](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.
Note that AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries
installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the
nvml library to be installed, but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks.

sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface

trials.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or similarly named association field shown by sacctmgr) refers to the association-level group limits that apply specifically to GRES (Generic RESources — e.g., GPUs, licenses, burst buffers). It is how Slurm records or displays the GRES-related group/TRES limits for a user/account/association.

What association (group) GRES/TRES limits are
- TRES = Trackable RESource. GRES is the TRES type for generic resources (typically gpu, license, etc.).
- Association/group limits control aggregate and per-entity use of resources for an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition).
- Common GRES-related limits:
  - GrpTRES (or Assoc group TRES): aggregate limits for the association, e.g. GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8 (at most 8 GPUs in total across that association).
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPerAcct: per-user or per-account maximums (can be type- and model-qualified, e.g. gres/gpu:tesla=1).
  - MaxTRESPerJob: limit of a TRES per single job (e.g. a job cannot request > 4 GPUs).
  - Other related fields: GrpJobs, MaxJobs, etc., which affect job counts rather than TRES counts.

How the limits are expressed (syntax)
- Limits are given as comma-separated TRES=VALUE pairs. Example forms:
  - GrpTRES=cpu=128,mem=512G,gres/gpu=8
  - MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
  - MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=4
- GRES type qualification: you can qualify a GRES by model/type: gres/gpu:tesla or simply gres/gpu. The qualified form targets a specific GRES subtype.

Enforcement and precedence
- When Slurm considers starting a job, it checks association/group limits. If starting that job would exceed any applicable group limit, the job is not considered for allocation (remains pending).
- Precedence order for limits: job QOS / partition QOS and association levels are checked in a defined hierarchy. In general the first-defined limit in the precedence list is used (user association → account association(s) → cluster defaults), with some exceptions documented for certain limits (see Slurm docs).
- Changing limits:
  - If you lower a limit, running jobs are not killed to satisfy the new limit; the new limit is enforced for new allocations.
  - If you delete an association, jobs belonging to it are cancelled immediately.

Important GRES caveat (common pitfall)
- Type-specific limits vs generic requests: if you set a limit for a specific GRES type (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) but a user submits with --gres=gpu (no model specified), Slurm may not enforce the type-specific limit. In short: a type-specific limit will not block a generic request for a different/unspecified type. This is a known design limitation; if you need strict enforcement, require users to request specific types (via job_submit plugin or policies).

How to view and change these limits
- View defined GRES types: sacctmgr show tres
- View association limits: sacctmgr show association (use format options to display TRES/GrpTRES/MaxTRES* fields)
- Set/modify limits via sacctmgr. Example (run as admin):
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16
  - sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
- To remove a TRES limit assign -1 (or use sacctmgr syntax to remove that entry).

Recommendations / best practices
- Decide whether you want generic or model-specific enforcement. If model-specific enforcement is required, either:
  - require users to request a model in --gres (enforce with job_submit plugin), or
  - implement a lua job_submit plugin to rewrite/validate requests.
- Use sacctmgr show tres and show association formats regularly to audit active limits.
- Use GrpTRES for aggregate quotas and MaxTRESPerUser/MaxTRESPerJob for per-user or per-job caps.

References / where to read more
- sacctmgr and resource_limits docs in the Slurm manual (commands: sacctmgr show tres, sacctmgr show association; docs: "Resource Limits" and "sacctmgr" pages).

If you want, I can:
- show the current GRES and association limits on your cluster (sac t mgr / sacctmgr queries), or
- give exact sacctmgr command examples tailored to a user/account name you supply.

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.

SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin

SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.

## Configuration [#Configuration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the
slurm.conf configuration file. The configuration parameters of
interest are GresTypes and Gres .
For more details, see [GresTypes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) and [Gres](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) in the slurm.conf man page.
Note that the GRES specification for each node works in the same fashion
as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.

```text

```
Each compute node with generic resources typically contain a gres.conf
file describing which resources are available on the node, their count,
associated device files and cores which should be used with those resources.
There are cases where you may want to define a Generic Resource on a node
without specifying a quantity of that GRES. For example, the filesystem type
of a node doesn't decrease in value as jobs run on that node.
You can use the no_consume flag to allow users to request a GRES
without having a defined count that gets used as it is requested.
To view available gres.conf configuration parameters, see the
[gres.conf man page](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.conf.html).

If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the

installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the
nvml library to be installed, but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).
This database can serve as a central storehouse of user and
computer information for multiple computers at a single site.
Slurm account information is recorded based upon four parameters

account . user is the login name.

the ClusterName parameter in the slurm.conf configuration file.
partition is the name of a Slurm partition on that cluster.

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or similarly named association field shown by sacctmgr) refers to the association-level group limits that apply specifically to GRES (Generic RESources — e.g., GPUs, licenses, burst buffers). It is how Slurm records or displays the GRES-related group/TRES limits for a user/account/association.

What association (group) GRES/TRES limits are
- TRES = Trackable RESource. GRES is the TRES type for generic resources (typically gpu, license, etc.).
- Association/group limits control aggregate and per-entity use of resources for an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition).
- Common GRES-related limits:
  - GrpTRES (or Assoc group TRES): aggregate limits for the association, e.g. GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8 (at most 8 GPUs in total across that association).
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPerAcct: per-user or per-account maximums (can be type- and model-qualified, e.g. gres/gpu:tesla=1).
  - MaxTRESPerJob: limit of a TRES per single job (e.g. a job cannot request > 4 GPUs).
  - Other related fields: GrpJobs, MaxJobs, etc., which affect job counts rather than TRES counts.

How the limits are expressed (syntax)
- Limits are given as comma-separated TRES=VALUE pairs. Example forms:
  - GrpTRES=cpu=128,mem=512G,gres/gpu=8
  - MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
  - MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=4
- GRES type qualification: you can qualify a GRES by model/type: gres/gpu:tesla or simply gres/gpu. The qualified form targets a specific GRES subtype.

Enforcement and precedence
- When Slurm considers starting a job, it checks association/group limits. If starting that job would exceed any applicable group limit, the job is not considered for allocation (remains pending).
- Precedence order for limits: job QOS / partition QOS and association levels are checked in a defined hierarchy. In general the first-defined limit in the precedence list is used (user association → account association(s) → cluster defaults), with some exceptions documented for certain limits (see Slurm docs).
- Changing limits:
  - If you lower a limit, running jobs are not killed to satisfy the new limit; the new limit is enforced for new allocations.
  - If you delete an association, jobs belonging to it are cancelled immediately.

Important GRES caveat (common pitfall)
- Type-specific limits vs generic requests: if you set a limit for a specific GRES type (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) but a user submits with --gres=gpu (no model specified), Slurm may not enforce the type-specific limit. In short: a type-specific limit will not block a generic request for a different/unspecified type. This is a known design limitation; if you need strict enforcement, require users to request specific types (via job_submit plugin or policies).

How to view and change these limits
- View defined GRES types: sacctmgr show tres
- View association limits: sacctmgr show association (use format options to display TRES/GrpTRES/MaxTRES* fields)
- Set/modify limits via sacctmgr. Example (run as admin):
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16
  - sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
- To remove a TRES limit assign -1 (or use sacctmgr syntax to remove that entry).

Recommendations / best practices
- Decide whether you want generic or model-specific enforcement. If model-specific enforcement is required, either:
  - require users to request a model in --gres (enforce with job_submit plugin), or
  - implement a lua job_submit plugin to rewrite/validate requests.
- Use sacctmgr show tres and show association formats regularly to audit active limits.
- Use GrpTRES for aggregate quotas and MaxTRESPerUser/MaxTRESPerJob for per-user or per-job caps.

References / where to read more
- sacctmgr and resource_limits docs in the Slurm manual (commands: sacctmgr show tres, sacctmgr show association; docs: "Resource Limits" and "sacctmgr" pages).

If you want, I can:
- show the current GRES and association limits on your cluster (sac t mgr / sacctmgr queries), or
- give exact sacctmgr command examples tailored to a user/account name you supply.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or similarly named association field shown by sacctmgr) refers to the association-level group limits that apply specifically to GRES (Generic RESources — e.g., GPUs, licenses, burst buffers). It is how Slurm records or displays the GRES-related group/TRES limits for a user/account/association.

What association (group) GRES/TRES limits are
- TRES = Trackable RESource. GRES is the TRES type for generic resources (typically gpu, license, etc.).
- Association/group limits control aggregate and per-entity use of resources for an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition).
- Common GRES-related limits:
  - GrpTRES (or Assoc group TRES): aggregate limits for the association, e.g. GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8 (at most 8 GPUs in total across that association).
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPerAcct: per-user or per-account maximums (can be type- and model-qualified, e.g. gres/gpu:tesla=1).
  - MaxTRESPerJob: limit of a TRES per single job (e.g. a job cannot request > 4 GPUs).
  - Other related fields: GrpJobs, MaxJobs, etc., which affect job counts rather than TRES counts.

How the limits are expressed (syntax)
- Limits are given as comma-separated TRES=VALUE pairs. Example forms:
  - GrpTRES=cpu=128,mem=512G,gres/gpu=8
  - MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
  - MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=4
- GRES type qualification: you can qualify a GRES by model/type: gres/gpu:tesla or simply gres/gpu. The qualified form targets a specific GRES subtype.

Enforcement and precedence
- When Slurm considers starting a job, it checks association/group limits. If starting that job would exceed any applicable group limit, the job is not considered for allocation (remains pending).
- Precedence order for limits: job QOS / partition QOS and association levels are checked in a defined hierarchy. In general the first-defined limit in the precedence list is used (user association → account association(s) → cluster defaults), with some exceptions documented for certain limits (see Slurm docs).
- Changing limits:
  - If you lower a limit, running jobs are not killed to satisfy the new limit; the new limit is enforced for new allocations.
  - If you delete an association, jobs belonging to it are cancelled immediately.

Important GRES caveat (common pitfall)
- Type-specific limits vs generic requests: if you set a limit for a specific GRES type (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) but a user submits with --gres=gpu (no model specified), Slurm may not enforce the type-specific limit. In short: a type-specific limit will not block a generic request for a different/unspecified type. This is a known design limitation; if you need strict enforcement, require users to request specific types (via job_submit plugin or policies).

How to view and change these limits
- View defined GRES types: sacctmgr show tres
- View association limits: sacctmgr show association (use format options to display TRES/GrpTRES/MaxTRES* fields)
- Set/modify limits via sacctmgr. Example (run as admin):
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16
  - sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
- To remove a TRES limit assign -1 (or use sacctmgr syntax to remove that entry).

Recommendations / best practices
- Decide whether you want generic or model-specific enforcement. If model-specific enforcement is required, either:
  - require users to request a model in --gres (enforce with job_submit plugin), or
  - implement a lua job_submit plugin to rewrite/validate requests.
- Use sacctmgr show tres and show association formats regularly to audit active limits.
- Use GrpTRES for aggregate quotas and MaxTRESPerUser/MaxTRESPerJob for per-user or per-job caps.

References / where to read more
- sacctmgr and resource_limits docs in the Slurm manual (commands: sacctmgr show tres, sacctmgr show association; docs: "Resource Limits" and "sacctmgr" pages).

If you want, I can:
- show the current GRES and association limits on your cluster (sac t mgr / sacctmgr queries), or
- give exact sacctmgr command examples tailored to a user/account name you supply.

## Association specific limits and scheduling policies [#assoc](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
These represent the limits and scheduling policies relevant to Associations.
When dealing with Associations, most of these limits are available
not only for the user association, but also for each cluster and account.
Limits and policies are applied in the following order:
1. The option specified for the user association.
2. The option specified for the account.
3. The option specified for the cluster.
4. If nothing is configured at the above levels, no limit will be applied.
These are just the limits and policies for Associations. For a more
complete description of the columns available to be displayed, see the

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.
Note: The precedence order specified above is respected except for the
following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even
if the job is enforced with...

When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this
situation an additional lua job submit plugin to check the user request may
become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a
limit set of MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 , the limit won't be
enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.
This is due to a design limitation. The only way to enforce such a limit

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in

as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources

If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,

installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" is an accounting/association-level concept for GRES (generic resources, e.g., GPUs) that appears in the association/group resource limits exposed by Slurm accounting (sacctmgr/sacct). It expresses the group-level GRES/TRES limits or usage that apply to an association (the association is the combination of user/account/cluster/partition).
- Association/group GRES limits are enforced at job allocation time: if starting a job would cause any group limit to be exceeded, that job will not be considered for scheduling. Limits are applied according to Slurm’s association/limit hierarchy (QOS/partition → job QOS → user association → account association(s) → cluster, etc.).
- GRES limits can be expressed using TRES syntax (examples: gres/gpu=2 or gres/gpu:tesla=1). A notable caveat: a type-specific limit (for example MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) does not prevent a user from requesting a generic --gres=gpu:2 and thereby obtaining two of that model; enforcing that requires a job_submit plugin or forcing users to request specific types.

Key behavior and admin notes
- Which fields control these limits: association/group-level fields such as GrpTRES (and other Grp* fields like GrpJobs) are used to limit aggregate resources for an association. These are evaluated when the scheduler considers a job for allocation.
- Enforcement prerequisites and effects:
  - AccountingStorageEnforce must include limits (i.e., AccountingStorageEnforce=limits) in slurm.conf for Slurm to enforce association limits.
  - When limits are lowered, running jobs are not retroactively killed to satisfy the new lower limits; new/queued jobs are blocked if they would exceed the lowered limits.
  - Deleting an association will cancel running or pending jobs that belong to that association immediately.
- Scheduling-time semantics: group limits are tested when a job is being considered. If the job would exceed the group limit, it won’t be scheduled even if preemption of other jobs would have freed enough resources.
- GRES type-vs-generic limit caveat: type-aware limits (gres/gpu:MODEL=...) only apply when jobs request that specific type. If users request generic GRES (gres/gpu without a model), the type-specific limit may not be enforced; use a job_submit plugin to require model-specific requests if you need strict enforcement.

How to view/change these limits
- Use sacctmgr to view and edit association limits (the sacctmgr man page and the Resource Limits documentation show the fields and syntax). Typical fields include GrpTRES, GrpJobs and the Max/Min TRES settings; GRES is expressed in TRES form (gres/...).
- Use sacctmgr show association (or sacctmgr list/show account/user with WithAssoc) to inspect current association limits/GrpTRES values; use sacctmgr modify (or add) to change them. Consult the sacctmgr documentation for exact command-line format.

Where to read the authoritative details
- See Slurm’s Resource Limits documentation (resource_limits) for the limit hierarchy and GRES/TRES examples, and the sacctmgr man page for association fields (GrpTRES, GrpJobs, etc.) and sacctmgr syntax.

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS

After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" is an accounting/association-level concept for GRES (generic resources, e.g., GPUs) that appears in the association/group resource limits exposed by Slurm accounting (sacctmgr/sacct). It expresses the group-level GRES/TRES limits or usage that apply to an association (the association is the combination of user/account/cluster/partition).
- Association/group GRES limits are enforced at job allocation time: if starting a job would cause any group limit to be exceeded, that job will not be considered for scheduling. Limits are applied according to Slurm’s association/limit hierarchy (QOS/partition → job QOS → user association → account association(s) → cluster, etc.).
- GRES limits can be expressed using TRES syntax (examples: gres/gpu=2 or gres/gpu:tesla=1). A notable caveat: a type-specific limit (for example MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) does not prevent a user from requesting a generic --gres=gpu:2 and thereby obtaining two of that model; enforcing that requires a job_submit plugin or forcing users to request specific types.

Key behavior and admin notes
- Which fields control these limits: association/group-level fields such as GrpTRES (and other Grp* fields like GrpJobs) are used to limit aggregate resources for an association. These are evaluated when the scheduler considers a job for allocation.
- Enforcement prerequisites and effects:
  - AccountingStorageEnforce must include limits (i.e., AccountingStorageEnforce=limits) in slurm.conf for Slurm to enforce association limits.
  - When limits are lowered, running jobs are not retroactively killed to satisfy the new lower limits; new/queued jobs are blocked if they would exceed the lowered limits.
  - Deleting an association will cancel running or pending jobs that belong to that association immediately.
- Scheduling-time semantics: group limits are tested when a job is being considered. If the job would exceed the group limit, it won’t be scheduled even if preemption of other jobs would have freed enough resources.
- GRES type-vs-generic limit caveat: type-aware limits (gres/gpu:MODEL=...) only apply when jobs request that specific type. If users request generic GRES (gres/gpu without a model), the type-specific limit may not be enforced; use a job_submit plugin to require model-specific requests if you need strict enforcement.

How to view/change these limits
- Use sacctmgr to view and edit association limits (the sacctmgr man page and the Resource Limits documentation show the fields and syntax). Typical fields include GrpTRES, GrpJobs and the Max/Min TRES settings; GRES is expressed in TRES form (gres/...).
- Use sacctmgr show association (or sacctmgr list/show account/user with WithAssoc) to inspect current association limits/GrpTRES values; use sacctmgr modify (or add) to change them. Consult the sacctmgr documentation for exact command-line format.

Where to read the authoritative details
- See Slurm’s Resource Limits documentation (resource_limits) for the limit hierarchy and GRES/TRES examples, and the sacctmgr man page for association fields (GrpTRES, GrpJobs, etc.) and sacctmgr syntax.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being allocated/run; the job remains in the queue (typically in PENDING) and will not be scheduled until all active holds on it are removed.
- Holds are additive: a job can have multiple hold types at once. Removing one hold does not schedule the job if any other hold remains (or other scheduling constraints still block it).

Hold types and semantics
- UserHold
  - Intended for the job owner (or a user with appropriate privileges).
  - Commonly placed at submission time with sbatch --hold or later by the job owner (or by an admin acting on behalf).
  - The job owner (and admins) can release a UserHold.
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators (e.g., site policy or manual admin intervention).
  - Ordinary users cannot remove an AdminHold; only admins can release it.
- SystemHold
  - Placed by Slurm/system components for system-level reasons (maintenance, controller action, etc.).
  - Typically cleared by the system or by administrators when the underlying condition is resolved.

Commands and inspection
- Place a hold:
  - sbatch --hold (submit job in held state)
  - scontrol hold <jobid> (place a hold on an existing job)
- Clear a hold:
  - scontrol release <jobid> (release holds; permission rules apply — admins can clear Admin/System holds; owners can clear UserHold)
- Inspect hold/state:
  - squeue shows job state and often a reason column (held jobs display a hold-related reason).
  - scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed job fields (including hold info).
- Job arrays and components:
  - scontrol operations on an ArrayJobID apply to all elements by default; you can target individual elements with the element-specific jobid (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID).

Behavioral notes / interactions
- Holds prevent scheduling even if resources are available and any dependencies are satisfied. Releasing the hold only makes the job eligible again; it may still remain pending for other reasons (resources, dependencies, QOS limits, reservations, etc.).
- Holds do not terminate or cancel a job. A held job stays in the queue until released or explicitly cancelled.
- Holding a running job is not the same as suspending it; to stop a running job you would use job suspension/requeue mechanisms (scontrol suspend/requeue), not a hold.
- Permissions matter: who can set/release which hold type follows the Owner vs Admin vs System separation; admins have broader authority.

Practical tips
- Use sbatch --hold if you want a job submitted but prevent it from starting until you explicitly release it.
- Use scontrol show job and squeue to confirm which hold type(s) are present and why a job is not starting.
- If a job remains pending after release, check resource availability, dependencies, partition/reservation constraints, and QOS/limits.

Commands referenced
- sbatch --hold
- scontrol hold <jobid>
- scontrol release <jobid>
- squeue
- scontrol show job <jobid>
results.judge_reason: Used correct tool and provided accurate, comprehensive explanation.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text

```

```text

```

trials.agent_response:
Summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being allocated/run; the job remains in the queue (typically in PENDING) and will not be scheduled until all active holds on it are removed.
- Holds are additive: a job can have multiple hold types at once. Removing one hold does not schedule the job if any other hold remains (or other scheduling constraints still block it).

Hold types and semantics
- UserHold
  - Intended for the job owner (or a user with appropriate privileges).
  - Commonly placed at submission time with sbatch --hold or later by the job owner (or by an admin acting on behalf).
  - The job owner (and admins) can release a UserHold.
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators (e.g., site policy or manual admin intervention).
  - Ordinary users cannot remove an AdminHold; only admins can release it.
- SystemHold
  - Placed by Slurm/system components for system-level reasons (maintenance, controller action, etc.).
  - Typically cleared by the system or by administrators when the underlying condition is resolved.

Commands and inspection
- Place a hold:
  - sbatch --hold (submit job in held state)
  - scontrol hold <jobid> (place a hold on an existing job)
- Clear a hold:
  - scontrol release <jobid> (release holds; permission rules apply — admins can clear Admin/System holds; owners can clear UserHold)
- Inspect hold/state:
  - squeue shows job state and often a reason column (held jobs display a hold-related reason).
  - scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed job fields (including hold info).
- Job arrays and components:
  - scontrol operations on an ArrayJobID apply to all elements by default; you can target individual elements with the element-specific jobid (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID).

Behavioral notes / interactions
- Holds prevent scheduling even if resources are available and any dependencies are satisfied. Releasing the hold only makes the job eligible again; it may still remain pending for other reasons (resources, dependencies, QOS limits, reservations, etc.).
- Holds do not terminate or cancel a job. A held job stays in the queue until released or explicitly cancelled.
- Holding a running job is not the same as suspending it; to stop a running job you would use job suspension/requeue mechanisms (scontrol suspend/requeue), not a hold.
- Permissions matter: who can set/release which hold type follows the Owner vs Admin vs System separation; admins have broader authority.

Practical tips
- Use sbatch --hold if you want a job submitted but prevent it from starting until you explicitly release it.
- Use scontrol show job and squeue to confirm which hold type(s) are present and why a job is not starting.
- If a job remains pending after release, check resource availability, dependencies, partition/reservation constraints, and QOS/limits.

Commands referenced
- sbatch --hold
- scontrol hold <jobid>
- scontrol release <jobid>
- squeue
- scontrol show job <jobid>

## Other Command Use [#other_commands](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
The following Slurm commands do not currently recognize job arrays and their
use requires the use of Slurm job IDs, which are unique for each array element:
sbcast, sprio, sreport, sshare and sstat.
The sacct, sattach and strigger commands have been modified to permit
specification of either job IDs or job array elements.

and ArrayTaskId fields. Both fields are displayed with a value of "N/A" if
the job is not part of a job array.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being allocated/run; the job remains in the queue (typically in PENDING) and will not be scheduled until all active holds on it are removed.
- Holds are additive: a job can have multiple hold types at once. Removing one hold does not schedule the job if any other hold remains (or other scheduling constraints still block it).

Hold types and semantics
- UserHold
  - Intended for the job owner (or a user with appropriate privileges).
  - Commonly placed at submission time with sbatch --hold or later by the job owner (or by an admin acting on behalf).
  - The job owner (and admins) can release a UserHold.
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators (e.g., site policy or manual admin intervention).
  - Ordinary users cannot remove an AdminHold; only admins can release it.
- SystemHold
  - Placed by Slurm/system components for system-level reasons (maintenance, controller action, etc.).
  - Typically cleared by the system or by administrators when the underlying condition is resolved.

Commands and inspection
- Place a hold:
  - sbatch --hold (submit job in held state)
  - scontrol hold <jobid> (place a hold on an existing job)
- Clear a hold:
  - scontrol release <jobid> (release holds; permission rules apply — admins can clear Admin/System holds; owners can clear UserHold)
- Inspect hold/state:
  - squeue shows job state and often a reason column (held jobs display a hold-related reason).
  - scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed job fields (including hold info).
- Job arrays and components:
  - scontrol operations on an ArrayJobID apply to all elements by default; you can target individual elements with the element-specific jobid (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID).

Behavioral notes / interactions
- Holds prevent scheduling even if resources are available and any dependencies are satisfied. Releasing the hold only makes the job eligible again; it may still remain pending for other reasons (resources, dependencies, QOS limits, reservations, etc.).
- Holds do not terminate or cancel a job. A held job stays in the queue until released or explicitly cancelled.
- Holding a running job is not the same as suspending it; to stop a running job you would use job suspension/requeue mechanisms (scontrol suspend/requeue), not a hold.
- Permissions matter: who can set/release which hold type follows the Owner vs Admin vs System separation; admins have broader authority.

Practical tips
- Use sbatch --hold if you want a job submitted but prevent it from starting until you explicitly release it.
- Use scontrol show job and squeue to confirm which hold type(s) are present and why a job is not starting.
- If a job remains pending after release, check resource availability, dependencies, partition/reservation constraints, and QOS/limits.

Commands referenced
- sbatch --hold
- scontrol hold <jobid>
- scontrol release <jobid>
- squeue
- scontrol show job <jobid>
