results.prompt: Explain how scancel sends signals to jobs and steps
results.agent_response:
Short answer: scancel is a client that asks slurmctld to deliver signals; slurmctld tells the slurmd(s) on the node(s) to signal the tracked processes for the targeted job(s)/step(s). The slurmd uses the configured proctrack (e.g., proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux) mechanism to find the task PIDs (or the job’s cgroup) and then send the requested signals to those PIDs (or the group).

Details and important behaviors
- Targets: you can target whole jobs (1234), individual steps (1234.1), array or array-index forms (1237_4), users, partitions, states, etc. Cancelling a job step (1234.1) does not by itself cancel the whole job/allocation; cancelling the job releases the allocation.
- Default cancel sequence (no --signal): scancel jobID performs a polite cancel:
  - sends SIGCONT to all steps to wake them (if stopped),
  - then sends SIGTERM,
  - waits the KillWait time configured in slurm.conf,
  - and if processes are still running finally sends SIGKILL.
  This gives steps a chance to clean up before forcible termination.
- --signal: you can request an explicit signal (name or number) to send instead of the default cancel sequence. Example: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 sends SIGTERM to step 1 of job 1234.
  - If you send a SIGNAL=KILL to an entire job, Slurm will kill active steps (SIGKILL) but that signal form by itself does not necessarily show as a normal job-cancel operation (see docs for exact semantics).
- --batch (-b): by default signals other than SIGKILL are NOT sent to the batch step (the job’s shell script). Using --batch causes scancel to signal only the batch shell step (useful when the shell should trap the signal) and not other steps.
- Granularity: scancel can signal individual steps (only those will get the signal) or whole jobs (all active steps). Use the job.step syntax to address steps.
- How delivery is implemented: slurmd invokes the proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux plugin to enumerate the PIDs for the job/step. The proctrack plugin then issues the kernel signals (or operates via the cgroup interface) to reach every task in the job/step. On systems with cgroups/systemd, Slurm often confines tasks in a cgroup and signals the set of PIDs in that cgroup; on other systems it will signal the recorded PIDs directly.
- Cleanup vs allocation release: cancelling a job (scancel without --signal) releases the allocation. Sending a signal to steps (using --signal) may not release the allocation unless you explicitly cancel the job.

Examples
- scancel 1234
  - cancel job 1234: SIGCONT → SIGTERM → wait KillWait → SIGKILL
- scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
  - send SIGTERM to steps 1 and 3 only
- scancel --signal=KILL 1235
  - send SIGKILL to all steps of job 1235 (see docs: this will kill active steps but that signal form alone is treated differently from a full job cancel)
- scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236
  - send SIGUSR1 to the batch shell process only (so the shell can trap it)

If you want precise, version-specific edge cases (exact behavior for KILL vs cancel, or how signals interact with particular proctrack/cgroup configs), tell me your Slurm version and whether you use proctrack/cgroup (cgroups v1/v2) or proctrack/linux and I can point to the exact doc excerpts for that setup.

Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job

flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the

## Following systemd rules [#systemd_rules](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
Systemd is currently the most widely used init mechanism. For this reason
Slurm needs to find a way to coexist with the rules of systemd. The designers of
systemd have conceived a new rule called the "single-writer" rule, which implies
that every cgroup has one single owner and nobody else should write to it. Read
more about this in [systemd.io Cgroup Delegation Documentation](https://systemd.io/CGROUP_DELEGATION). In practice this means that the systemd
daemon, started when the kernel boots and which takes pid 1, will consider
itself the absolute owner and single writer of the entire cgroup tree.

cgroup directly, nor should another process be creating directories or moving
pids around, without systemd being aware of it.

trials.agent_response:
Short answer: scancel is a client that asks slurmctld to deliver signals; slurmctld tells the slurmd(s) on the node(s) to signal the tracked processes for the targeted job(s)/step(s). The slurmd uses the configured proctrack (e.g., proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux) mechanism to find the task PIDs (or the job’s cgroup) and then send the requested signals to those PIDs (or the group).

Details and important behaviors
- Targets: you can target whole jobs (1234), individual steps (1234.1), array or array-index forms (1237_4), users, partitions, states, etc. Cancelling a job step (1234.1) does not by itself cancel the whole job/allocation; cancelling the job releases the allocation.
- Default cancel sequence (no --signal): scancel jobID performs a polite cancel:
  - sends SIGCONT to all steps to wake them (if stopped),
  - then sends SIGTERM,
  - waits the KillWait time configured in slurm.conf,
  - and if processes are still running finally sends SIGKILL.
  This gives steps a chance to clean up before forcible termination.
- --signal: you can request an explicit signal (name or number) to send instead of the default cancel sequence. Example: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 sends SIGTERM to step 1 of job 1234.
  - If you send a SIGNAL=KILL to an entire job, Slurm will kill active steps (SIGKILL) but that signal form by itself does not necessarily show as a normal job-cancel operation (see docs for exact semantics).
- --batch (-b): by default signals other than SIGKILL are NOT sent to the batch step (the job’s shell script). Using --batch causes scancel to signal only the batch shell step (useful when the shell should trap the signal) and not other steps.
- Granularity: scancel can signal individual steps (only those will get the signal) or whole jobs (all active steps). Use the job.step syntax to address steps.
- How delivery is implemented: slurmd invokes the proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux plugin to enumerate the PIDs for the job/step. The proctrack plugin then issues the kernel signals (or operates via the cgroup interface) to reach every task in the job/step. On systems with cgroups/systemd, Slurm often confines tasks in a cgroup and signals the set of PIDs in that cgroup; on other systems it will signal the recorded PIDs directly.
- Cleanup vs allocation release: cancelling a job (scancel without --signal) releases the allocation. Sending a signal to steps (using --signal) may not release the allocation unless you explicitly cancel the job.

Examples
- scancel 1234
  - cancel job 1234: SIGCONT → SIGTERM → wait KillWait → SIGKILL
- scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
  - send SIGTERM to steps 1 and 3 only
- scancel --signal=KILL 1235
  - send SIGKILL to all steps of job 1235 (see docs: this will kill active steps but that signal form alone is treated differently from a full job cancel)
- scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236

Systemd is currently the most widely used init mechanism. For this reason
Slurm needs to find a way to coexist with the rules of systemd. The designers of
systemd have conceived a new rule called the "single-writer" rule, which implies
that every cgroup has one single owner and nobody else should write to it. Read

itself the absolute owner and single writer of the entire cgroup tree.

### Main differences between cgroup/v1 and cgroup/v2 [#differences](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroups.html)
The three main differences between v1 and v2 are:

Based on the current cluster state, short answer: scancel is a client that asks slurmctld to deliver signals; slurmctld tells the slurmd(s) on the node(s) to signal the tracked processes for the targeted job(s)/step(s). The slurmd uses the configured proctrack (e.g., proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux) mechanism to find the task PIDs (or the job’s cgroup) and then send the requested signals to those PIDs (or the group).

Details and important behaviors
- Targets: you can target whole jobs (1234), individual steps (1234.1), array or array-index forms (1237_4), users, partitions, states, etc. Cancelling a job step (1234.1) does not by itself cancel the whole job/allocation; cancelling the job releases the allocation.
- Default cancel sequence (no --signal): scancel jobID performs a polite cancel:
  - sends SIGCONT to all steps to wake them (if stopped),
  - then sends SIGTERM,
  - waits the KillWait time configured in slurm.conf,
  - and if processes are still running finally sends SIGKILL.
  This gives steps a chance to clean up before forcible termination.
- --signal: you can request an explicit signal (name or number) to send instead of the default cancel sequence. Example: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 sends SIGTERM to step 1 of job 1234.
  - If you send a SIGNAL=KILL to an entire job, Slurm will kill active steps (SIGKILL) but that signal form by itself does not necessarily show as a normal job-cancel operation (see docs for exact semantics).
- --batch (-b): by default signals other than SIGKILL are NOT sent to the batch step (the job’s shell script). Using --batch causes scancel to signal only the batch shell step (useful when the shell should trap the signal) and not other steps.
- Granularity: scancel can signal individual steps (only those will get the signal) or whole jobs (all active steps). Use the job.step syntax to address steps.
- How delivery is implemented: slurmd invokes the proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux plugin to enumerate the PIDs for the job/step. The proctrack plugin then issues the kernel signals (or operates via the cgroup interface) to reach every task in the job/step. On systems with cgroups/systemd, Slurm often confines tasks in a cgroup and signals the set of PIDs in that cgroup; on other systems it will signal the recorded PIDs directly.
- Cleanup vs allocation release: cancelling a job (scancel without --signal) releases the allocation. Sending a signal to steps (using --signal) may not release the allocation unless you explicitly cancel the job.

Examples
- scancel 1234
  - cancel job 1234: SIGCONT → SIGTERM → wait KillWait → SIGKILL
- scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
  - send SIGTERM to steps 1 and 3 only
- scancel --signal=KILL 1235
  - send SIGKILL to all steps of job 1235 (see docs: this will kill active steps but that signal form alone is treated differently from a full job cancel)
- scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236
  - send SIGUSR1 to the batch shell process only (so the shell can trap it)

If you want precise, version-specific edge cases (exact behavior for KILL vs cancel, or how signals interact with particular proctrack/cgroup configs), tell me your Slurm version and whether you use proctrack/cgroup (cgroups v1/v2) or proctrack/linux and I can point to the exact doc excerpts for that setup.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer: scancel is a client that asks slurmctld to deliver signals; slurmctld tells the slurmd(s) on the node(s) to signal the tracked processes for the targeted job(s)/step(s). The slurmd uses the configured proctrack (e.g., proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux) mechanism to find the task PIDs (or the job’s cgroup) and then send the requested signals to those PIDs (or the group).

Details and important behaviors
- Targets: you can target whole jobs (1234), individual steps (1234.1), array or array-index forms (1237_4), users, partitions, states, etc. Cancelling a job step (1234.1) does not by itself cancel the whole job/allocation; cancelling the job releases the allocation.
- Default cancel sequence (no --signal): scancel jobID performs a polite cancel:
  - sends SIGCONT to all steps to wake them (if stopped),
  - then sends SIGTERM,
  - waits the KillWait time configured in slurm.conf,
  - and if processes are still running finally sends SIGKILL.
  This gives steps a chance to clean up before forcible termination.
- --signal: you can request an explicit signal (name or number) to send instead of the default cancel sequence. Example: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 sends SIGTERM to step 1 of job 1234.
  - If you send a SIGNAL=KILL to an entire job, Slurm will kill active steps (SIGKILL) but that signal form by itself does not necessarily show as a normal job-cancel operation (see docs for exact semantics).
- --batch (-b): by default signals other than SIGKILL are NOT sent to the batch step (the job’s shell script). Using --batch causes scancel to signal only the batch shell step (useful when the shell should trap the signal) and not other steps.
- Granularity: scancel can signal individual steps (only those will get the signal) or whole jobs (all active steps). Use the job.step syntax to address steps.
- How delivery is implemented: slurmd invokes the proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux plugin to enumerate the PIDs for the job/step. The proctrack plugin then issues the kernel signals (or operates via the cgroup interface) to reach every task in the job/step. On systems with cgroups/systemd, Slurm often confines tasks in a cgroup and signals the set of PIDs in that cgroup; on other systems it will signal the recorded PIDs directly.
- Cleanup vs allocation release: cancelling a job (scancel without --signal) releases the allocation. Sending a signal to steps (using --signal) may not release the allocation unless you explicitly cancel the job.

Examples
- scancel 1234
  - cancel job 1234: SIGCONT → SIGTERM → wait KillWait → SIGKILL
- scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
  - send SIGTERM to steps 1 and 3 only
- scancel --signal=KILL 1235
  - send SIGKILL to all steps of job 1235 (see docs: this will kill active steps but that signal form alone is treated differently from a full job cancel)
- scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236
  - send SIGUSR1 to the batch shell process only (so the shell can trap it)

If you want precise, version-specific edge cases (exact behavior for KILL vs cancel, or how signals interact with particular proctrack/cgroup configs), tell me your Slurm version and whether you use proctrack/cgroup (cgroups v1/v2) or proctrack/linux and I can point to the exact doc excerpts for that setup.

Control Group is a mechanism provided by the kernel to organize processes
hierarchically and distribute system resources along the hierarchy in a
controlled and configurable manner. Slurm can make use of cgroups to constrain
different resources to jobs, steps and tasks, and to get accounting about these

Systemd is currently the most widely used init mechanism. For this reason
Slurm needs to find a way to coexist with the rules of systemd. The designers of
systemd have conceived a new rule called the "single-writer" rule, which implies

itself the absolute owner and single writer of the entire cgroup tree.

results.prompt: Compare srun, sbatch, and salloc from the Slurm docs
results.agent_response:
I looked up the Slurm docs for srun, sbatch, and salloc and summarized the practical differences and typical uses below.

Purpose / primary role
- sbatch — Batch submission: submit a job script to the scheduler for queued/executed batch jobs. sbatch returns a job ID and the script runs later under Slurm (outputs go to slurm-<jobid>.out unless overridden).
- salloc — Interactive allocation: request and hold a job allocation (nodes/CPUs/etc.) and run a user command (or open an interactive shell/xterm). The allocation is held until the command or shell exits.
- srun — Job-step launcher / task launcher: start tasks inside an existing allocation (or, if no allocation exists, srun can obtain an allocation and directly launch tasks). Commonly used inside sbatch scripts or inside an salloc session to launch parallel processes.

Typical workflows / when to use each
- Production/scheduled runs: write a batch script and use sbatch. Inside the script use srun to launch the parallel MPI/OMP tasks or serial commands as job steps.
- Interactive debugging or ad-hoc use: use salloc to get nodes/resource and either run srun inside the allocation or get a shell to work interactively on the allocated nodes.
- Single-command launch or step-level control: use srun when you want to launch a parallel job step directly (either inside an allocation or as a one-off allocation+launch).

Blocking / lifecycle differences
- sbatch: non-blocking submit; sbatch returns immediately with a job ID; the job runs later under normal queue lifecycle.
- salloc: blocks while waiting for allocation, then blocks while the allocation/command runs; relinquishes resources when the command/shell exits.
- srun: blocks while the launched tasks run (unless used with –background); if no existing allocation, srun may allocate resources and run, then release them when finished.

Interaction/roles together
- Typical batch script: sbatch myscript.sh -> inside script: srun -nN ./parallel_program
- Interactive allocation: salloc -N4 bash  (now you have an interactive shell on allocated nodes), then srun -n8 ./prog
- Direct launch: srun -N2 -n4 ./prog can be run without sbatch/salloc (Slurm will obtain needed resources for that step).

Other practical notes
- Output: sbatch jobs produce batch output files (slurm-<jobid>.out) by default. salloc/srun interactive runs send stdout/stderr to your terminal unless redirected.
- Environment: allocations set SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, etc.; srun job-steps inherit the allocation environment when run inside sbatch/salloc.
- Flexibility: srun can be used for fine-grained step control; sbatch is for queuing scripts; salloc is for interactive control and debugging.

If you want, I can paste short canonical examples from the docs (sbatch script example, salloc interactive example, srun examples) or show the exact manpage snippets used. Which would you prefer?

Based on the current cluster state, i looked up the Slurm docs for srun, sbatch, and salloc and summarized the practical differences and typical uses below.

Purpose / primary role
- sbatch — Batch submission: submit a job script to the scheduler for queued/executed batch jobs. sbatch returns a job ID and the script runs later under Slurm (outputs go to slurm-<jobid>.out unless overridden).
- salloc — Interactive allocation: request and hold a job allocation (nodes/CPUs/etc.) and run a user command (or open an interactive shell/xterm). The allocation is held until the command or shell exits.
- srun — Job-step launcher / task launcher: start tasks inside an existing allocation (or, if no allocation exists, srun can obtain an allocation and directly launch tasks). Commonly used inside sbatch scripts or inside an salloc session to launch parallel processes.

Typical workflows / when to use each
- Production/scheduled runs: write a batch script and use sbatch. Inside the script use srun to launch the parallel MPI/OMP tasks or serial commands as job steps.
- Interactive debugging or ad-hoc use: use salloc to get nodes/resource and either run srun inside the allocation or get a shell to work interactively on the allocated nodes.
- Single-command launch or step-level control: use srun when you want to launch a parallel job step directly (either inside an allocation or as a one-off allocation+launch).

Blocking / lifecycle differences
- sbatch: non-blocking submit; sbatch returns immediately with a job ID; the job runs later under normal queue lifecycle.
- salloc: blocks while waiting for allocation, then blocks while the allocation/command runs; relinquishes resources when the command/shell exits.
- srun: blocks while the launched tasks run (unless used with –background); if no existing allocation, srun may allocate resources and run, then release them when finished.

Interaction/roles together
- Typical batch script: sbatch myscript.sh -> inside script: srun -nN ./parallel_program
- Interactive allocation: salloc -N4 bash  (now you have an interactive shell on allocated nodes), then srun -n8 ./prog
- Direct launch: srun -N2 -n4 ./prog can be run without sbatch/salloc (Slurm will obtain needed resources for that step).

Other practical notes
- Output: sbatch jobs produce batch output files (slurm-<jobid>.out) by default. salloc/srun interactive runs send stdout/stderr to your terminal unless redirected.
- Environment: allocations set SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, etc.; srun job-steps inherit the allocation environment when run inside sbatch/salloc.
- Flexibility: srun can be used for fine-grained step control; sbatch is for queuing scripts; salloc is for interactive control and debugging.

results.prompt: Compare srun, sbatch, and salloc from the Slurm docs
results.agent_response:
Summary comparison (from the Slurm docs)

Purpose
- sbatch: Submit a batch script to the scheduler (non-interactive). The script runs later as a queued batch job.
- salloc: Request an interactive job allocation (a set of nodes/CPUs). When allocation is granted, run a command (or drop you into a shell) while holding those resources.
- srun: Launch job steps / parallel tasks. Can be used inside an existing allocation (sbatch or salloc) or used standalone to obtain an allocation and run a command.

Key behavioral differences
- Interactivity
  - sbatch: non-interactive (submit-and-return; job runs later).
  - salloc: interactive (waits until resources allocated, then runs command or shell; holds allocation until command exits).
  - srun: can be interactive when run from a shell (it will run the command and return); commonly used interactively inside an salloc shell or in a batch script to create job steps.

- Allocation vs launch
  - sbatch: submits a job request (scheduler handles allocation when resources available).
  - salloc: explicitly requests an allocation now (blocks until granted), then you get to use it interactively.
  - srun: launches tasks / job steps; if not already inside an allocation it can implicitly request an allocation for the command.

- Typical usage patterns
  - sbatch: long-running or repeatable batch workflows; use job scripts with #SBATCH directives. Returns a job ID immediately.
  - salloc: debugging, interactive development, or launching an interactive parallel environment (e.g., get nodes, then run MPI tests or start an interactive job).
  - srun: start MPI/parallel tasks (srun -nN ...), used within sbatch scripts to launch steps, or used together with salloc to run on the allocated nodes.

- Relationship to each other
  - Common pattern: salloc (get allocation) → srun (launch steps interactively).
  - Common batch pattern: sbatch (submit job) → inside script use srun to run parallel tasks/steps.
  - srun can also be used as a lightweight submitter (it may create an implicit allocation and run the command immediately).

- Return/visibility
  - sbatch: prints "Submitted batch job <jobid>" and exits; job output is captured to files.
  - salloc: waits until allocation granted, prints allocation job id, then runs the command/shell; relinquishes after command exits.
  - srun: runs the command and exits when it finishes; when used standalone it behaves synchronously for that command.

When to pick which
- Use sbatch when you want to submit a non-interactive batch job or job array to run later.
- Use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (a shell or interactive environment on allocated nodes).
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (inside sbatch or salloc) or to run a single parallel command immediately (it can also obtain resources implicitly).

Examples
- sbatch my_script.sh          # submit batch script → queued job
- salloc -N4 --time=01:00 bash  # get 4-node allocation, drop to shell on allocated nodes
- salloc -N4 srun -n16 ./a.out # get allocation and immediately run a parallel job
- srun -n8 hostname            # run 8 tasks (will allocate if not already in an allocation, or run as a step if inside one)

Notes / caveats
- Inside a batch script you typically use srun to launch the parallel program so Slurm creates job steps and accounts resources correctly.
- srun and salloc can both create allocations if none exist, but salloc is intended to hold nodes for interactive use; srun is focused on launching steps/tasks.
- Resource request flags (-N, -n, -c, --gres, --time, etc.) are accepted by all three but their meanings depend on whether you are requesting an allocation (salloc/sbatch) or launching tasks (srun).

If you want, I can paste the official one-line descriptions or short examples from the sbatch/salloc/srun man pages.

Purpose
- sbatch: Submit a batch script to the scheduler (non-interactive). The script runs later as a queued batch job.
- salloc: Request an interactive job allocation (a set of nodes/CPUs). When allocation is granted, run a command (or drop you into a shell) while holding those resources.
- srun: Launch job steps / parallel tasks. Can be used inside an existing allocation (sbatch or salloc) or used standalone to obtain an allocation and run a command.

Key behavioral differences
- Interactivity
  - sbatch: non-interactive (submit-and-return; job runs later).
  - salloc: interactive (waits until resources allocated, then runs command or shell; holds allocation until command exits).
  - srun: can be interactive when run from a shell (it will run the command and return); commonly used interactively inside an salloc shell or in a batch script to create job steps.

- Allocation vs launch
  - sbatch: submits a job request (scheduler handles allocation when resources available).
  - salloc: explicitly requests an allocation now (blocks until granted), then you get to use it interactively.
  - srun: launches tasks / job steps; if not already inside an allocation it can implicitly request an allocation for the command.

- Typical usage patterns
  - sbatch: long-running or repeatable batch workflows; use job scripts with #SBATCH directives. Returns a job ID immediately.
  - salloc: debugging, interactive development, or launching an interactive parallel environment (e.g., get nodes, then run MPI tests or start an interactive job).
  - srun: start MPI/parallel tasks (srun -nN ...), used within sbatch scripts to launch steps, or used together with salloc to run on the allocated nodes.

- Relationship to each other
  - Common pattern: salloc (get allocation) → srun (launch steps interactively).
  - Common batch pattern: sbatch (submit job) → inside script use srun to run parallel tasks/steps.
  - srun can also be used as a lightweight submitter (it may create an implicit allocation and run the command immediately).

  - sbatch: prints "Submitted batch job <jobid>" and exits; job output is captured to files.
  - salloc: waits until allocation granted, prints allocation job id, then runs the command/shell; relinquishes after command exits.
  - srun: runs the command and exits when it finishes; when used standalone it behaves synchronously for that command.

When to pick which
- Use sbatch when you want to submit a non-interactive batch job or job array to run later.
- Use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (a shell or interactive environment on allocated nodes).
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (inside sbatch or salloc) or to run a single parallel command immediately (it can also obtain resources implicitly).

- salloc -N4 srun -n16 ./a.out # get allocation and immediately run a parallel job

results.prompt: Explain sbcast and when it helps stage files to allocated nodes
results.agent_response:
What sbcast is (short)
- sbcast is a Slurm utility that transmits a file from the node where you run it to every node in the currently active Slurm allocation. It must be run from inside a job allocation (batch job or the shell from salloc/sbatch). The destination path should be on each node’s local filesystem (for example /tmp or $SLURM_TMPDIR).

When it helps (common, practical cases)
- Reduce shared-FS contention: when many tasks on many nodes would simultaneously read the same file from a shared filesystem (NFS/GPFS), sbcast stages a local copy on each node and avoids I/O hot spots.
- Distribute a single executable or small dataset to all allocated nodes (binaries, single data shard, model weights, small VM/container rootfs).
- Stage runtime dependencies: use --send-libs to also broadcast required shared libraries for a standalone binary.
- Use per-node local scratch: when your job needs good local I/O throughput or low-latency access to a file on each node.
- Faster than many ad-hoc per-node scp calls for small-to-moderate size files because Slurm uses a fanout distribution tree and optional compression.

When sbcast is not a good fit
- Very large files or many many small files: sbcast can be slower than a high-performance parallel filesystem, and many sbcast calls (one per file) can overload slurmctld. Tar/pack files first or use the shared FS if it scales better.
- Files that must be available cluster-wide outside the allocation: sbcast only targets nodes in your current allocation.
- If you already have an efficient distribution mechanism (CVMFS, preloaded images, container registry, cluster-wide shared FS), use that instead.

Key options and tips
- --compress / -C: enable compression (lz4 by default); helpful for compressible content.
- --fanout / -F N: tune parallel tree fanout (how many child transfers each node spawns); useful for very large allocations or networks with specific topology.
- --send-libs: autodetect and transmit required shared libraries for an executable.
- --preserve / -p: preserve mode and timestamps.
- --force / -f: overwrite existing files on nodes.
- Tar multiple files into one archive before broadcasting (reduce slurmctld RPCs and overhead), then extract on nodes.
- Put destination on local tmp ($SLURM_TMPDIR or /tmp); check node-local disk free space before staging.
- Avoid looping sbcast calls from scripts (each sbcast triggers an RPC to slurmctld — can overload the controller).

Minimal usage pattern (conceptual)
- Inside your job script or salloc shell:
  1) sbcast /path/on/submit/node/mybin /tmp/mybin
  2) srun chmod +x /tmp/mybin && srun /tmp/mybin  (or use $SLURM_TMPDIR instead of /tmp)

Performance cautions
- sbcast sends RPCs to slurmctld; lots of simultaneous or repeated sbcast calls can degrade the controller. Limit calls and bundle files where possible.
- For very large payloads, benchmark sbcast vs your parallel FS — performance depends on file size, node count, network topology, and slurm.conf BcastParameters.

In short
- Use sbcast when you need a single, consistent local copy of a file on every node in your allocation to avoid shared-FS hotspots or to satisfy local-disk-only requirements. For many files or very large files, bundle them or prefer an alternative distribution mechanism.

It must be run from inside a job allocation (batch job or the shell from salloc/sbatch). The destination path should be on each node’s local filesystem (for example /tmp or $SLURM_TMPDIR).

When it helps (common, practical cases)
- Reduce shared-FS contention: when many tasks on many nodes would simultaneously read the same file from a shared filesystem (NFS/GPFS), sbcast stages a local copy on each node and avoids I/O hot spots.
- Distribute a single executable or small dataset to all allocated nodes (binaries, single data shard, model weights, small VM/container rootfs).
- Stage runtime dependencies: use --send-libs to also broadcast required shared libraries for a standalone binary.
- Use per-node local scratch: when your job needs good local I/O throughput or low-latency access to a file on each node.
- Faster than many ad-hoc per-node scp calls for small-to-moderate size files because Slurm uses a fanout distribution tree and optional compression.

When sbcast is not a good fit
- Very large files or many many small files: sbcast can be slower than a high-performance parallel filesystem, and many sbcast calls (one per file) can overload slurmctld. Tar/pack files first or use the shared FS if it scales better.
- Files that must be available cluster-wide outside the allocation: sbcast only targets nodes in your current allocation.
- If you already have an efficient distribution mechanism (CVMFS, preloaded images, container registry, cluster-wide shared FS), use that instead.

Key options and tips
- --compress / -C: enable compression (lz4 by default); helpful for compressible content.
- --fanout / -F N: tune parallel tree fanout (how many child transfers each node spawns); useful for very large allocations or networks with specific topology.
- --send-libs: autodetect and transmit required shared libraries for an executable.
- --preserve / -p: preserve mode and timestamps.
- --force / -f: overwrite existing files on nodes.
- Tar multiple files into one archive before broadcasting (reduce slurmctld RPCs and overhead), then extract on nodes.
- Put destination on local tmp ($SLURM_TMPDIR or /tmp); check node-local disk free space before staging.
- Avoid looping sbcast calls from scripts (each sbcast triggers an RPC to slurmctld — can overload the controller).

Minimal usage pattern (conceptual)
- Inside your job script or salloc shell:
  1) sbcast /path/on/submit/node/mybin /tmp/mybin
  2) srun chmod +x /tmp/mybin && srun /tmp/mybin  (or use $SLURM_TMPDIR instead of /tmp)

Performance cautions
- sbcast sends RPCs to slurmctld; lots of simultaneous or repeated sbcast calls can degrade the controller. Limit calls and bundle files where possible.
- For very large payloads, benchmark sbcast vs your parallel FS — performance depends on file size, node count, network topology, and slurm.conf BcastParameters.

In short
- Use sbcast when you need a single, consistent local copy of a file on every node in your allocation to avoid shared-FS hotspots or to satisfy local-disk-only requirements. For many files or very large files, bundle them or prefer an alternative distribution mechanism.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
Summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. It’s how Slurm advertises and allocates non-CPU resources such as GPUs, MPS slots, MIG instances, license tokens, shards, etc.
- Node-level configuration lives in slurm.conf (Gres= on NodeName lines) and optionally per-node gres.conf (detailed device mapping / AutoDetect). The scheduler matches job requests against the configured GRES.

Key GRES syntax (node config)
- In slurm.conf you typically set: NodeName=node[01-08] Gres=gpu:4,mps:200
- In gres.conf each device can be described; Slurm supports AutoDetect (nvml/rsmi/oneapi) to discover GPU devices.
- GRES element format (job-side requests): name[:type:count]
  - name: GRES name (commonly "gpu")
  - type: optional string to distinguish device types (e.g., v100, a100, or a MIG profile substring)
  - count: number required (integer)
  - Examples: gpu:2   gpu:tesla:2   mps:50

Requesting GPUs at submit time
- --gres (generic): --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - Example: sbatch --gres=gpu:2  (requests 2 GPUs per allocated node by the select plugin semantics)
  - Example with type: --gres=gpu:V100:2 (requests GPUs whose type string contains "V100")
- Convenience / GPU-specific options (shortcuts; require select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N
    - Requests N GPUs for the job allocation (total GPUs for the job). Often equivalent to requesting --gres=gpu:N but semantics depend on whether you combine with -N/-n.
  - --gpus-per-node=N
    - Equivalent to --gres for GPUs: request N GPUs on each allocated node.
  - --gpus-per-task=N
    - Request N GPUs for each task; requires you also set a task count (e.g., --ntasks or srun task counts).
  - --gpus-per-socket, --gpus-per-core also exist for socket/core-level placement in clusters that support them.

How counts map into allocations (common patterns)
- Single-node 2 GPUs: sbatch --gpus=2 or sbatch --gres=gpu:2
- Two nodes, 1 GPU each: sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=1  (get 2 nodes × 1 GPU)
- MPI with one GPU per rank: sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks-per-node=4  (4 tasks on node, each gets 1 GPU — requires enough GPUs on node)
- If you use --gpus (total) plus multiple nodes, scheduler may place them across nodes to satisfy the total; use --gpus-per-node to guarantee per-node counts.

MIG, MPS, sharding and partial-GPU resources
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG instances. MIG profiles can be exposed as separate GRES; type in name[:type:count] can match a MIG profile substring.
- MPS/sharding: Slurm can expose sharable resources like mps or shard in slurm.conf/gres.conf. You request them with --gres=mps:50 (counts are configured by admin). MPS/shard allocations have special semantics and require appropriate plugins.
- Note: requesting a fractional GPU (percent) is admin-configured via sharding/MPS; plain "gpu:0.5" is not supported — you request integer counts of the configured GRES units.

Environment variables and device visibility
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps to limit each step’s visible GPU devices to the ones allocated on that node. This is how Slurm ensures distinct assignments between jobs.
- The exact env vars available can vary by Slurm version and local configuration; always check your job environment if you rely on a specific variable.

Accounting and monitoring
- If AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled, Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil (NVML/rsmi required) for accounting.
- TRES name for GPUs is typically gres/gpu (and can show up in sacct output if accounting is configured).

Requirements & gotchas
- select/cons_tres plugin: the modern --gpus* options and many GRES features require the select/cons_tres plugin; jobs that request GPU options on systems not configured with that plugin will be rejected.
- Types must match admin configuration: if admins used a custom GRES type string in gres.conf (or used MIG profile substrings), you must match that type string when requesting specific types.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES maps to device indices visible inside the job, not necessarily the physical device IDs you see with nvidia-smi on the whole node. cgroups may be used to restrict device files too.
- If your job is pending with a GPU request, use sinfo and squeue to inspect partition/node GPU availability (and pending reason). If unsure which type to request, ask your cluster admins or inspect node gres with sinfo or node slurmd logs.

Practical examples
- Simple 2-GPU batch script:
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
  #SBATCH -t 02:00:00
  ...
- Request 1 GPU per task for 8 MPI ranks (8 GPUs total, assigned per rank):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Two nodes, 2 GPUs per node:
  sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=2 myscript.sh
- Request specific GPU type:
  sbatch --gres=gpu:A100:4 my_a100_job.sh

If you want, I can:
- Show exact local examples based on your cluster’s gres configuration (I’d read sinfo/gres or show gres.conf), or
- Help convert a particular MPI/CUDA job script to the correct --gpus/--gres usage for one-GPU-per-rank or multi-GPU-per-node patterns.

Which would you prefer?

trials.agent_response:
Summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. It’s how Slurm advertises and allocates non-CPU resources such as GPUs, MPS slots, MIG instances, license tokens, shards, etc.
- Node-level configuration lives in slurm.conf (Gres= on NodeName lines) and optionally per-node gres.conf (detailed device mapping / AutoDetect). The scheduler matches job requests against the configured GRES.

Key GRES syntax (node config)
- In slurm.conf you typically set: NodeName=node[01-08] Gres=gpu:4,mps:200
- In gres.conf each device can be described; Slurm supports AutoDetect (nvml/rsmi/oneapi) to discover GPU devices.
- GRES element format (job-side requests): name[:type:count]
  - name: GRES name (commonly "gpu")
  - type: optional string to distinguish device types (e.g., v100, a100, or a MIG profile substring)
  - count: number required (integer)
  - Examples: gpu:2   gpu:tesla:2   mps:50

Requesting GPUs at submit time
- --gres (generic): --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - Example: sbatch --gres=gpu:2  (requests 2 GPUs per allocated node by the select plugin semantics)
  - Example with type: --gres=gpu:V100:2 (requests GPUs whose type string contains "V100")
- Convenience / GPU-specific options (shortcuts; require select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N
    - Requests N GPUs for the job allocation (total GPUs for the job). Often equivalent to requesting --gres=gpu:N but semantics depend on whether you combine with -N/-n.
  - --gpus-per-node=N
    - Equivalent to --gres for GPUs: request N GPUs on each allocated node.
  - --gpus-per-task=N
    - Request N GPUs for each task; requires you also set a task count (e.g., --ntasks or srun task counts).
  - --gpus-per-socket, --gpus-per-core also exist for socket/core-level placement in clusters that support them.

How counts map into allocations (common patterns)
- Single-node 2 GPUs: sbatch --gpus=2 or sbatch --gres=gpu:2
- Two nodes, 1 GPU each: sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=1  (get 2 nodes × 1 GPU)
- MPI with one GPU per rank: sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks-per-node=4  (4 tasks on node, each gets 1 GPU — requires enough GPUs on node)
- If you use --gpus (total) plus multiple nodes, scheduler may place them across nodes to satisfy the total; use --gpus-per-node to guarantee per-node counts.

MIG, MPS, sharding and partial-GPU resources
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG instances. MIG profiles can be exposed as separate GRES; type in name[:type:count] can match a MIG profile substring.
- MPS/sharding: Slurm can expose sharable resources like mps or shard in slurm.conf/gres.conf. You request them with --gres=mps:50 (counts are configured by admin). MPS/shard allocations have special semantics and require appropriate plugins.
- Note: requesting a fractional GPU (percent) is admin-configured via sharding/MPS; plain "gpu:0.5" is not supported — you request integer counts of the configured GRES units.

Environment variables and device visibility
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps to limit each step’s visible GPU devices to the ones allocated on that node. This is how Slurm ensures distinct assignments between jobs.
- The exact env vars available can vary by Slurm version and local configuration; always check your job environment if you rely on a specific variable.

Accounting and monitoring
- If AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled, Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil (NVML/rsmi required) for accounting.
- TRES name for GPUs is typically gres/gpu (and can show up in sacct output if accounting is configured).

Requirements & gotchas
- select/cons_tres plugin: the modern --gpus* options and many GRES features require the select/cons_tres plugin; jobs that request GPU options on systems not configured with that plugin will be rejected.
- Types must match admin configuration: if admins used a custom GRES type string in gres.conf (or used MIG profile substrings), you must match that type string when requesting specific types.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES maps to device indices visible inside the job, not necessarily the physical device IDs you see with nvidia-smi on the whole node. cgroups may be used to restrict device files too.
- If your job is pending with a GPU request, use sinfo and squeue to inspect partition/node GPU availability (and pending reason). If unsure which type to request, ask your cluster admins or inspect node gres with sinfo or node slurmd logs.

Practical examples
- Simple 2-GPU batch script:
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
  #SBATCH -t 02:00:00
  ...
- Request 1 GPU per task for 8 MPI ranks (8 GPUs total, assigned per rank):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Two nodes, 2 GPUs per node:
  sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=2 myscript.sh
- Request specific GPU type:
  sbatch --gres=gpu:A100:4 my_a100_job.sh

If you want, I can:
- Show exact local examples based on your cluster’s gres configuration (I’d read sinfo/gres or show gres.conf), or
- Help convert a particular MPI/CUDA job script to the correct --gpus/--gres usage for one-GPU-per-rank or multi-GPU-per-node patterns.

Which would you prefer?

Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores
while jobs use sockets.

restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

Based on the current cluster state, summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. It’s how Slurm advertises and allocates non-CPU resources such as GPUs, MPS slots, MIG instances, license tokens, shards, etc.
- Node-level configuration lives in slurm.conf (Gres= on NodeName lines) and optionally per-node gres.conf (detailed device mapping / AutoDetect). The scheduler matches job requests against the configured GRES.

Key GRES syntax (node config)
- In slurm.conf you typically set: NodeName=node[01-08] Gres=gpu:4,mps:200
- In gres.conf each device can be described; Slurm supports AutoDetect (nvml/rsmi/oneapi) to discover GPU devices.
- GRES element format (job-side requests): name[:type:count]
  - name: GRES name (commonly "gpu")
  - type: optional string to distinguish device types (e.g., v100, a100, or a MIG profile substring)
  - count: number required (integer)
  - Examples: gpu:2   gpu:tesla:2   mps:50

Requesting GPUs at submit time
- --gres (generic): --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - Example: sbatch --gres=gpu:2  (requests 2 GPUs per allocated node by the select plugin semantics)
  - Example with type: --gres=gpu:V100:2 (requests GPUs whose type string contains "V100")
- Convenience / GPU-specific options (shortcuts; require select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N
    - Requests N GPUs for the job allocation (total GPUs for the job). Often equivalent to requesting --gres=gpu:N but semantics depend on whether you combine with -N/-n.
  - --gpus-per-node=N
    - Equivalent to --gres for GPUs: request N GPUs on each allocated node.
  - --gpus-per-task=N
    - Request N GPUs for each task; requires you also set a task count (e.g., --ntasks or srun task counts).
  - --gpus-per-socket, --gpus-per-core also exist for socket/core-level placement in clusters that support them.

How counts map into allocations (common patterns)
- Single-node 2 GPUs: sbatch --gpus=2 or sbatch --gres=gpu:2
- Two nodes, 1 GPU each: sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=1  (get 2 nodes × 1 GPU)
- MPI with one GPU per rank: sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks-per-node=4  (4 tasks on node, each gets 1 GPU — requires enough GPUs on node)
- If you use --gpus (total) plus multiple nodes, scheduler may place them across nodes to satisfy the total; use --gpus-per-node to guarantee per-node counts.

MIG, MPS, sharding and partial-GPU resources
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG instances. MIG profiles can be exposed as separate GRES; type in name[:type:count] can match a MIG profile substring.
- MPS/sharding: Slurm can expose sharable resources like mps or shard in slurm.conf/gres.conf. You request them with --gres=mps:50 (counts are configured by admin). MPS/shard allocations have special semantics and require appropriate plugins.
- Note: requesting a fractional GPU (percent) is admin-configured via sharding/MPS; plain "gpu:0.5" is not supported — you request integer counts of the configured GRES units.

Environment variables and device visibility
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps to limit each step’s visible GPU devices to the ones allocated on that node. This is how Slurm ensures distinct assignments between jobs.
- The exact env vars available can vary by Slurm version and local configuration; always check your job environment if you rely on a specific variable.

Accounting and monitoring
- If AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled, Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil (NVML/rsmi required) for accounting.
- TRES name for GPUs is typically gres/gpu (and can show up in sacct output if accounting is configured).

Requirements & gotchas
- select/cons_tres plugin: the modern --gpus* options and many GRES features require the select/cons_tres plugin; jobs that request GPU options on systems not configured with that plugin will be rejected.
- Types must match admin configuration: if admins used a custom GRES type string in gres.conf (or used MIG profile substrings), you must match that type string when requesting specific types.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES maps to device indices visible inside the job, not necessarily the physical device IDs you see with nvidia-smi on the whole node. cgroups may be used to restrict device files too.
- If your job is pending with a GPU request, use sinfo and squeue to inspect partition/node GPU availability (and pending reason). If unsure which type to request, ask your cluster admins or inspect node gres with sinfo or node slurmd logs.

Practical examples
- Simple 2-GPU batch script:
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
  #SBATCH -t 02:00:00
  ...
- Request 1 GPU per task for 8 MPI ranks (8 GPUs total, assigned per rank):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Two nodes, 2 GPUs per node:
  sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=2 myscript.sh
- Request specific GPU type:
  sbatch --gres=gpu:A100:4 my_a100_job.sh

If you want, I can:
- Show exact local examples based on your cluster’s gres configuration (I’d read sinfo/gres or show gres.conf), or
- Help convert a particular MPI/CUDA job script to the correct --gpus/--gres usage for one-GPU-per-rank or multi-GPU-per-node patterns.

Which would you prefer?

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

## AutoDetect [#AutoDetect](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.
Note that AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries
installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the
nvml library to be installed, but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks.

## Accounting [#Accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
GPU memory and GPU utilization can be tracked as
[TRES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html) for tasks using GPU
resources. If `AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu` is configured,
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil will automatically be configured and gathered from
GPU jobs. gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil can also be set individually when
gres/gpu is not set.
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil are only available for NVIDIA GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=nvml`, and AMD GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=rsmi`.
NVML does not support utilization metrics for MIGs, so Slurm does not
provide gpumem or gpuutil accounting for MIG devices. See
[NVIDIA's MIG User Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/mig-user-guide/).

## Socket Affinity Configuration [#Socket_Affinity](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores
while jobs use sockets.
To prevent administrators from specify a core affinity for the device that
Slurm cannot currently respect, Slurm validates that any specified `Cores` align with socket boundaries and will generate
errors if they do not.

## MIG Management [#MIG_Management](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").
Several options are available for configuring shards in the gres.conf file
as listed below with examples following that:

## Running Jobs [#Running_Jobs](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Jobs will not be allocated any generic resources unless specifically
requested at job submit time using the options:
--gres
Generic resources required per node
--gpus
GPUs required per job
--gpus-per-node
GPUs required per node. Equivalent to the --gres option for GPUs.
--gpus-per-socket
GPUs required per socket. Requires the job to specify a task socket.
--gpus-per-task
GPUs required per task. Requires the job to specify a task count.

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. It’s how Slurm advertises and allocates non-CPU resources such as GPUs, MPS slots, MIG instances, license tokens, shards, etc.
- Node-level configuration lives in slurm.conf (Gres= on NodeName lines) and optionally per-node gres.conf (detailed device mapping / AutoDetect). The scheduler matches job requests against the configured GRES.

Key GRES syntax (node config)
- In slurm.conf you typically set: NodeName=node[01-08] Gres=gpu:4,mps:200
- In gres.conf each device can be described; Slurm supports AutoDetect (nvml/rsmi/oneapi) to discover GPU devices.
- GRES element format (job-side requests): name[:type:count]
  - name: GRES name (commonly "gpu")
  - type: optional string to distinguish device types (e.g., v100, a100, or a MIG profile substring)
  - count: number required (integer)
  - Examples: gpu:2   gpu:tesla:2   mps:50

Requesting GPUs at submit time
- --gres (generic): --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - Example: sbatch --gres=gpu:2  (requests 2 GPUs per allocated node by the select plugin semantics)
  - Example with type: --gres=gpu:V100:2 (requests GPUs whose type string contains "V100")
- Convenience / GPU-specific options (shortcuts; require select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N
    - Requests N GPUs for the job allocation (total GPUs for the job). Often equivalent to requesting --gres=gpu:N but semantics depend on whether you combine with -N/-n.
  - --gpus-per-node=N
    - Equivalent to --gres for GPUs: request N GPUs on each allocated node.
  - --gpus-per-task=N
    - Request N GPUs for each task; requires you also set a task count (e.g., --ntasks or srun task counts).
  - --gpus-per-socket, --gpus-per-core also exist for socket/core-level placement in clusters that support them.

How counts map into allocations (common patterns)
- Single-node 2 GPUs: sbatch --gpus=2 or sbatch --gres=gpu:2
- Two nodes, 1 GPU each: sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=1  (get 2 nodes × 1 GPU)
- MPI with one GPU per rank: sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks-per-node=4  (4 tasks on node, each gets 1 GPU — requires enough GPUs on node)
- If you use --gpus (total) plus multiple nodes, scheduler may place them across nodes to satisfy the total; use --gpus-per-node to guarantee per-node counts.

MIG, MPS, sharding and partial-GPU resources
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG instances. MIG profiles can be exposed as separate GRES; type in name[:type:count] can match a MIG profile substring.
- MPS/sharding: Slurm can expose sharable resources like mps or shard in slurm.conf/gres.conf. You request them with --gres=mps:50 (counts are configured by admin). MPS/shard allocations have special semantics and require appropriate plugins.
- Note: requesting a fractional GPU (percent) is admin-configured via sharding/MPS; plain "gpu:0.5" is not supported — you request integer counts of the configured GRES units.

Environment variables and device visibility
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps to limit each step’s visible GPU devices to the ones allocated on that node. This is how Slurm ensures distinct assignments between jobs.
- The exact env vars available can vary by Slurm version and local configuration; always check your job environment if you rely on a specific variable.

Accounting and monitoring
- If AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled, Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil (NVML/rsmi required) for accounting.
- TRES name for GPUs is typically gres/gpu (and can show up in sacct output if accounting is configured).

Requirements & gotchas
- select/cons_tres plugin: the modern --gpus* options and many GRES features require the select/cons_tres plugin; jobs that request GPU options on systems not configured with that plugin will be rejected.
- Types must match admin configuration: if admins used a custom GRES type string in gres.conf (or used MIG profile substrings), you must match that type string when requesting specific types.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES maps to device indices visible inside the job, not necessarily the physical device IDs you see with nvidia-smi on the whole node. cgroups may be used to restrict device files too.
- If your job is pending with a GPU request, use sinfo and squeue to inspect partition/node GPU availability (and pending reason). If unsure which type to request, ask your cluster admins or inspect node gres with sinfo or node slurmd logs.

Practical examples
- Simple 2-GPU batch script:
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
  #SBATCH -t 02:00:00
  ...
- Request 1 GPU per task for 8 MPI ranks (8 GPUs total, assigned per rank):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Two nodes, 2 GPUs per node:
  sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=2 myscript.sh
- Request specific GPU type:
  sbatch --gres=gpu:A100:4 my_a100_job.sh

- Show exact local examples based on your cluster’s gres configuration (I’d read sinfo/gres or show gres.conf), or
- Help convert a particular MPI/CUDA job script to the correct --gpus/--gres usage for one-GPU-per-rank or multi-GPU-per-node patterns.

If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.

## Accounting [#Accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
GPU memory and GPU utilization can be tracked as
[TRES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html) for tasks using GPU
resources. If `AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu` is configured,
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil will automatically be configured and gathered from
GPU jobs. gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil can also be set individually when
gres/gpu is not set.
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil are only available for NVIDIA GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=nvml`, and AMD GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=rsmi`.
NVML does not support utilization metrics for MIGs, so Slurm does not
provide gpumem or gpuutil accounting for MIG devices. See

## Socket Affinity Configuration [#Socket_Affinity](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores
while jobs use sockets.
To prevent administrators from specify a core affinity for the device that
Slurm cannot currently respect, Slurm validates that any specified `Cores` align with socket boundaries and will generate
errors if they do not.

Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.

Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be

Jobs will not be allocated any generic resources unless specifically
requested at job submit time using the options:
--gres
Generic resources required per node
--gpus
GPUs required per job

GPUs required per node. Equivalent to the --gres option for GPUs.
--gpus-per-socket
GPUs required per socket. Requires the job to specify a task socket.
--gpus-per-task

srun commands.

## Accounting [#Accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
GPU memory and GPU utilization can be tracked as
[TRES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html) for tasks using GPU
resources. If `AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu` is configured,
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil will automatically be configured and gathered from
GPU jobs. gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil can also be set individually when
gres/gpu is not set.
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil are only available for NVIDIA GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=nvml`, and AMD GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=rsmi`.
NVML does not support utilization metrics for MIGs, so Slurm does not
provide gpumem or gpuutil accounting for MIG devices. See
[NVIDIA's MIG User Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/mig-user-guide/).

## MIG Management [#MIG_Management](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`
in slurm.conf as if the MIGs were regular GPUs, like this:
`NodeName=tux[1-16] gres=gpu:2`. An optional

## Environment Variables [#env_var](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm environment variables will be set independently for each component of
the job by appending "_HET_GROUP_" and a sequence number to the usual name.
In addition, the "SLURM_JOB_ID" environment variable will contain the job ID
of the heterogeneous job leader and "SLURM_HET_SIZE" will contain the number of
components in the job. Note that if using srun with a single specific
het group (for instance --het-group=1) "SLURM_JOB_ID" will contain the job
ID of the heterogeneous job leader. The job ID for a specific heterogeneous
component is set in "SLURM_JOB_ID_HET_GROUP_<component_id>". For example:

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.
The order of precedence for determining what configuration source to use
is as follows:
- The slurmd --conf-server $host[:$port] option
- The -f $config_file option
- The SLURM_CONF environment variable (if set)
- A local slurm config file: The default slurm config file (likely /etc/slurm.conf)

slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be
consistent across all nodes in the cluster.
The file location can be modified at execution time by setting the SLURM_CONF
environment variable. The Slurm daemons also allow you to override
both the built-in and environment-provided location using the "-f"
option on the command line.
The contents of the file are case insensitive except for the names of nodes
and partitions. Any text following a "#" in the configuration file is treated
as a comment through the end of that line.

results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
Summary first
- --gres=gpu:N (the historical generic-resource form) requests N GPUs per node for your job step.
- Slurm also provides user-friendly aliases: --gpus=<count> (GPUs per job/allocation), --gpus-per-node=<count> (GPUs per node), and --gpus-per-task=<count> (GPUs attached to each task).
- Slurm will allocate whole GPU devices unless your cluster is configured for sharing (MPS, sharding, or MIG slices). Slurm then sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job to make only the allocated device(s) visible.

Details

1) The request forms and what they mean
- --gres=gpu[:<type>:]<count>
  - The gres option is a per-node generic-resource request. By default that means "<count> GPUs per node".
- --gpus=<count>
  - Requests <count> GPUs for the whole job/allocation (total across nodes).
- --gpus-per-node=<count>
  - Equivalent to asking for that many GPUs on every node in the allocation.
- --gpus-per-task=<count>
  - Requests that many GPUs for each task (requires supplying a task count). Slurm tries to place/assign GPUs so each task gets the requested number.

Note: the --gpu* options require the select/cons_tres plugin (and proper gres.conf / slurm.conf) on the cluster; otherwise the request will be rejected.

2) How Slurm chooses devices and what your job sees
- Device mapping: GPUs are configured via gres.conf (or autodetected). Slurm maps the logical "gpu" gres units to physical device files (/dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidia1, or MIG slice devices) on each node.
- Visibility: for each job step that runs on a node, Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to a comma-separated list of node-local device indices that the step may use. This is done per node and per step:
  - For sbatch the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES you see in the job environment reflects the allocation on node 0 of the allocation (sbatch sets the environment only from node 0).
  - When tasks are launched on other nodes, the step-launch environment for those tasks will also have CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set on that node to the devices allocated there.
- Device numbering is node-local. "GPU 0" on nodeA is independent of "GPU 0" on nodeB.
- If the cluster is configured to use cgroups to restrict device node access, Slurm may also hide or whitelist /dev/nvidia* devices inside the job's cgroup in addition to setting CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.

3) Whole-device vs sharing
- By default Slurm allocates whole GPUs (one gres unit = whole device).
- Sharing options:
  - MPS (CUDA Multi-Process Service): when configured, Slurm can allocate fractional MPS resources (configured via gres/mps).
  - Sharding: Slurm's sharding feature lets you configure many shards per GPU and allocate them as GRES; this does not fence the hardware — it's a logical share.
  - MIG (NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU): Slurm can be configured (AutoDetect=nvml, and correct gres.conf) to detect and allocate MIG slices as separate GRES units. Behavior depends on how the system admin set up gres.conf.
- If your site supports any of the above, you must check how the cluster exposes those resources (gres type names, environment vars, or device files).

4) Binding GPUs to tasks (common patterns)
- If you want 1 GPU per MPI rank / per process:
  - Use --gpus-per-task=1 and launch one task per rank (e.g., srun --ntasks=NUM_RANKS ...). Slurm will attempt to assign distinct GPUs to each task.
- If you want N GPUs on each node for a single multi-GPU job:
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:N -N1 or sbatch --gpus-per-node=N -N1
- If you request a total number of GPUs (--gpus=TOTAL) across multiple nodes, Slurm will distribute GPUs across nodes to satisfy the count and your other constraints (node count, partitions, etc.).
- Newer Slurm versions provide --gpu-bind (and related options) to control how GPUs are selected/mapped to tasks (see your cluster docs / man page).

5) How to confirm what you got (debugging tips)
- Inside a job step run:
  - echo $CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
  - nvidia-smi -L
  - nvidia-smi topo - or nvidia-smi (shows devices visible and UUIDs)
- From the controller/admin side use: scontrol show job <jobid> (AllocTRES, GresDetail) or scontrol show node to inspect gres configuration (admins). As a user, check your job environment variables as above.

6) Practical examples
- Request 2 GPUs on a single node:
  - sbatch --gpus-per-node=2 -N1 ...
  - or sbatch --gres=gpu:2 -N1 ...
- Request 8 GPUs total and let scheduler pick nodes:
  - sbatch --gpus=8 ...
  - The scheduler may give 4 nodes × 2 GPUs each, or 2 nodes × 4 GPUs each, depending on availability and constraints.
- Request 1 GPU per task for a 16-rank job:
  - sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks=16 ...
  - or srun --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks=16 ...

7) Version / site differences
- Exact environment variables exposed (besides CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) and support for MIG/MPS/sharding depend on Slurm version and how your cluster is configured (gres.conf, slurm.conf, and cgroup settings). Some clusters also set SLURM_JOB_GPUS or SLURM_STEP_GPUS — check your cluster's srun/sbatch man pages or ask your admin.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact GRES configuration or current gpu partition state on your cluster (sinfo / scontrol show node) — or
- give exact example sbatch/srun lines for your workflow (single-GPU training, multi-GPU DDP, MPI+GPU), or
- explain how to force a particular mapping with --gpu-bind.

Which would you like?

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
node.

## Environment Variables [#env_var](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm environment variables will be set independently for each component of
the job by appending "_HET_GROUP_" and a sequence number to the usual name.
In addition, the "SLURM_JOB_ID" environment variable will contain the job ID
of the heterogeneous job leader and "SLURM_HET_SIZE" will contain the number of
components in the job. Note that if using srun with a single specific
het group (for instance --het-group=1) "SLURM_JOB_ID" will contain the job
ID of the heterogeneous job leader. The job ID for a specific heterogeneous

```text

### Special case - manual startup [#manual_startup](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
Starting slurmd from systemd creates the slurmd unit with its own cgroup.
Then slurmd starts the slurmstepd.scope which in turn creates a new cgroup
tree. Any new process spawned for a job is migrated into this scope. If,
instead of starting slurmd from systemd, one starts slurmd manually from the
command line, things are different. The slurmd will be spawned into the same
terminal's cgroup and will share the cgroup tree with the terminal process
itself (and possibly with other user processes).
This situation is detected by slurmd by reading the INVOCATION_ID
environment variable. This variable is normally set by systemd when it starts

trials.agent_response:
Summary first
- --gres=gpu:N (the historical generic-resource form) requests N GPUs per node for your job step.
- Slurm also provides user-friendly aliases: --gpus=<count> (GPUs per job/allocation), --gpus-per-node=<count> (GPUs per node), and --gpus-per-task=<count> (GPUs attached to each task).
- Slurm will allocate whole GPU devices unless your cluster is configured for sharing (MPS, sharding, or MIG slices). Slurm then sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job to make only the allocated device(s) visible.

Details

1) The request forms and what they mean
- --gres=gpu[:<type>:]<count>
  - The gres option is a per-node generic-resource request. By default that means "<count> GPUs per node".
- --gpus=<count>
  - Requests <count> GPUs for the whole job/allocation (total across nodes).
- --gpus-per-node=<count>
  - Equivalent to asking for that many GPUs on every node in the allocation.
- --gpus-per-task=<count>
  - Requests that many GPUs for each task (requires supplying a task count). Slurm tries to place/assign GPUs so each task gets the requested number.

Note: the --gpu* options require the select/cons_tres plugin (and proper gres.conf / slurm.conf) on the cluster; otherwise the request will be rejected.

2) How Slurm chooses devices and what your job sees
- Device mapping: GPUs are configured via gres.conf (or autodetected). Slurm maps the logical "gpu" gres units to physical device files (/dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidia1, or MIG slice devices) on each node.
- Visibility: for each job step that runs on a node, Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to a comma-separated list of node-local device indices that the step may use. This is done per node and per step:
  - For sbatch the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES you see in the job environment reflects the allocation on node 0 of the allocation (sbatch sets the environment only from node 0).
  - When tasks are launched on other nodes, the step-launch environment for those tasks will also have CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set on that node to the devices allocated there.
- Device numbering is node-local. "GPU 0" on nodeA is independent of "GPU 0" on nodeB.
- If the cluster is configured to use cgroups to restrict device node access, Slurm may also hide or whitelist /dev/nvidia* devices inside the job's cgroup in addition to setting CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.

3) Whole-device vs sharing
- By default Slurm allocates whole GPUs (one gres unit = whole device).
- Sharing options:
  - MPS (CUDA Multi-Process Service): when configured, Slurm can allocate fractional MPS resources (configured via gres/mps).
  - Sharding: Slurm's sharding feature lets you configure many shards per GPU and allocate them as GRES; this does not fence the hardware — it's a logical share.
  - MIG (NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU): Slurm can be configured (AutoDetect=nvml, and correct gres.conf) to detect and allocate MIG slices as separate GRES units. Behavior depends on how the system admin set up gres.conf.
- If your site supports any of the above, you must check how the cluster exposes those resources (gres type names, environment vars, or device files).

4) Binding GPUs to tasks (common patterns)
- If you want 1 GPU per MPI rank / per process:
  - Use --gpus-per-task=1 and launch one task per rank (e.g., srun --ntasks=NUM_RANKS ...). Slurm will attempt to assign distinct GPUs to each task.
- If you want N GPUs on each node for a single multi-GPU job:
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:N -N1 or sbatch --gpus-per-node=N -N1
- If you request a total number of GPUs (--gpus=TOTAL) across multiple nodes, Slurm will distribute GPUs across nodes to satisfy the count and your other constraints (node count, partitions, etc.).
- Newer Slurm versions provide --gpu-bind (and related options) to control how GPUs are selected/mapped to tasks (see your cluster docs / man page).

5) How to confirm what you got (debugging tips)
- Inside a job step run:
  - echo $CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
  - nvidia-smi -L
  - nvidia-smi topo - or nvidia-smi (shows devices visible and UUIDs)
- From the controller/admin side use: scontrol show job <jobid> (AllocTRES, GresDetail) or scontrol show node to inspect gres configuration (admins). As a user, check your job environment variables as above.

6) Practical examples
- Request 2 GPUs on a single node:
  - sbatch --gpus-per-node=2 -N1 ...
  - or sbatch --gres=gpu:2 -N1 ...
- Request 8 GPUs total and let scheduler pick nodes:
  - sbatch --gpus=8 ...
  - The scheduler may give 4 nodes × 2 GPUs each, or 2 nodes × 4 GPUs each, depending on availability and constraints.
- Request 1 GPU per task for a 16-rank job:
  - sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks=16 ...
  - or srun --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks=16 ...

7) Version / site differences
- Exact environment variables exposed (besides CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) and support for MIG/MPS/sharding depend on Slurm version and how your cluster is configured (gres.conf, slurm.conf, and cgroup settings). Some clusters also set SLURM_JOB_GPUS or SLURM_STEP_GPUS — check your cluster's srun/sbatch man pages or ask your admin.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact GRES configuration or current gpu partition state on your cluster (sinfo / scontrol show node) — or
- give exact example sbatch/srun lines for your workflow (single-GPU training, multi-GPU DDP, MPI+GPU), or
- explain how to force a particular mapping with --gpu-bind.

Which would you like?

Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
