- Medium-term: reduce recent usage (fewer or smaller jobs), or let historical usage decay; that will raise her fairshare factor.
- Administrative options: adjust account shares, change the account/QOS assigned to jobs, or alter PriorityWeightFairshare if policy should favor age/QOS more; those are cluster-config changes and require admin/operator action.

results.prompt: Explain topology placement constraints for current nodes
results.agent_response:
Short answer first
- The cluster topology shows a single switch (switch0) connecting all four nodes: cpu-node-01, cpu-node-02, gpu-node-01, gpu-node-02. Because all nodes are on the same switch, there are no multi‑switch placement constraints to enforce — all nodes are topologically “adjacent” from Slurm’s point of view.

Current node/partition state (from sinfo)
- gpu-node-01 — partition=gpu — STATE=down — GRES=gpu:4 — (hardware failure) — not usable.
- gpu-node-02 — partition=gpu — STATE=alloc — 32/32 CPUs allocated, 128G — currently allocated (not idle).
- cpu-node-01 — partition=cpu — STATE=drain — 0/64 CPUs — under maintenance (not usable).
- cpu-node-02 — partition=cpu — STATE=mix — 48/64 allocated, 200G/256G used — partially available (16 CPUs free).

What that means for topology placement constraints
- No cross-switch constraints: because every node is on the same switch, Slurm cannot/does not need to prefer nodes on a particular switch to reduce inter-switch latency — all nodes are already on the same fabric.
- Effective constraints come from partition, node state, and resources (GRES/CPUs/memory), not from multi-switch topology. For example, GPU jobs are limited by the gpu partition and by gpu-node-01 being down and gpu-node-02 being currently allocated — there are no idle GPU nodes available now.
- Partial/“mix” nodes (cpu-node-02) can satisfy smaller multi‑task requests but will not satisfy requests that require whole nodes or reserved nodes unless enough free CPUs/GPU resources exist on that node.
- If you request topology-aware allocations (block/tree or plane distributions or CPU affinity), Slurm can still apply distribution/affinity within the single-switch topology (for example using --distribution=plane or -m plane with cpu-bind). But because the fabric is flat, you won’t get cross-switch placement benefits — topology-aware allocation will only arrange tasks among the nodes attached to this single switch.
- Topology enforcement (e.g., strict block allocation) requires a configured topology plugin (topology/block) and a topology.conf defining blocks. The controller config we checked did not show an explicit TopologyPlugin entry in the brief output; if you require strict block placement you should enable/configure TopologyPlugin and topology.conf.

Practical implications / recommendations
- For GPU jobs: currently no idle GPU nodes (gpu-node-01 is down, gpu-node-02 is allocated) — GPU submissions will wait unless gpu-node-02 becomes free or hardware is repaired.
- For low-latency multi‑node MPI jobs: with all nodes on the same switch you already have minimal switch-level latency, but you must still account for available nodes (cpu-node-02 only partially free).
- If you need strict contiguous or hierarchical block placement for future scale, define blocks in topology.conf and enable topology/block (then test with small allocations). Otherwise use --distribution (plane/block/cyclic) and CPU affinity flags to control per-node task packing/affinity.
- If you want, I can list current idle-capable nodes (or GPU availability) or show the full topology.conf/config — which would you like?

results.agent_response:
Summary of current topology and how placement constraints will behave

Current cluster facts (from topology and sinfo)
- Topology: single leaf switch "switch0" contains: cpu-node-01, cpu-node-02, gpu-node-01, gpu-node-02.
- Partition context (sinfo):
  - gpu partition: 2 nodes (gpu-node-01, gpu-node-02), both show in state alloc, each with 32 CPUs, 128G memory, gpu:4.
  - cpu partition: 2 nodes (cpu-node-01, cpu-node-02), both show in state alloc, each with 64 CPUs, 256G memory.
- Net effect: all four compute nodes are children of the same switch (no separate leaf switches) and currently all nodes are allocated (no idle nodes shown).

What "topology placement constraints" mean here
- Topology-aware scheduling (topology/tree or topology/block plugins) tries to allocate resources on the smallest switch-level (leaf) that satisfies a job’s request so as to minimize network contention and maximize locality.
- Because all nodes live under the same leaf switch (switch0), topology will not prevent a job from spanning these nodes due to switch boundaries — there are no multiple leaf switches to restrict spanning.
- However, partition boundaries still apply: typical Slurm usage restricts a job to one partition at submission time. So a job submitted to the gpu partition will only see gpu-node-* nodes, and a cpu-partition job will only see cpu-node-* nodes even though the network switch is shared.
- Node availability still matters: although the topology allows spanning all nodes, the scheduler can only allocate nodes that are idle/available. Right now all nodes are allocated, so topology won’t help until idle nodes exist.

User controls and options that affect placement
- --switches=count[@time] (srun/sbatch/salloc): request a maximum number of leaf switches and a wait time for an optimized placement; only meaningful if the tree topology plugin is active.
- TopologyParam and TopologyPlugin settings (in slurm.conf) can change behavior (e.g., TopoOptional allows jobs to span leaves without a common parent).

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
Slurm includes support for creating a federation of clusters
and scheduling jobs in a peer-to-peer fashion between them. Jobs submitted to a

results.prompt: Explain scheduler health using diagnostics, controller ping, and queue pressure
results.agent_response:
Short answer: use sdiag to measure scheduler behavior (cycle times, backfill efficiency, queue depth), scontrol ping to verify the controller is responsive and has low RPC latency, and squeue/sinfo/sprio to measure queue pressure and the reasons jobs are stuck. Combine those signals to decide whether the scheduler is healthy, overloaded, misconfigured, or blocked by resources/policy.

What each tool tells you
- sdiag
  - Purpose: scheduler diagnostics / health summary.
  - Key signals to read: scheduling cycle time (min/avg/max), backfill efficiency (percent), queue depth/backlog statistics, number of scheduling decisions, and any reported scheduling failures or long-running cycles.
  - Interpretation:
    - Low/short cycle times (milliseconds → single-digit seconds) and high backfill efficiency (close to 100%) usually mean the scheduler is keeping up and using idle resources well.
    - Rising average or max cycle times, wide variance, or many long cycles indicate slurmctld CPU/lock contention, heavy scheduling load, or pathological job patterns (very large numbers of small jobs, many small reservations).
    - Low backfill efficiency indicates idle capacity that the scheduler cannot use (often due to inaccurate time limits on running jobs, strict constraints, or complex placement policies).

- scontrol ping
  - Purpose: verify the controller (slurmctld) process is responsive to RPCs.
  - What to expect: a quick success response (typically sub-millisecond to low milliseconds on a healthy controller on the same LAN) or a failure/time-out if the controller is unreachable or overloaded.
  - Interpretation:
    - Successful, low-latency pings => controller responsive.
    - Increased latency (tens to hundreds of ms) or failed pings => network problems, slurmctld overloaded, or RPC backlog. Investigate slurmctld CPU, process state, system load, and network latency.
    - If ping fails, check slurmctld logs, system load, and whether slurmctld or munge crashed.

- squeue (and sinfo, sprio)
  - Purpose: measure queue pressure and why jobs are pending.
  - Useful queries:
    - squeue --states=PD,R to get counts and ages of pending/running jobs.
    - squeue -o "%i %u %t %M %S %R" to show jobID, user, state, time, submit/start time, and Reason.
    - squeue --states=PD -o "%i %u %M %R" | head to surface the oldest pending jobs and their Reason codes.
    - sinfo -Nel to see node states (idle/alloc/drain/down) and whether nodes are available to satisfy pending requests.
    - sprio to see whether backlog is due to priority/fairshare.
  - Key things to inspect:
    - Pending job counts and longest pending age: a small queue with short pending times is healthy; large backlogs and very old jobs indicate resource shortage or policy limits.
    - Pending reason codes: Resources (not enough nodes/gpus/cpus), QOS/Assoc limits (policy), License (no free license), PartitionDown/NodeDown, ReqNodeNotAvail, or Priority-related reasons all point to different fixes.
    - Whether many jobs are waiting for the same small set of resources (e.g., all want 8 GPUs on a specific partition) — that’s a resource mismatch, not necessarily scheduler fault.
    - sprio/sdiag/sshow to understand priority/fairshare impacts.

How to combine signals (triage logic)
- Controller responsiveness (scontrol ping)
  - If ping fails or is very slow → stop here: controller or network issue. Fix slurmctld, restore munge, or resolve network problems before other fixes.
- Scheduler internals (sdiag)
  - If sdiag shows long scheduling cycles and low backfill efficiency while controller ping is fine → slurmctld is overwhelmed (CPU, lock contention, pathological job patterns). Actions: raise slurmctld resources (CPU/cores), tune scheduling parameters (reduce expensive plugins or adjust scheduling interval), or investigate job submission patterns (coalesce very many tiny jobs).
  - If sdiag is healthy but queue is large → likely resource shortage or policy limits (not scheduler responsiveness). Check squeue reasons and sinfo.
- Queue pressure (squeue + sinfo + sprio)

trials.agent_response:
After reviewing the Slurm cluster, short answer: use sdiag to measure scheduler behavior (cycle times, backfill efficiency, queue depth), scontrol ping to verify the controller is responsive and has low RPC latency, and squeue/sinfo/sprio to measure queue pressure and the reasons jobs are stuck. Combine those signals to decide whether the scheduler is healthy, overloaded, misconfigured, or blocked by resources/policy.

What each tool tells you
- sdiag
  - Purpose: scheduler diagnostics / health summary.
  - Key signals to read: scheduling cycle time (min/avg/max), backfill efficiency (percent), queue depth/backlog statistics, number of scheduling decisions, and any reported scheduling failures or long-running cycles.
  - Interpretation:
    - Low/short cycle times (milliseconds → single-digit seconds) and high backfill efficiency (close to 100%) usually mean the scheduler is keeping up and using idle resources well.
    - Rising average or max cycle times, wide variance, or many long cycles indicate slurmctld CPU/lock contention, heavy scheduling load, or pathological job patterns (very large numbers of small jobs, many small reservations).
    - Low backfill efficiency indicates idle capacity that the scheduler cannot use (often due to inaccurate time limits on running jobs, strict constraints, or complex placement policies).

- scontrol ping
  - Purpose: verify the controller (slurmctld) process is responsive to RPCs.
  - What to expect: a quick success response (typically sub-millisecond to low milliseconds on a healthy controller on the same LAN) or a failure/time-out if the controller is unreachable or overloaded.
  - Interpretation:
    - Successful, low-latency pings => controller responsive.
    - Increased latency (tens to hundreds of ms) or failed pings => network problems, slurmctld overloaded, or RPC backlog. Investigate slurmctld CPU, process state, system load, and network latency.
    - If ping fails, check slurmctld logs, system load, and whether slurmctld or munge crashed.

- squeue (and sinfo, sprio)
  - Purpose: measure queue pressure and why jobs are pending.
  - Useful queries:
    - squeue --states=PD,R to get counts and ages of pending/running jobs.
    - squeue -o "%i %u %t %M %S %R" to show jobID, user, state, time, submit/start time, and Reason.
    - squeue --states=PD -o "%i %u %M %R" | head to surface the oldest pending jobs and their Reason codes.
    - sinfo -Nel to see node states (idle/alloc/drain/down) and whether nodes are available to satisfy pending requests.
    - sprio to see whether backlog is due to priority/fairshare.
  - Key things to inspect:
    - Pending job counts and longest pending age: a small queue with short pending times is healthy; large backlogs and very old jobs indicate resource shortage or policy limits.
    - Pending reason codes: Resources (not enough nodes/gpus/cpus), QOS/Assoc limits (policy), License (no free license), PartitionDown/NodeDown, ReqNodeNotAvail, or Priority-related reasons all point to different fixes.
    - Whether many jobs are waiting for the same small set of resources (e.g., all want 8 GPUs on a specific partition) — that’s a resource mismatch, not necessarily scheduler fault.
    - sprio/sdiag/sshow to understand priority/fairshare impacts.

How to combine signals (triage logic)
- Controller responsiveness (scontrol ping)
  - If ping fails or is very slow → stop here: controller or network issue. Fix slurmctld, restore munge, or resolve network problems before other fixes.
- Scheduler internals (sdiag)
  - If sdiag shows long scheduling cycles and low backfill efficiency while controller ping is fine → slurmctld is overwhelmed (CPU, lock contention, pathological job patterns). Actions: raise slurmctld resources (CPU/cores), tune scheduling parameters (reduce expensive plugins or adjust scheduling interval), or investigate job submission patterns (coalesce very many tiny jobs).
  - If sdiag is healthy but queue is large → likely resource shortage or policy limits (not scheduler responsiveness). Check squeue reasons and sinfo.
- Queue pressure (squeue + sinfo + sprio)
  - If most pending jobs show Reason=Resources and sinfo reports few idle nodes → capacity problem. Consider adding nodes, changing partition sizing, or encouraging smaller jobs/more flexible requests.
  - If many jobs blocked by Assoc/Acct/QOS limits → adjust accounting or QOS policies.
  - If Reason=ReqNodeNotAvail or PartitionDown → resolve node health/reservations/drain states.
  - If Reason=License or GRES-related → check scontrol_license and apportioned licenses/gres availability.

Concrete checklist and commands to run (quick triage)
1. Verify controller reachable:
   - scontrol ping
   - If this fails/timeouts, check slurmctld, munge, system logs.
2. Get scheduler diagnostics:
   - sdiag
   - Look at scheduling cycle times, backfill efficiency, queue depth.
3. Inspect queue pressure:
   - squeue --states=PD -o "%i %u %t %M %S %R" | head
   - squeue --states=PD -O "jobid,name,user,prio,timeused,reason"
   - sinfo -Nel
   - sprio
4. Look for policy/resource blocks:
   - If squeue Reason shows AssociationJobLimit/AssocMax*Limit -> run sacctmgr show associations or sacctmgr list to inspect limits.
   - If licenses are implicated -> scontrol_license
5. If sdiag shows long cycles and scontrol ping is slow but squeue doesn’t indicate resource shortage:
   - Check slurmctld host CPU/memory, disk I/O, and slurmctld logs (/var/log/slurmctld.log).
   - Consider increasing slurmctld CPUs or tuning scheduler plugins and scheduling interval.

Common warning signs of unhealthy scheduler
- scontrol ping fails or has high latency.
- sdiag: average/max scheduling cycle time much larger than normal; rapidly growing queue depth; backfill efficiency dropping.
- squeue: sustained large pending backlog, many old pending jobs, pending reasons pointing to resources/policies rather than transient placement.
- sprio: priority starvation where fairshare/QOS causes large waits.
- Many node drains or frequent node state flaps visible in sinfo or sinfo_reasons.

Metrics to collect for longer investigation
- Regular sdiag snapshots (cycle times, backfill efficiency) over time.
- scontrol ping response times / failures.
- squeue pending counts and oldest pending age by partition/user.
- slurmctld host metrics: CPU, RSS, context switches, run queue, disk I/O, and network latency.
- slurmctld logs around times of long cycles or failures.

When to escalate to operator/admin
- scontrol ping fails or is inconsistent → immediate operator action.
- sdiag shows severe scheduler thrashing (very long cycles, scheduler loops) or persistent low backfill despite idle nodes → needs config or capacity change.
- Queue pressure caused by account/QOS/limits or license exhaustion → admin/policy change.

results.prompt: Explain relevant Slurm configuration for scheduling and accounting
results.agent_response:
Good question — scheduling and accounting are tightly linked in Slurm. Below is a concise, actionable overview of the most relevant slurm.conf / slurmdbd / sacctmgr settings and where they interact, plus checks and common pitfalls.

High-level components
- slurmctld (scheduler): governed by slurm.conf and priority plugin settings.
- slurmd (node agents): report usage and enforce cgroups.
- slurmdbd (accounting DB daemon): stores historical usage and is required for fairshare, age, and many accounting-based features.
- sacctmgr / sreport / sshare / sprio: admin tools to inspect and manage accounting, shares, and priorities.

Scheduling configuration (slurm.conf and plugins)
1. Priority plugin
- PriorityType
  - Common value: priority/multifactor — the Multifactor plugin composes priority from age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, site factors, and requested TRES.
- Priority weights (how factors combine)
  - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - The composite job priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + ... (weights are numeric).
- PriorityFlags
  - Toggles behavior (examples: NO_FAIR_TREE to use classic fairshare, SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME, etc.).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife
  - Controls decay of historical usage for fairshare. Example: 7-0 means a 7‑day half-life. 0 disables decay (requires other usage reset policy).
- PriorityCalcPeriod / PriorityUsageResetPeriod / PriorityMaxAge
  - Control recalculation cadence, when usage is reset, and the max age factor value.

2. Fairshare and accounting dependency
- Fairshare requires slurmdbd (AccountingStorage) and properly configured association shares.
- sacctmgr is used to set "Fairshare" (Share) values on accounts/users/associations.
- If you want fairshare-based scheduling, ensure AccountingStorageType points to slurmdbd and slurmdbd is running.

3. QOS and partition factors
- QOS definitions (sacctmgr) can set priorities, limits, preemption behavior, and priority caps.
- Partition factors and per-partition PriorityWeightPartition influence job order by partition.

4. Job size / age / nice / site factors
- PriorityFavorSmall (YES/NO) controls whether small jobs get more priority.
- Age factor grows while a job is eligible to run; PriorityMaxAge caps it.
- Site / job_submit plugins allow custom site_factor or submission-time modifications.

5. Preemption and backfill
- PreemptType / PreemptMode / PreemptExemptTime set how preemption works (requeue, suspend, preempt).
- Backfill: the scheduler supports backfilling; relevant settings live in scheduler plugin parameters (multifactor scheduling uses scheduler logic and backfill capability).

6. TRES-based weighting
- You can weight specific TRES (e.g., GPUs, CPUs) via TRES weights so jobs requesting expensive TRES are evaluated differently.

Accounting configuration (slurmdbd, slurm.conf, job accounting)
1. AccountingStorage
- slurm.conf keys:
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost / Port /User /Loc depending on DB backend
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: controls enforcement level on job submit (values like associations, all, nojobs, nosteps). Use to block submissions that violate associations/limits.
- slurmdbd.conf: DB connection settings, auth, and retention configuration.

2. Job usage collection and completion logging
- JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency: configure how resource usage (RSS, maxrss, CPU) is gathered.
- JobCompType / JobCompLoc (job completion logging plugin) — where completion records are sent if not using slurmdbd.

3. sacctmgr associations, accounts, QOS
- Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, set DefaultQOS, set Share/Fairshare, set limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.).
- Grp* limits are checked when considering starting jobs — these can block allocation if limits would be exceeded.
- DefaultQOS, QOSMaxJobs, QOSMaxSubmitJobs etc. control per-user/ per-account behavior.

4. Reporting and tools
- sshare shows fairshare and effective shares.
- sprio shows priority breakdown per job and the active weights.
- sreport generates accounting usage (CPU/GPU-hours) reports.
- sacct for historical job records; sacct requires accounting data (slurmdbd or jobcomp to storage).

Practical examples (typical lines)
- slurm.conf (examples)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityFavorSmall=YES
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.edu
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
- sacctmgr (examples)
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=clustername Description="Research group"
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100
  - sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultAccount=mygroup

Checks and diagnostics (read-only commands)
- scontrol show config — view current slurm.conf settings (PriorityType, AccountingStorageType, JobAcctGatherType).
- sprio -w — view current priority weights and plugin behavior.
- sshare -l — check fairshare allocation and recent usage.
- sdiag — scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics.
- scontrol ping — check controller responsiveness.
- sacctmgr list associations — inspect accounts, shares, and limits.

Common pitfalls and recommendations
- Fairshare/age requires slurmdbd; without it fairshare/age factors are not computed.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is 0 you must manage usage resets (PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
- Changing slurm.conf requires restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld to take effect; slurmdbd config changes require restart of slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce can block users unintentionally — test changes in a staging environment first.
- Ensure JobAcctGatherType is enabled and frequent enough to capture required metrics (increase frequency for finer accounting).
- When tuning weights, use sprio and sshare to observe results and iterate: small changes to PriorityWeightFairshare can have large effects.

If you want, I can:
- Show the cluster’s current config snippets (scontrol show config) and priority/fairshare state (sprio, sshare) to make concrete recommendations.  
- Or provide a sample minimal slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf snippet for a typical research cluster tuned for fairshare.

Which would you like next?

desirable to relocate them.

updated host info and finish normally.

The "include" key word can be used with modifiers within the specified
pathname. These modifiers would be replaced with cluster name or other
information depending on which modifier is specified. If the included file
is not an absolute path name (i.e. it does not start with a slash), it will
searched for in the same directory as the slurm.conf file.

EXAMPLE

ClusterName=linux include /home/slurm/etc/%c_config # Above line interpreted as # "include /home/slurm/etc/linux_config"
```

The following slurm.conf parameters are used to configure the Multifactor Job
Priority Plugin. See slurm.conf(5) man page for more details.
PriorityType
Set this value to "priority/multifactor" to enable the Multifactor Job
Priority Plugin.
PriorityDecayHalfLife
This determines the contribution of historical usage on the
composite usage value. The larger the number, the longer past usage
affects fair-share. If set to 0 no decay will be applied. This is helpful if
you want to enforce hard time limits per association. If set to 0
PriorityUsageResetPeriod must be set to some interval.
The unit is a time string (i.e. min, hr:min:00, days-hr:min:00, or
days-hr). The default value is 7-0 (7 days).

and operation of the [Slurm Accounting Database](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html).
The age factor represents the length of time a job has been sitting in the
queue and eligible to run. In general, the longer a job waits in the queue, the
larger its age factor grows. However, the age factor for a dependent job will
not change while it waits for the job it depends on to complete. Also, the age
factor will not change when scheduling is withheld for a job whose node or time
limits exceed the cluster's current limits.

will max out to 1.0.

trials.agent_response:
Good question — scheduling and accounting are tightly linked in Slurm. Below is a concise, actionable overview of the most relevant slurm.conf / slurmdbd / sacctmgr settings and where they interact, plus checks and common pitfalls.

High-level components
- slurmctld (scheduler): governed by slurm.conf and priority plugin settings.
- slurmd (node agents): report usage and enforce cgroups.
- slurmdbd (accounting DB daemon): stores historical usage and is required for fairshare, age, and many accounting-based features.
- sacctmgr / sreport / sshare / sprio: admin tools to inspect and manage accounting, shares, and priorities.

Scheduling configuration (slurm.conf and plugins)
1. Priority plugin
- PriorityType
  - Common value: priority/multifactor — the Multifactor plugin composes priority from age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, site factors, and requested TRES.
- Priority weights (how factors combine)
  - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - The composite job priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + ... (weights are numeric).
- PriorityFlags
  - Toggles behavior (examples: NO_FAIR_TREE to use classic fairshare, SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME, etc.).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife
  - Controls decay of historical usage for fairshare. Example: 7-0 means a 7‑day half-life. 0 disables decay (requires other usage reset policy).
- PriorityCalcPeriod / PriorityUsageResetPeriod / PriorityMaxAge
  - Control recalculation cadence, when usage is reset, and the max age factor value.

2. Fairshare and accounting dependency
- Fairshare requires slurmdbd (AccountingStorage) and properly configured association shares.
- sacctmgr is used to set "Fairshare" (Share) values on accounts/users/associations.
- If you want fairshare-based scheduling, ensure AccountingStorageType points to slurmdbd and slurmdbd is running.

3. QOS and partition factors
- QOS definitions (sacctmgr) can set priorities, limits, preemption behavior, and priority caps.
- Partition factors and per-partition PriorityWeightPartition influence job order by partition.

4. Job size / age / nice / site factors
- PriorityFavorSmall (YES/NO) controls whether small jobs get more priority.
- Age factor grows while a job is eligible to run; PriorityMaxAge caps it.
- Site / job_submit plugins allow custom site_factor or submission-time modifications.

5. Preemption and backfill
- PreemptType / PreemptMode / PreemptExemptTime set how preemption works (requeue, suspend, preempt).
- Backfill: the scheduler supports backfilling; relevant settings live in scheduler plugin parameters (multifactor scheduling uses scheduler logic and backfill capability).

6. TRES-based weighting
- You can weight specific TRES (e.g., GPUs, CPUs) via TRES weights so jobs requesting expensive TRES are evaluated differently.

Accounting configuration (slurmdbd, slurm.conf, job accounting)
1. AccountingStorage
- slurm.conf keys:
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost / Port /User /Loc depending on DB backend
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: controls enforcement level on job submit (values like associations, all, nojobs, nosteps). Use to block submissions that violate associations/limits.
- slurmdbd.conf: DB connection settings, auth, and retention configuration.

2. Job usage collection and completion logging
- JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency: configure how resource usage (RSS, maxrss, CPU) is gathered.
- JobCompType / JobCompLoc (job completion logging plugin) — where completion records are sent if not using slurmdbd.

3. sacctmgr associations, accounts, QOS
- Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, set DefaultQOS, set Share/Fairshare, set limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.).
- Grp* limits are checked when considering starting jobs — these can block allocation if limits would be exceeded.
- DefaultQOS, QOSMaxJobs, QOSMaxSubmitJobs etc. control per-user/ per-account behavior.

4. Reporting and tools
- sshare shows fairshare and effective shares.
- sprio shows priority breakdown per job and the active weights.
- sreport generates accounting usage (CPU/GPU-hours) reports.
- sacct for historical job records; sacct requires accounting data (slurmdbd or jobcomp to storage).

Practical examples (typical lines)
- slurm.conf (examples)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityFavorSmall=YES
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.edu
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
- sacctmgr (examples)
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=clustername Description="Research group"
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100
  - sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultAccount=mygroup

Checks and diagnostics (read-only commands)
- scontrol show config — view current slurm.conf settings (PriorityType, AccountingStorageType, JobAcctGatherType).
- sprio -w — view current priority weights and plugin behavior.
- sshare -l — check fairshare allocation and recent usage.
- sdiag — scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics.
- scontrol ping — check controller responsiveness.
- sacctmgr list associations — inspect accounts, shares, and limits.

Common pitfalls and recommendations
- Fairshare/age requires slurmdbd; without it fairshare/age factors are not computed.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is 0 you must manage usage resets (PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
- Changing slurm.conf requires restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld to take effect; slurmdbd config changes require restart of slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce can block users unintentionally — test changes in a staging environment first.
- Ensure JobAcctGatherType is enabled and frequent enough to capture required metrics (increase frequency for finer accounting).
- When tuning weights, use sprio and sshare to observe results and iterate: small changes to PriorityWeightFairshare can have large effects.

If you want, I can:
- Show the cluster’s current config snippets (scontrol show config) and priority/fairshare state (sprio, sshare) to make concrete recommendations.  
- Or provide a sample minimal slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf snippet for a typical research cluster tuned for fairshare.

Which would you like next?

## RELOCATING CONTROLLERS[#SECTION_RELOCATING-CONTROLLERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
If the cluster's computers used for the primary or backup controller
will be out of service for an extended period of time, it may be
desirable to relocate them.
In order to do so, follow this procedure:
1. Stop the Slurm daemons on the old controller and nodes.
2. Modify the slurm.conf file appropriately.
3. Copy the files from the StateSaveLocation to the new controller or ensure
that they are accessible to the new controller via a shared drive.
4. Distribute the updated slurm.conf file to all nodes.
5. Restart the Slurm daemons on the new controller and nodes.
There should be no loss of any pending jobs. Any running jobs will get the
updated host info and finish normally.
Ensure that any nodes added to the cluster have the current
slurm.conf file installed.

## INCLUDE MODIFIERS[#SECTION_INCLUDE-MODIFIERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The "include" key word can be used with modifiers within the specified
pathname. These modifiers would be replaced with cluster name or other
information depending on which modifier is specified. If the included file
is not an absolute path name (i.e. it does not start with a slash), it will
searched for in the same directory as the slurm.conf file.
%c [#OPT_%c](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) Cluster name specified in the slurm.conf will be used.
EXAMPLE
```text
ClusterName=linux include /home/slurm/etc/%c_config # Above line interpreted as # "include /home/slurm/etc/linux_config"
```

## Age Factor[#age](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
Note: Computing the age factor requires the installation
and operation of the [Slurm Accounting Database](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html).
The age factor represents the length of time a job has been sitting in the
queue and eligible to run. In general, the longer a job waits in the queue, the
larger its age factor grows. However, the age factor for a dependent job will
not change while it waits for the job it depends on to complete. Also, the age
factor will not change when scheduling is withheld for a job whose node or time
limits exceed the cluster's current limits.
At some configurable length of time ( PriorityMaxAge ), the age factor
will max out to 1.0.

trials.agent_response:
Based on the current cluster state, good question — scheduling and accounting are tightly linked in Slurm. Below is a concise, actionable overview of the most relevant slurm.conf / slurmdbd / sacctmgr settings and where they interact, plus checks and common pitfalls.

High-level components
- slurmctld (scheduler): governed by slurm.conf and priority plugin settings.
- slurmd (node agents): report usage and enforce cgroups.
- slurmdbd (accounting DB daemon): stores historical usage and is required for fairshare, age, and many accounting-based features.
- sacctmgr / sreport / sshare / sprio: admin tools to inspect and manage accounting, shares, and priorities.

Scheduling configuration (slurm.conf and plugins)
1. Priority plugin
- PriorityType
  - Common value: priority/multifactor — the Multifactor plugin composes priority from age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, site factors, and requested TRES.
- Priority weights (how factors combine)
  - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - The composite job priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + ... (weights are numeric).
- PriorityFlags
  - Toggles behavior (examples: NO_FAIR_TREE to use classic fairshare, SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME, etc.).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife
  - Controls decay of historical usage for fairshare. Example: 7-0 means a 7‑day half-life. 0 disables decay (requires other usage reset policy).
- PriorityCalcPeriod / PriorityUsageResetPeriod / PriorityMaxAge
  - Control recalculation cadence, when usage is reset, and the max age factor value.

2. Fairshare and accounting dependency
- Fairshare requires slurmdbd (AccountingStorage) and properly configured association shares.
- sacctmgr is used to set "Fairshare" (Share) values on accounts/users/associations.
- If you want fairshare-based scheduling, ensure AccountingStorageType points to slurmdbd and slurmdbd is running.

3. QOS and partition factors
- QOS definitions (sacctmgr) can set priorities, limits, preemption behavior, and priority caps.
- Partition factors and per-partition PriorityWeightPartition influence job order by partition.

4. Job size / age / nice / site factors
- PriorityFavorSmall (YES/NO) controls whether small jobs get more priority.
- Age factor grows while a job is eligible to run; PriorityMaxAge caps it.
- Site / job_submit plugins allow custom site_factor or submission-time modifications.

5. Preemption and backfill
- PreemptType / PreemptMode / PreemptExemptTime set how preemption works (requeue, suspend, preempt).
- Backfill: the scheduler supports backfilling; relevant settings live in scheduler plugin parameters (multifactor scheduling uses scheduler logic and backfill capability).

6. TRES-based weighting
- You can weight specific TRES (e.g., GPUs, CPUs) via TRES weights so jobs requesting expensive TRES are evaluated differently.

Accounting configuration (slurmdbd, slurm.conf, job accounting)
1. AccountingStorage
- slurm.conf keys:
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost / Port /User /Loc depending on DB backend
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: controls enforcement level on job submit (values like associations, all, nojobs, nosteps). Use to block submissions that violate associations/limits.
- slurmdbd.conf: DB connection settings, auth, and retention configuration.

2. Job usage collection and completion logging
- JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency: configure how resource usage (RSS, maxrss, CPU) is gathered.
- JobCompType / JobCompLoc (job completion logging plugin) — where completion records are sent if not using slurmdbd.

3. sacctmgr associations, accounts, QOS
- Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, set DefaultQOS, set Share/Fairshare, set limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.).
- Grp* limits are checked when considering starting jobs — these can block allocation if limits would be exceeded.
- DefaultQOS, QOSMaxJobs, QOSMaxSubmitJobs etc. control per-user/ per-account behavior.

4. Reporting and tools
- sshare shows fairshare and effective shares.
- sprio shows priority breakdown per job and the active weights.
- sreport generates accounting usage (CPU/GPU-hours) reports.
- sacct for historical job records; sacct requires accounting data (slurmdbd or jobcomp to storage).

Practical examples (typical lines)
- slurm.conf (examples)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityFavorSmall=YES
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.edu
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
- sacctmgr (examples)
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=clustername Description="Research group"
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100
  - sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultAccount=mygroup

Checks and diagnostics (read-only commands)
- scontrol show config — view current slurm.conf settings (PriorityType, AccountingStorageType, JobAcctGatherType).
- sprio -w — view current priority weights and plugin behavior.
- sshare -l — check fairshare allocation and recent usage.
- sdiag — scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics.
- scontrol ping — check controller responsiveness.
- sacctmgr list associations — inspect accounts, shares, and limits.

Common pitfalls and recommendations
- Fairshare/age requires slurmdbd; without it fairshare/age factors are not computed.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is 0 you must manage usage resets (PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
- Changing slurm.conf requires restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld to take effect; slurmdbd config changes require restart of slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce can block users unintentionally — test changes in a staging environment first.
- Ensure JobAcctGatherType is enabled and frequent enough to capture required metrics (increase frequency for finer accounting).
- When tuning weights, use sprio and sshare to observe results and iterate: small changes to PriorityWeightFairshare can have large effects.

If you want, I can:
- Show the cluster’s current config snippets (scontrol show config) and priority/fairshare state (sprio, sshare) to make concrete recommendations.  
- Or provide a sample minimal slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf snippet for a typical research cluster tuned for fairshare.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be
consistent across all nodes in the cluster.
The file location can be modified at execution time by setting the SLURM_CONF
environment variable. The Slurm daemons also allow you to override
both the built-in and environment-provided location using the "-f"
option on the command line.
The contents of the file are case insensitive except for the names of nodes
and partitions. Any text following a "#" in the configuration file is treated
as a comment through the end of that line.

## NODE CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODE-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.
Nodes which register to the system with less than the configured resources
(e.g. too little memory), will be placed in the "DOWN" state to
avoid scheduling jobs on them.

slurmdbd.conf is an ASCII file which describes Slurm Database
Daemon (SlurmDBD) configuration information.
The file will always be located in the same directory as the slurm.conf .
The contents of the file are case insensitive except for the names of nodes
and files. Any text following a "#" in the configuration file is treated
as a comment through the end of that line.
Changes to the configuration file take effect upon restart of
SlurmDBD or daemon receipt of the SIGHUP signal unless otherwise noted.
This file should be only on the machine where SlurmDBD executes, owned by the
SlurmUser or root, and have permissions set to 600 or 640.

user ID, the configuration file will initially be read as user root, but will

## NODESET CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODESET-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The nodeset configuration allows you to define a name for a specific set of
nodes which can be used to simplify the partition configuration section,
especially for heterogeneous or condo-style systems. Each nodeset may be defined
by an explicit list of nodes, and/or by filtering the nodes by a particular
configured feature. If both Feature= and Nodes= are used the
nodeset shall be the union of the two subsets.
Note that the nodesets are only used to simplify the partition definitions
at present, and are not usable outside of the partition configuration.

## RELOCATING CONTROLLERS[#SECTION_RELOCATING-CONTROLLERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
If the cluster's computers used for the primary or backup controller
will be out of service for an extended period of time, it may be
desirable to relocate them.
In order to do so, follow this procedure:
1. Stop the Slurm daemons on the old controller and nodes.
2. Modify the slurm.conf file appropriately.
3. Copy the files from the StateSaveLocation to the new controller or ensure
that they are accessible to the new controller via a shared drive.
4. Distribute the updated slurm.conf file to all nodes.
5. Restart the Slurm daemons on the new controller and nodes.
There should be no loss of any pending jobs. Any running jobs will get the
updated host info and finish normally.
Ensure that any nodes added to the cluster have the current
slurm.conf file installed.
CAUTION: If two nodes are simultaneously configured as the
primary controller...

## RELOCATING CONTROLLERS[#SECTION_RELOCATING-CONTROLLERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
If the cluster's computers used for the primary or backup controller
will be out of service for an extended period of time, it may be
desirable to relocate them.
In order to do so, follow this procedure:
1. Stop the Slurm daemons on the old controller and nodes.
2. Modify the slurm.conf file appropriately.
3. Copy the files from the StateSaveLocation to the new controller or ensure
that they are accessible to the new controller via a shared drive.
4. Distribute the updated slurm.conf file to all nodes.
5. Restart the Slurm daemons on the new controller and nodes.
There should be no loss of any pending jobs. Any running jobs will get the
updated host info and finish normally.
Ensure that any nodes added to the cluster have the current
slurm.conf file installed.

## Age Factor[#age](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
Note: Computing the age factor requires the installation
and operation of the [Slurm Accounting Database](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html).
The age factor represents the length of time a job has been sitting in the
queue and eligible to run. In general, the longer a job waits in the queue, the
larger its age factor grows. However, the age factor for a dependent job will
not change while it waits for the job it depends on to complete. Also, the age
factor will not change when scheduling is withheld for a job whose node or time
limits exceed the cluster's current limits.
At some configurable length of time ( PriorityMaxAge ), the age factor
will max out to 1.0.

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.
The job's priority is an integer that ranges between 0 and

positioned in the queue, and the sooner the j...

There are nine factors in the Multifactor Job Priority plugin that
influence job priority:
Age

Association
a factor associated with each association
Fair-share
the difference between the portion of the computing resource that has been promised and the amount of resources that has been consumed

the number of nodes or CPUs a job is allocated

QOS

## Job Size Factor[#jobsize](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job size factor correlates to the number of nodes or CPUs the job has
requested. This factor can be configured to favor larger jobs or smaller jobs
based on the state of the PriorityFavorSmall boolean in the slurm.conf
file. When PriorityFavorSmall is NO, the larger the job, the greater
its job size factor will be. A job that requests all the nodes on the machine
will get a job size factor of 1.0. When the PriorityFavorSmall Boolean
is YES, the single node job will receive the 1.0 job size factor.
The PriorityFlags value of SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME alters this
behavior as follows. The job size in CPUs is divided by the time limit in
minutes. The result is divided by the total number of CPUs in the system.

After reviewing the Slurm cluster, good question — scheduling and accounting are tightly linked in Slurm. Below is a concise, actionable overview of the most relevant slurm.conf / slurmdbd / sacctmgr settings and where they interact, plus checks and common pitfalls.

High-level components
- slurmctld (scheduler): governed by slurm.conf and priority plugin settings.
- slurmd (node agents): report usage and enforce cgroups.
- slurmdbd (accounting DB daemon): stores historical usage and is required for fairshare, age, and many accounting-based features.
- sacctmgr / sreport / sshare / sprio: admin tools to inspect and manage accounting, shares, and priorities.

Scheduling configuration (slurm.conf and plugins)
1. Priority plugin
- PriorityType
  - Common value: priority/multifactor — the Multifactor plugin composes priority from age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, site factors, and requested TRES.
- Priority weights (how factors combine)
  - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - The composite job priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + ... (weights are numeric).
- PriorityFlags
  - Toggles behavior (examples: NO_FAIR_TREE to use classic fairshare, SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME, etc.).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife
  - Controls decay of historical usage for fairshare. Example: 7-0 means a 7‑day half-life. 0 disables decay (requires other usage reset policy).
- PriorityCalcPeriod / PriorityUsageResetPeriod / PriorityMaxAge
  - Control recalculation cadence, when usage is reset, and the max age factor value.

2. Fairshare and accounting dependency
- Fairshare requires slurmdbd (AccountingStorage) and properly configured association shares.
- sacctmgr is used to set "Fairshare" (Share) values on accounts/users/associations.
- If you want fairshare-based scheduling, ensure AccountingStorageType points to slurmdbd and slurmdbd is running.

3. QOS and partition factors
- QOS definitions (sacctmgr) can set priorities, limits, preemption behavior, and priority caps.
- Partition factors and per-partition PriorityWeightPartition influence job order by partition.

4. Job size / age / nice / site factors
- PriorityFavorSmall (YES/NO) controls whether small jobs get more priority.
- Age factor grows while a job is eligible to run; PriorityMaxAge caps it.
- Site / job_submit plugins allow custom site_factor or submission-time modifications.

5. Preemption and backfill
- PreemptType / PreemptMode / PreemptExemptTime set how preemption works (requeue, suspend, preempt).
- Backfill: the scheduler supports backfilling; relevant settings live in scheduler plugin parameters (multifactor scheduling uses scheduler logic and backfill capability).

6. TRES-based weighting
- You can weight specific TRES (e.g., GPUs, CPUs) via TRES weights so jobs requesting expensive TRES are evaluated differently.

Accounting configuration (slurmdbd, slurm.conf, job accounting)
1. AccountingStorage
- slurm.conf keys:
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost / Port /User /Loc depending on DB backend
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: controls enforcement level on job submit (values like associations, all, nojobs, nosteps). Use to block submissions that violate associations/limits.
- slurmdbd.conf: DB connection settings, auth, and retention configuration.

2. Job usage collection and completion logging
- JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency: configure how resource usage (RSS, maxrss, CPU) is gathered.
- JobCompType / JobCompLoc (job completion logging plugin) — where completion records are sent if not using slurmdbd.

3. sacctmgr associations, accounts, QOS
- Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, set DefaultQOS, set Share/Fairshare, set limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.).
- Grp* limits are checked when considering starting jobs — these can block allocation if limits would be exceeded.
- DefaultQOS, QOSMaxJobs, QOSMaxSubmitJobs etc. control per-user/ per-account behavior.

4. Reporting and tools
- sshare shows fairshare and effective shares.
- sprio shows priority breakdown per job and the active weights.
- sreport generates accounting usage (CPU/GPU-hours) reports.
- sacct for historical job records; sacct requires accounting data (slurmdbd or jobcomp to storage).

Practical examples (typical lines)
- slurm.conf (examples)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityFavorSmall=YES
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.edu
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
- sacctmgr (examples)
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=clustername Description="Research group"
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100
  - sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultAccount=mygroup

Checks and diagnostics (read-only commands)
- scontrol show config — view current slurm.conf settings (PriorityType, AccountingStorageType, JobAcctGatherType).
- sprio -w — view current priority weights and plugin behavior.
- sshare -l — check fairshare allocation and recent usage.
- sdiag — scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics.
- scontrol ping — check controller responsiveness.
- sacctmgr list associations — inspect accounts, shares, and limits.

Common pitfalls and recommendations
- Fairshare/age requires slurmdbd; without it fairshare/age factors are not computed.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is 0 you must manage usage resets (PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
- Changing slurm.conf requires restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld to take effect; slurmdbd config changes require restart of slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce can block users unintentionally — test changes in a staging environment first.
- Ensure JobAcctGatherType is enabled and frequent enough to capture required metrics (increase frequency for finer accounting).
- When tuning weights, use sprio and sshare to observe results and iterate: small changes to PriorityWeightFairshare can have large effects.

If you want, I can:
- Show the cluster’s current config snippets (scontrol show config) and priority/fairshare state (sprio, sshare) to make concrete recommendations.  
- Or provide a sample minimal slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf snippet for a typical research cluster tuned for fairshare.

The "include" key word can be used with modifiers within the specified
pathname. These modifiers would be replaced with cluster name or other
information depending on which modifier is specified. If the included file
is not an absolute path name (i.e. it does not start with a slash), it will
searched for in the same directory as the slurm.conf file.

EXAMPLE

ClusterName=linux include /home/slurm/etc/%c_config # Above line interpreted as # "include /home/slurm/etc/linux_config"
```

PriorityType

Priority Plugin.
PriorityDecayHalfLife
This determines the contribution of historical usage on the
composite usage value. The larger the number, the longer past usage
affects fair-share. If set to 0 no decay will be applied. This is helpful if
you want to enforce hard time limits per association. If set to 0
PriorityUsageResetPeriod must be set to some interval.
The unit is a time string (i.e. min, hr:min:00, days-hr:min:00, or
days-hr). The default value is 7-0 (7 days).

Note: Computing the age factor requires the installation
and operation of the [Slurm Accounting Database](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html).
The age factor represents the length of time a job has been sitting in the
queue and eligible to run. In general, the longer a job waits in the queue, the
larger its age factor grows. However, the age factor for a dependent job will
not change while it waits for the job it depends on to complete. Also, the age
factor will not change when scheduling is withheld for a job whose node or time
limits exceed the cluster's current limits.

results.prompt: Explain relevant Slurm configuration for scheduling and accounting
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact reference of the Slurm configuration knobs that are most relevant when you design scheduling policy and accounting. I include what each setting does, typical values or choices, and practical notes (what you must enable to get full accounting/fairshare behavior).

High-level picture
- Scheduling (slurmctld / slurm.conf): controls how jobs are prioritized/selected and when/backfill decisions are made (PriorityType, SchedulerType, SchedInterval, select/cons_res).
- Accounting (slurmdbd + slurm.conf + sacctmgr): records job completions and usage to a database, enforces association/QoS/limit policies, and enables reporting/fairshare state.
- Interaction: PriorityType can include fairshare; fairshare state is stored/updated in the accounting DB (SlurmDBD) so accurate fairshare requires accounting enabled.

Key scheduling-related slurm.conf parameters
- PriorityType
  - Defines which priority plugins are used (common plugins: priority/multifactor, priority/basic). Use multifactor to combine age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, etc.
  - Example: PriorityType=priority/multifactor
- Priority weights and tuning (when using multifactor)
  - PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife (controls how historical usage decays for fairshare), and PriorityFlags to tweak behavior (e.g., ignore certain classes).
  - Tuning notes: raise WeightFairshare to favor users with low historical usage; adjust decay half-life to control how quickly past usage becomes irrelevant.
- SchedulerType
  - Controls which scheduler implementation runs (e.g., sched/builtin or sched/backfill). Use sched/backfill to enable backfill behavior.
  - Example: SchedulerType=sched/backfill
- SchedInterval
  - How often the scheduler rebuilds the feasible set and reorders pending jobs (seconds). Shorter interval = more responsive but more CPU used by slurmctld.
- SelectType / SelectTypeParameters
  - Resource selection plugin (select/cons_res is common). SelectTypeParameters sets how allocation is done (e.g., CR_Core, CR_Socket, CR_CPU_Memory); important for correct packing and for TRES accounting.
- Preemption / Backfill / Topology
  - You can enable preemption plugins and backfill tuning via SchedulerType and SchedulerParameters. Preemption behavior is controlled by PreemptType/PreemptMode / associated QOS settings.
- Resource definitions that affect scheduling
  - NodeName / PartitionName: node sizes, CPUs, memory, GRES (GPUs) and partitions determine which jobs are eligible.
  - DefMemPerCPU, OverSubscribe and MaxCPUsPerNode influence packing and per-job resource limits.
- TRES (Trackable RESources)
  - Slurm uses TRES names (cpu, mem, gres/gpu, license, etc.) for limits, accounting and QOS. Define GRES on nodes (e.g., Gres=gpu:4) so GPUs are visible and charged.

Key accounting-related parameters (slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf)
- AccountingStorageType
  - Tells slurmctld how to store accounting. Typical production configuration: AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd and run slurmdbd as middle tier into MySQL/MariaDB.
- AccountingStorageEnforce
  - Comma-separated enforcement options to require valid associations/limits at submission time (examples: associations and limits). Controls whether submissions are rejected or allowed to pend when they violate association/QoS/limit rules.
  - Use carefully: enabling strict enforcement can cause job submissions to be rejected if sacctmgr associations/limits are not configured.
- JobAcctGatherType (and gather plugin)
  - Controls how resource usage for running jobs is gathered (commonly jobacct_gather/linux). The gather plugin supplies per-job CPU, memory, I/O and GPU accounting used for billing/fairshare.
  - JobAcctGatherParams (plugin-specific) tune sampling frequency or enabled metrics.
- JobCompType
  - Where job completion records are sent. Use jobcomp/slurmdbd to write completion records into the accounting DB via slurmdbd.
- slurmdbd.conf (SlurmDBD)
  - DbdHost, StorageType (mysql/mariadb), StorageUser/StoragePass, LogFile, PurgeJobAfter, Archive options.
  - slurmdbd sits between slurmctld and the SQL DB; it is strongly recommended for security and scalability.
- sacctmgr (account/association/QoS setup)
  - To enable limits and enforcement you must create accounts, users, and associations with sacctmgr, and add QOS objects and limits (MaxWall, MaxTRESPerUser, GrpTRES, etc.).
- QOS and limits
  - QOS objects give per-QOS priorities and limits. QOS flags include DenyOnLimit (reject on submit if limits violated), EnforceUsageThreshold, and UsageThreshold.
  - Limits often use TRES names: MaxTRESPerUser, MaxTRESPerAccount, GrpTRES, etc.
- Fairshare / sshare
  - Fairshare state is stored in the accounting DB. Use sshare to view fairshare effective shares and historical usage. PriorityType must include fairshare and slurmdbd/accounting must be enabled for it to work correctly.
- Reporting and tools
  - sacct (historical job accounting), sreport (aggregated usage reports), sshare (fairshare view), sacctmgr (manage accounts/QoS/associations).

Minimal example (typical lines in slurm.conf)
- Scheduler/priority/accounting essentials:
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SchedInterval=30
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - SelectType=select/cons_res
  - SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd

What you must do to enable functional accounting + fairshare
1. Install and configure slurmdbd and a SQL database (MySQL/MariaDB). Configure slurmdbd.conf with StorageType, StorageUser, StoragePass, and DbdHost.
2. Point slurmctld at slurmdbd: set AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd in slurm.conf.
3. Enable job accounting & job completion plugins: JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux and JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd.
4. Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, and associations and to define QOS objects and limits. If you want enforcement, set AccountingStorageEnforce appropriately.
5. Tune PriorityType weights and PriorityDecayHalfLife to shape fairshare behavior; use sshare to inspect fairshare allocations.

Practical tuning tips
- Start with moderate SchedInterval (20–60s) and increase scheduler interval only if slurmctld CPU usage is a problem.
- If backfill is valuable for utilization, enable SchedulerType=sched/backfill and test with realistic job mixes.
- Test AccountingStorageEnforce in “audit” mode first (don’t immediately reject jobs) so you can verify sacctmgr associations and limits are correct.
- Use QOS DenyOnLimit for strict control of runaway submissions; use EnforceUsageThreshold for automatic throttling before hard deny.
- For GPU clusters, ensure nodes declare GRES=gpu:N and that TRES accounting is configured so fairshare and limits count GPU hours.

Where to read more (official docs)
- slurm.conf reference and parameters (PriorityType, AccountingStorageEnforce, JobAcctGatherType, JobCompType, etc.): https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html
- slurmdbd.conf (database/back-end) reference: https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmdbd.conf.html
- QOS and resource limits: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Accounting and reporting: https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html

If you want, I can:
- Inspect your current cluster’s slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf (read-only) and highlight the exact parameters you have set and what they mean; or
- Show the current accounting/fairshare state (ssh-less read) by calling scontrol_show_config, scontrol_ping, sshare, or sdiag and summarize recommended tuning changes.

Which of those would you like me to do next?

trials.agent_response:
Below is a compact reference of the Slurm configuration knobs that are most relevant when you design scheduling policy and accounting. I include what each setting does, typical values or choices, and practical notes (what you must enable to get full accounting/fairshare behavior).

High-level picture
- Scheduling (slurmctld / slurm.conf): controls how jobs are prioritized/selected and when/backfill decisions are made (PriorityType, SchedulerType, SchedInterval, select/cons_res).
- Accounting (slurmdbd + slurm.conf + sacctmgr): records job completions and usage to a database, enforces association/QoS/limit policies, and enables reporting/fairshare state.
- Interaction: PriorityType can include fairshare; fairshare state is stored/updated in the accounting DB (SlurmDBD) so accurate fairshare requires accounting enabled.

Key scheduling-related slurm.conf parameters
- PriorityType
  - Defines which priority plugins are used (common plugins: priority/multifactor, priority/basic). Use multifactor to combine age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, etc.
  - Example: PriorityType=priority/multifactor
- Priority weights and tuning (when using multifactor)
  - PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife (controls how historical usage decays for fairshare), and PriorityFlags to tweak behavior (e.g., ignore certain classes).
  - Tuning notes: raise WeightFairshare to favor users with low historical usage; adjust decay half-life to control how quickly past usage becomes irrelevant.
- SchedulerType
  - Controls which scheduler implementation runs (e.g., sched/builtin or sched/backfill). Use sched/backfill to enable backfill behavior.
  - Example: SchedulerType=sched/backfill
- SchedInterval
  - How often the scheduler rebuilds the feasible set and reorders pending jobs (seconds). Shorter interval = more responsive but more CPU used by slurmctld.
- SelectType / SelectTypeParameters
  - Resource selection plugin (select/cons_res is common). SelectTypeParameters sets how allocation is done (e.g., CR_Core, CR_Socket, CR_CPU_Memory); important for correct packing and for TRES accounting.
- Preemption / Backfill / Topology
  - You can enable preemption plugins and backfill tuning via SchedulerType and SchedulerParameters. Preemption behavior is controlled by PreemptType/PreemptMode / associated QOS settings.
- Resource definitions that affect scheduling
  - NodeName / PartitionName: node sizes, CPUs, memory, GRES (GPUs) and partitions determine which jobs are eligible.
  - DefMemPerCPU, OverSubscribe and MaxCPUsPerNode influence packing and per-job resource limits.
- TRES (Trackable RESources)
  - Slurm uses TRES names (cpu, mem, gres/gpu, license, etc.) for limits, accounting and QOS. Define GRES on nodes (e.g., Gres=gpu:4) so GPUs are visible and charged.

Key accounting-related parameters (slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf)
- AccountingStorageType
  - Tells slurmctld how to store accounting. Typical production configuration: AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd and run slurmdbd as middle tier into MySQL/MariaDB.
- AccountingStorageEnforce
  - Comma-separated enforcement options to require valid associations/limits at submission time (examples: associations and limits). Controls whether submissions are rejected or allowed to pend when they violate association/QoS/limit rules.
  - Use carefully: enabling strict enforcement can cause job submissions to be rejected if sacctmgr associations/limits are not configured.
- JobAcctGatherType (and gather plugin)
  - Controls how resource usage for running jobs is gathered (commonly jobacct_gather/linux). The gather plugin supplies per-job CPU, memory, I/O and GPU accounting used for billing/fairshare.
  - JobAcctGatherParams (plugin-specific) tune sampling frequency or enabled metrics.
- JobCompType
  - Where job completion records are sent. Use jobcomp/slurmdbd to write completion records into the accounting DB via slurmdbd.
- slurmdbd.conf (SlurmDBD)
  - DbdHost, StorageType (mysql/mariadb), StorageUser/StoragePass, LogFile, PurgeJobAfter, Archive options.
  - slurmdbd sits between slurmctld and the SQL DB; it is strongly recommended for security and scalability.
- sacctmgr (account/association/QoS setup)
  - To enable limits and enforcement you must create accounts, users, and associations with sacctmgr, and add QOS objects and limits (MaxWall, MaxTRESPerUser, GrpTRES, etc.).
- QOS and limits
  - QOS objects give per-QOS priorities and limits. QOS flags include DenyOnLimit (reject on submit if limits violated), EnforceUsageThreshold, and UsageThreshold.
  - Limits often use TRES names: MaxTRESPerUser, MaxTRESPerAccount, GrpTRES, etc.
- Fairshare / sshare
  - Fairshare state is stored in the accounting DB. Use sshare to view fairshare effective shares and historical usage. PriorityType must include fairshare and slurmdbd/accounting must be enabled for it to work correctly.
- Reporting and tools
  - sacct (historical job accounting), sreport (aggregated usage reports), sshare (fairshare view), sacctmgr (manage accounts/QoS/associations).

Minimal example (typical lines in slurm.conf)
- Scheduler/priority/accounting essentials:
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SchedInterval=30
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - SelectType=select/cons_res
  - SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd

What you must do to enable functional accounting + fairshare
1. Install and configure slurmdbd and a SQL database (MySQL/MariaDB). Configure slurmdbd.conf with StorageType, StorageUser, StoragePass, and DbdHost.
2. Point slurmctld at slurmdbd: set AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd in slurm.conf.
3. Enable job accounting & job completion plugins: JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux and JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd.
4. Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, and associations and to define QOS objects and limits. If you want enforcement, set AccountingStorageEnforce appropriately.
5. Tune PriorityType weights and PriorityDecayHalfLife to shape fairshare behavior; use sshare to inspect fairshare allocations.

Practical tuning tips
- Start with moderate SchedInterval (20–60s) and increase scheduler interval only if slurmctld CPU usage is a problem.
- If backfill is valuable for utilization, enable SchedulerType=sched/backfill and test with realistic job mixes.
- Test AccountingStorageEnforce in “audit” mode first (don’t immediately reject jobs) so you can verify sacctmgr associations and limits are correct.
- Use QOS DenyOnLimit for strict control of runaway submissions; use EnforceUsageThreshold for automatic throttling before hard deny.
- For GPU clusters, ensure nodes declare GRES=gpu:N and that TRES accounting is configured so fairshare and limits count GPU hours.

Where to read more (official docs)
- slurm.conf reference and parameters (PriorityType, AccountingStorageEnforce, JobAcctGatherType, JobCompType, etc.): https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html
- slurmdbd.conf (database/back-end) reference: https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmdbd.conf.html
- QOS and resource limits: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Accounting and reporting: https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html

nodes which can be used to simplify the partition configuration section,

configured feature. If both Feature= and Nodes= are used the

## RELOCATING CONTROLLERS[#SECTION_RELOCATING-CONTROLLERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
If the cluster's computers used for the primary or backup controller
will be out of service for an extended period of time, it may be
desirable to relocate them.
In order to do so, follow this procedure:
1. Stop the Slurm daemons on the old controller and nodes.
2. Modify the slurm.conf file appropriately.
3. Copy the files from the StateSaveLocation to the new controller or ensure
that they are accessible to the new controller via a shared drive.
4. Distribute the updated slurm.conf file to all nodes.
5. Restart the Slurm daemons on the new controller and nodes.
There should be no loss of any pending jobs. Any running jobs will get the
updated host info and finish normally.
Ensure that any nodes added to the cluster have the current
slurm.conf file installed.
